Matrix Haar measure has \(\operatorname{vol}_G(K)=1\); central multiplicative Haar measure has \(\operatorname{vol}_Z(\mathcal O^\times)=1\). We first construct the compatible measure on the quotient.

Lemma 1.23h. There is a positive bi-invariant Haar measure on \(Q\), uniquely normalized by \(\operatorname{vol}_Q(\bar K)=1\). It satisfies the exact fiber formula

\[ \int_G f(g)\,dg =\int_Q\int_Z f(zg)\,dz\,d\bar g \qquad(f\in C_c^\infty(G)). \tag{1.39a} \]

Proof. The quotient map is open: the inverse image of the image of an open set \(A\subset G\) is \(ZA\), a union of open translates. The scalar centre is closed, since its matrix entries satisfy the closed conditions that every off-diagonal entry is zero and all diagonal entries agree. If \(xZ\ne yZ\), continuity of multiplication gives an identity neighbourhood \(W\) with \(W^{-1}x^{-1}yW\cap Z=\varnothing\). The images of \(xW\) and \(yW\) in the quotient are disjoint open neighbourhoods: an intersection would give \(w_1^{-1}x^{-1}yw_2\in Z\). Thus \(Q\) is Hausdorff. On the open locus with a specified matrix entry nonzero, dividing by that entry supplies a continuous local section with that entry equal to \(1\). These charts identify open sets with open subsets of affine matrix hyperplanes, so \(Q\) is locally compact and has a compact-open basis. It is a group because \(Z\) is central. The images \(\bar J_r\) of \(J_r=1+\varpi^rM_n(\mathcal O)\) form a basis of compact open identity subgroups and are contained in \(\bar K\).

Define the mass of every left coset \(x\bar J_r\) to be

\[ [\bar K:\bar J_r]^{-1}. \tag{1.39b} \]

The finite index is well defined because \(\bar J_r\) is open in the compact group \(\bar K\). Refinement to a smaller subgroup partitions each coset into exactly its subgroup index many equal pieces; multiplication of finite indices proves consistency of these masses. Every compactly supported locally constant function on \(Q\) is a finite linear combination of indicators of cosets of one sufficiently small \(\bar J_r\): take a common right-invariance subgroup by compactness, then partition its compact support into finitely many such open cosets. Thus (1.39b) defines a positive left-invariant integral with \(\bar K\)-mass one. It is the unique such integral, since left invariance and the same coset partitions determine every compact-open test.

For \(g\in G\), the intersection of \(\bar K\) and \(\bar g\bar K\bar g^{-1}\) is exactly the image of \(K\cap gKg^{-1}\). Indeed if \(k=zghg^{-1}\), \(k,h\in K\), then determinant valuation gives \(n\,v(z)=0\), so \(v(z)=0\) and \(z\in\mathcal O^\times I_n\). Such a scalar belongs to both compact groups and can be absorbed into \(h\). Also \(Z\cap K=\mathcal O^\times I_n\) is contained in that intersection. Hence the two quotient indices equal the corresponding ordinary indices:

\[ [\bar K:\bar K\cap\bar g\bar K\bar g^{-1}] =[K:K\cap gKg^{-1}], \quad [\bar g\bar K\bar g^{-1}:\bar K\cap\bar g\bar K\bar g^{-1}] =[gKg^{-1}:K\cap gKg^{-1}]. \tag{1.39c} \]

Bi-invariance of \(G\)'s matrix measure makes the two ordinary compact groups have the same volume \(1\), so these indices agree. Therefore conjugation preserves the normalized quotient measure: the ratio of the masses of \(\bar K\) and its conjugate is the ratio of these two indices. Conjugation followed by left translation gives right translation, proving bi-invariance. The valuation equation here is an equation of integers; it is valid also when the field characteristic divides \(n\).

For \(f\in C_c^\infty(G)\), its central-fiber integral \(qf(\bar g)=\int_Z f(zg)\,dz\) is well defined, compactly supported, and locally constant. Right invariance by a common compact open subgroup of \(f\) gives this last assertion on its quotient image. The functional \(F(f)=\int_Qqf\,d\bar g\) is positive and left \(G\)-invariant. Left invariance fixes its value on each translate of a compact-open subgroup. Partitioning \(K\) into cosets of a sufficiently small common subgroup and then partitioning arbitrary test supports proves that any such functional is a scalar multiple of matrix Haar integration. Here \(q1_K=1_{\bar K}\): the relevant central fiber is a translate of \(\mathcal O^\times I_n\), whose Haar mass is exactly \(1\). Thus \(F(1_K)=1=\operatorname{vol}_G(K)\). The scalar is \(1\), proving (1.39a). \(\square\)

Use this quotient measure in the coefficient and convolution integrals below. In Lemma 1.23r, \(c_\rho>0\) is the constant defined by the Schur-orthogonality integral and \(d_\rho=c_\rho^{-1}\). The identities \(f_{vw}*f_{v'w'}=H(v',w)f_{vw'}\), \(\rho(f_{vw})u=H(u,w)v\), and \(e=f_{ww}\) for \(H(w,w)=1\) consequently contain every normalization constant. Rescaling the quotient Haar measure rescales \(c_\rho\) and \(d_\rho\) inversely, leaving these identities unchanged.

Write \(q\) for the residue cardinality, \(\varpi\) for a uniformizer, and \(\nu(g)=|\det g|\). Let \(P\) be the upper parabolic of block sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_t\), and let \(I_P\) denote its normalized induction with covariance \(f(umg)=\delta_P(m)^{1/2}\rho(m)f(g)\) and right translation. A representation with unitary scalar centre is coefficient-tempered when every smooth coefficient lies in \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) modulo that centre for every \(\epsilon>0\). Its real norm twist is essentially coefficient-tempered. The exact modulus is \[ \delta_P(\operatorname{diag}(m_1,\ldots,m_t)) =\prod_{i<j}|\det m_i|^{n_j}|\det m_j|^{-n_i}. \tag{1.39d} \]

Compact support, duality and actual cuspidal quotients

Lemma 1.23i. If a smooth admissible representation \(V\) has every smooth coefficient compactly supported modulo \(Z_n\), then \(V_{U_i}=0\) for every standard proper two-block upper radical \(U_i\). Consequently the condition of zero proper Jacquet modules is preserved by ordinary smooth contragredience of irreducible admissible representations.

Proof. Fix \(i<n\), \(r\geq1\), \(J=J_r\), \(E=V^J\), and

\[ a=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi I_i,I_{n-i}),\qquad T=e_J\pi(a)e_J|_E. \tag{1.39e} \]

Choose bases of \(E\) and its dual. Extending a dual basis functional by composition with \(e_J\) gives an actual \(J\)-fixed smooth dual vector. All finitely many resulting coefficients vanish at \(a^b\) for every sufficiently large \(b\): its two elementary-divisor levels have gap \(b\), bounded on any compact subset of \(Z_n\backslash G_n\). A single \(N\) works for all these coefficients. Thus

\[ e_J\pi(a^b)e_J|_E=0,\qquad T^b=0\quad(b\geq N), \tag{1.39f} \]

the second equality being the proved probability semigroup identity.

Let \(p:V\to V_{U_i}\) be the ordinary quotient. Block elimination in each finite congruence quotient gives the probability-average identity

\[ e_J=e_{J\cap U_i}e_{J\cap M_i}e_{J\cap U_i^-}. \tag{1.39g} \]

Conjugating by \(a^{-b}\) expands upper entries to \(\varpi^{r-b}\mathcal O\), fixes the block diagonal group, and contracts lower entries to \(\varpi^{r+b}\mathcal O\). For \(v\in E\), the diagonal and contracted lower averages fix \(v\); the expanded upper average has the same Jacquet class as \(v\). Therefore

\[ p(e_J\pi(a^b)v)=a^b p(v)\quad(b\geq0), \tag{1.39h} \]

where \(a\) on the right is its invertible ordinary Levi action on the quotient. Equations (1.39f)–(1.39h) imply \(p(v)=0\). Every smooth vector is fixed by some \(J_r\), so \(p(V)=0\).

Now let \(V\) be irreducible admissible and Jacquet-zero. Lemma 1.20a gives compact-mod-center coefficient support. Smooth biduality identifies every coefficient of \(V^\vee\) with a coefficient of \(V\) composed with inversion. Inversion preserves compactness modulo the center. The assertion just proved gives zero proper two-block Jacquet modules for \(V^\vee\); further coinvariants and flag conjugation give every proper parabolic. In rank one the condition is vacuous. This proof uses neither Jacquet duality, second adjointness nor transpose-inverse identification. \(\square\)

Exact ordinary smooth duality

Lemma 1.23j. Ordinary smooth duality is exact on admissible smooth representations; it preserves admissibility and irreducibility, and evaluation is smooth biduality.

Proof. Restriction identifies \((V^\vee)^J\) with \((V^J)^*\), with inverse \(a\mapsto a\circ e_J\); these spaces are finite-dimensional. Given \(W\hookrightarrow V\), extend a \(J\)-fixed functional from \(W^J\) to \(V^J\), then compose with \(e_J\). Its restriction to \(W\) is the original functional. Restriction of smooth duals is therefore onto. The remaining exactness assertions follow from composition with a quotient and annihilators. Compact averaging lifts fixed vectors through a surjection, so submodules and quotients of admissible modules are admissible.

Evaluation \(V\to(V^\vee)^\vee\) is an isomorphism on every fixed space by finite-dimensional biduality, hence on their union. If \(V\) is irreducible and \(0\ne W\subset V^\vee\) is invariant, its annihilator in \(V\) is proper and invariant, hence zero. Detection of a \(J\)-fixed vector by \(W\) remains detection by its \(J\)-average. Thus \(W^J\) has zero annihilator in \(V^J\), so finite dimension gives \(W^J=(V^\vee)^J\). Taking the union proves \(W=V^\vee\). \(\square\)

Theorem 1.23k (actual unordered cuspidal quotient). Every irreducible smooth admissible \(\pi\) of \(G_n\) is an actual quotient

\[ \rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_t :=I_P(\rho_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\rho_t) \twoheadrightarrow\pi, \qquad n_1+\cdots+n_t=n, \tag{1.39i} \]

where each \(\rho_j\) is an irreducible admissible representation of \(G_{n_j}\) having zero every proper Jacquet module.

Proof. Apply Theorem 1.23e to the irreducible admissible \(\pi^\vee\), obtaining an embedding into \(I_P(\sigma_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\sigma_t)\) with Jacquet-zero factors. Lemma 1.23j and Lemma 1.23a give an onto map

\[ I_P(\sigma_1^\vee\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\sigma_t^\vee) \twoheadrightarrow(\pi^\vee)^\vee=\pi. \]

The factors are irreducible admissible by Lemma 1.23j and Jacquet-zero by Lemma 1.23i. This is (1.39i). The same upper \(P\) and same block order are used in normalized induction duality. No reflected permutation or inverse intertwiner is inserted. Transitivity was proved in (1.27v)–(1.27w). Finite length is unnecessary. \(\square\)

Real normalization and compatible unitary cuspidal blocks

Lemma 1.23l. An irreducible admissible Jacquet-zero \(\rho\) of \(G_d\) has a unique real number

\[ e(\rho)=-\frac{\log|\omega_\rho(\varpi)|}{d\log q} \tag{1.39j} \]

such that \(\tau=\rho\nu^{-e(\rho)}\) has unitary central character. The representation \(\tau\) has a compatible irreducible unitary Hilbert realization; every smooth coefficient is compactly supported modulo the center and lies in every \(L^p(Z_d\backslash G_d)\), \(0<p<\infty\). In particular it is square-integrable and coefficient-tempered.

Proof. A commuting endomorphism is scalar: restrict to a nonzero finite-dimensional fixed space, choose an eigenvalue, and use the invariant nonzero kernel of its difference from that scalar. Central elements therefore act by a smooth character \(\omega_\rho\). On \(\mathcal O^\times\) this character has finite image because an open central subgroup fixes a nonzero vector and is in its kernel. That image has modulus one. Since \(\nu(\varpi I_d)=q^{-d}\), the modulus of the central character of \(\rho\nu^{-e}\) at \(\varpi\) is \(|\omega_\rho(\varpi)|q^{de}\). It is one exactly for (1.39j). Units and the powers of \(\varpi\) exhaust the center. This proves existence and uniqueness, including the negative sign and division by \(d\). The real determinant twist preserves Jacquet vanishing and coefficient supports.

For \(d>1\), Lemma 1.20a gives compact coefficient support modulo the center. For \(d=1\), the quotient by the center is one point. With unitary central character, the absolute value of a coefficient is well defined on that quotient and bounded on its compact support. It lies in every stated \(L^p\).

Fix \(0\ne\ell\in\tau^\vee\) and define

\[ (v,w)_\ell= \int_{Z_d\backslash G_d} \ell(\tau(g)v)\overline{\ell(\tau(g)w)}\,d\bar g. \tag{1.39k} \]

The integrand is representative-independent and compactly supported. The quotient measure is right invariant: the matrix Haar density \(|\det g|^{-d}d^{d^2}g\) is bi-invariant, and right translation commutes with integration first over the central fibers. Thus this form is invariant. Its kernel is the invariant kernel of the coefficient map for \(\ell\); it is proper since \(\ell\ne0\), and hence zero by irreducibility.

The Hilbert completion \(H\) carries a strongly continuous unitary action: the dense smooth subspace has open stabilizers, and the unitary norm extends continuity to \(H\). Compact probability averaging is an orthogonal projection, and

\[ H^J=\overline{\tau^J}=\tau^J \tag{1.39l} \]

by admissibility. Every smooth vector of \(H\) therefore belongs to \(\tau\). The orthogonal projection onto a closed invariant subspace would commute with the action and preserve these fixed spaces. On the irreducible smooth \(\tau\) it is scalar and idempotent, hence zero or identity; density gives the same on \(H\). The completion is irreducible. A \(J\)-fixed smooth dual vector is represented by a vector in the finite-dimensional Hermitian space \(\tau^J\), and composing with the orthogonal projection \(e_J\) represents it on the entire \(\tau\). This proves compatibility. \(\square\)

Theorem 1.23k and Lemma 1.23l give, for every irreducible admissible \(\pi\), an actual quotient

\[ I_P((\tau_1\nu^{e_1})\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes (\tau_t\nu^{e_t}))\twoheadrightarrow\pi, \tag{1.39m} \]

with actual unitary square-integrable Jacquet-zero \(\tau_j\). The exponents have no proved ordering. Each supplied block's exponent is fixed by (1.39j); the entire list for \(\pi\) has no proved uniqueness here.

A compact section generates the full induction

Lemma 1.23m. If \(\rho=\rho_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\rho_t\) is the outer tensor product of irreducible admissible blocks, \(I_P(\rho)\) is finitely generated. One compact big-cell section generates it.

Proof. The tensor theorem used in Lemma 1.23d makes \(\rho\) irreducible and smooth under \(M\), so a nonzero \(v\) generates it. The block centers act by scalars.

Let \(N^-\) be the opposite lower block radical. Block elimination at the invertible successive trailing principal block pivots gives a unique factorization and continuous inverse for \(P\times N^-\to PN^-\). Its open image in \(P\backslash G_n\) is a chart identified with \(N^-\). Compactly supported locally constant functions \(N^-\to V_\rho\) give induced sections by the covariance law and extension by zero. Their common right stabilizer follows from a finite cover of the compact chart support on which that law and the open stabilizers of the finitely many vector values are fixed. The support is compact and open in the flag space, hence closed there too, so the zero extension is smooth.

Choose a compact open subgroup \(H\subset N^-\), with all lower block entries in a sufficiently small common power of \(\varpi\). Let \(F_v\) restrict to \(1_Hv\). Put

\[ a=\operatorname{diag}(I_{n_1},\varpi I_{n_2},\ldots, \varpi^{t-1}I_{n_t})\in Z(M). \tag{1.39n} \]

Conjugation by \(a\) contracts its \((i,j)\) lower block, \(i>j\), by \(\varpi^{i-j}\). Thus \(a^hHa^{-h}\), \(h\geq0\), is cofinal among identity neighborhoods of \(N^-\). With \(\rho(a)=\lambda\,\mathrm{id}\), \(\lambda\ne0\), (1.39d) gives

\[ \delta_P(a)=q^{\sum_{i<j}(j-i)n_i n_j},\qquad \kappa=\delta_P(a)^{1/2}\lambda\ne0. \tag{1.39o} \]

The section law at \(u a^h=a^h(a^{-h}ua^h)\) gives

\[ (\pi(a^h)F_v)(u)= \kappa^h1_{a^hHa^{-h}}(u)v. \tag{1.39p} \]

Right translation by \(m\in M\) multiplies the value by \(\delta_P(m)^{1/2}\rho(m)\) and conjugates the support by \(m\). As \(a\) commutes with \(m\), the span of \(F_v\) contains, after multiplication by a nonzero scalar, the function with value \(\rho(m)v\) and support \(m a^hHa^{-h}m^{-1}\), for every \(m,h\).

For any compact open subgroup \(L\subset N^-\), choose \(h\) with this support subgroup \(H'\subset L\). A finite right-coset partition of \(L\) by \(H'\), followed by right translation inside \(N^-\) and summation, gives \(1_L\rho(m)v\). Finite sums of \(\rho(m)v\) span \(V_\rho\), so the span contains \(1_Lw\) for every \(w\). Further right translations give \(1_{Lx}w\). Every compactly supported locally constant vector-valued function is a finite sum of these: it has finitely many values and one small common left-invariance subgroup on its compact support. We have generated every section supported compactly in this chart.

Translated charts cover the flag space, which is compact by the proved Iwasawa decomposition. Images of sufficiently small compact-open matrix neighborhoods give a compact-open basis of that space. Refine a finite chart cover to a finite disjoint compact-open partition, each piece lying compactly inside a chart. Any section is the sum of its restrictions to these pieces, extended by zero. Each is a translate of a section already generated, so \(F_v\) generates the entire induction. For \(t=1\), induction is \(\rho\), and its cyclicity proves the claim. \(\square\)

The compact picture alone would not prove finite generation: smooth sections have arbitrarily deep right levels. The contraction and coset partition explicitly generate those levels.

Finite heads and precise compact-corner tests

Lemma 1.23n. A nonzero finitely generated smooth admissible representation \(V\) has a finite semisimple maximal quotient. Choose a compact open \(J\) fixing a finite set of generators and \(E=V^J\). Then

\[ \operatorname{hd}(V)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^s Q_i^{m_i},\qquad \sum_i m_i\dim Q_i^J\leq\dim E,\qquad m_i=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,Q_i), \tag{1.39q} \]

where \(Q_i\) are distinct irreducible admissible quotients. Every map to a finite semisimple representation factors through this quotient. At least one \(Q_i\) exists. No finite-length assertion about \(V\) is made.

Proof. Set \(\mathcal H=C_c^\infty(G)\), \(e=e_J\) and \(A=e\mathcal He\). A group translate of a \(J\)-fixed vector is its Hecke translate by the normalized characteristic function of \(gJ\). Hence \(V=\mathcal HE\), and every quotient is generated by the image of \(E\). Averaging lifts fixed vectors, so any nonzero quotient has nonzero \(e\)-corner. Zorn's argument using finite generators produces a maximal proper submodule. Its irreducible quotient is admissible.

For an irreducible quotient \(Q\), \(eQ\) is a nonzero simple \(A\)-module: a nonzero \(A\)-submodule \(W\) generates \(Q\) under \(\mathcal H\), and applying \(e\) gives \(eQ=e\mathcal HeW=W\). This simple corner is a quotient of the finite-dimensional \(A\)-module \(E\). Decreasing dimension constructs a finite composition series of \(E\). Under a map from \(E\) onto any simple corner, the first term of this series with nonzero image gives an isomorphism from its simple successive quotient to that corner. Thus only finitely many simple quotient types occur.

A simple \(\mathcal H\)-module with nonzero \(e\)-corner is determined by that corner. For a simple \(A\)-module \(M\), form \(\mathcal He\otimes_A M\). Its corner is \(M\), which generates the module. Every proper submodule has zero corner, since a nonzero corner would equal \(M\) and generate the entire module. The sum of all proper submodules still has zero corner and is proper. It is the unique maximal submodule, and every simple module with that corner is a quotient by it. Thus only finitely many simple quotient types \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_s\) of \(V\) occur.

Restriction injects

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal H}(V,Q_i) \hookrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_A(E,eQ_i), \tag{1.39r} \]

as \(E\) generates \(V\). The target is finite-dimensional. Choose a basis of each space on the left and take the product of all these finitely many maps. Its image \(D\) is a submodule of the finite direct sum \(\bigoplus_iQ_i^{m_i}\).

A finite direct sum of simple modules and every submodule thereof are semisimple. One proof takes a simple submodule \(S\) of a nonzero submodule, obtainable by the finite-length descending argument inside that finite sum, and projects \(S\) to an ambient simple summand where it is nonzero. This gives a retraction onto \(S\); splitting it and iterating proves the statement. Thus \(D\) is finite semisimple. The product's kernel is the intersection of the kernels of every map to a simple quotient, by the chosen bases and finite list of types. Every map to a finite semisimple representation factors through \(D\).

Each \(Q_i\) has scalar endomorphisms by the compact-fixed eigenvalue argument. Consequently its multiplicity in \(D\) is \(\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(D,Q_i)=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,Q_i)\). Averaging \(V\twoheadrightarrow D\) makes \(eD\) a quotient of \(E\). Its dimension gives (1.39q). This identifies \(D=\operatorname{hd}(V)\). \(\square\)

Lemmas 1.23a and Lemma 1.23m let Lemma 1.23n apply to every induction in (1.39m): it has a nonzero finite semisimple head and \(\pi\) is one of its actual head constituents.

Corollary 1.23o (unique-head test). If \(V=\mathcal HeV\) is admissible and \(eV\) is simple over \(e\mathcal He\), then \(V\) has a unique maximal proper submodule and one irreducible quotient, with multiplicity one in the head.

Proof. A proper submodule \(W\) has \(eW=0\): otherwise its corner is all of \(eV\), forcing \(W=V\). The sum of all proper submodules has zero corner and is proper; it is the unique maximal submodule. Its quotient is simple. \(\square\)

Corollary 1.23p (finite-length test). If an admissible \(V\) has a compact open \(J\) such that every nonzero subquotient has nonzero \(J\)-fixed vectors, then \(V\) has finite length at most \(\dim V^J\).

Proof. Fixed vectors are exact by averaging. For every strict inclusion \(W\subsetneq W'\), the nonzero \((W'/W)^J\) gives \(\dim W'^J>\dim W^J\). An ascending or descending chain can therefore have at most \(\dim V^J\) strict steps. This ensures existence of a maximal proper submodule and termination of recursive maximal-submodule descent in a composition series of the claimed length. \(\square\)

Finite generation detects every nonzero quotient at the generating corner. The common-level test additionally requires that corner to detect every subquotient. Theorem 1.23v below establishes finite length by a finite family of Jacquet functors.

Rank-one data and the obstruction to arbitrary exchange

An irreducible smooth admissible \(G_1\)-representation is a character: a nonzero compact-fixed space is invariant under the abelian group, hence the entire finite-dimensional representation; commuting complex matrices have an eigenline, which is the whole irreducible space. Formula (1.39j) uniquely writes it as \(\chi_0|\cdot|^e\), with \(\chi_0\) unitary. Induction is then the representation itself. The classification, unique quotient and parameter uniqueness are completely proved in rank one.

The same one-block assertion holds for any Jacquet-zero irreducible \(\pi\). In fact it cannot be a quotient of a proper induction \(I_P(\rho)\) from an admissible module: such a quotient would dualize by Lemma 1.23j and Lemma 1.23a to a nonzero embedding \(\pi^\vee\hookrightarrow I_P(\rho^\vee)\). Normalized reciprocity would then give a nonzero map from the Jacquet module of \(\pi^\vee\), which is zero by Lemma 1.23i. This is impossible. Hence any ordered quotient datum for \(\pi\) must have the sole block \(\pi\), whose unique real normalization is Lemma 1.23l. This proves the full one-block classification assertion without an unproved exclusion of cuspidal subquotients from every proper induction.

Arbitrary exchange of inducing blocks already fails to give isomorphic modules in rank two. Put

\[ I_-=I_B(|\cdot|^{-1/2}\boxtimes|\cdot|^{1/2}),\qquad I_+=I_B(|\cdot|^{1/2}\boxtimes|\cdot|^{-1/2}). \tag{1.39s} \]

Here \(\delta_B^{1/2}(\operatorname{diag}(a,d))=|a/d|^{1/2}\). Thus \(I_-\) has trivial left covariance and contains the constant section \(\mathbf1\). The actually proved normalized reciprocity gives

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{G_2}(\mathbf1,I_+) =\operatorname{Hom}_{k^\times\times k^\times} (|\cdot|^{-1/2}\boxtimes|\cdot|^{1/2}, |\cdot|^{1/2}\boxtimes|\cdot|^{-1/2})=0. \tag{1.39t} \]

The characters are different because \(q>1\), so \(I_-\not\simeq I_+\). Smooth duality gives an actual \(I_+\twoheadrightarrow\mathbf1\), whereas \(\operatorname{Hom}_{G_2}(I_-,\mathbf1)=0\) by dualizing (1.39t). This uses no rank-two constituent classification. Thus an unproved blanket invariance of induction under adjacent exchanges cannot order (1.39m).

Coefficient idempotents and finite-length induction

Use the normalized quotient measure of Lemma 1.23h and the compact-coefficient unitary construction of Lemma 1.23l. The two-parabolic orbit calculation in Lemma 2.3p, equations (2.9cc)–(2.9ch), supplies its section filtration, additive-fibre kernel and exact density without a finite-length premise.

Lemma 1.23q (relative central-character convolution). Fix a smooth unitary character \(\omega:Z_n\to\mathbb C^\times\). Let \(\mathcal H_\omega(G_n)\) be the locally constant functions \(f:G_n\to\mathbb C\) compactly supported modulo \(Z_n\) with \(f(zg)=\omega(z)^{-1}f(g)\). They have convolution

\[ (f*h)(g)=\int_{Z_n\backslash G_n} f(x)h(x^{-1}g)\,d\bar x. \tag{1.39u} \]

On any smooth module \(V\) whose center acts by \(\omega\), they act by

\[ \pi_V(f)v=\int_{Z_n\backslash G_n}f(g)\pi_V(g)v\,d\bar g. \tag{1.39v} \]

These are well-defined associative operations, with actual finite vector-valued integrals.

Proof. Replacing \(x\) by \(zx\) in (1.39u) multiplies the first factor by \(\omega(z)^{-1}\) and the second by \(\omega(z)\), so their product is independent of the representative. The same cancellation holds in (1.39v). Local sections of the quotient exist explicitly: on the open set where the \((i,j)\)-entry is nonzero, choose the representative whose entry is \(1\), by dividing every matrix entry by that entry. These sections identify open subsets of \(Z_n\backslash G_n\) with open subsets of an affine matrix hyperplane. Thus the quotient is an \(l\)-space, and the displayed integrands are locally constant there. Their compact supports have finite compact-open partitions. The vector integrand in (1.39v) consequently takes finitely many vector values and its integral is a finite linear combination of those values.

The quotient group is unimodular: left and right translation commute with integration over central fibers of the bi-invariant matrix Haar measure. Products of compact quotient supports are compact. Finite partitions of such supports prove Fubini and the substitution rules directly, so the usual convolution calculation proves associativity and \(\pi_V(f*h)=\pi_V(f)\pi_V(h)\). Smaller common compact-open stabilizers of the functions and vectors justify every local-constancy refinement used in these calculations. No integration over the noncompact center itself is present. \(\square\)

Lemma 1.23r (Schur orthogonality with its proof). Let \(\rho\) be an irreducible admissible Jacquet-zero representation with unitary central character \(\omega\), and let \(H\) be its invariant Hermitian form from Lemma 1.23l, linear in the first variable. For a positive real constant \(c_\rho\), all smooth \(v,w,u,z\) satisfy

\[ \int_{Z_n\backslash G_n} H(v,\rho(g)w)H(\rho(g)u,z)\,d\bar g =c_\rho H(v,z)H(u,w). \tag{1.39w} \]

Proof. Each coefficient is compactly supported modulo the center, and the integrand has central weight \(\omega^{-1}\omega=1\), so the integral is finite. For fixed \(w,u\), call the resulting sesquilinear form in \(v,z\) \(B_{w,u}(v,z)\). Left Haar invariance makes it invariant under simultaneous translation of \(v,z\).

This invariant form is represented by an actual smooth commuting endomorphism, not an assumed bounded Hilbert operator. If \(v\) is \(J\)-fixed, invariance gives \(B_{w,u}(v,z)=B_{w,u}(v,e_Jz)\). The finite-dimensional Hermitian space \(\rho^J\) has a unique vector \(Tv\) representing this functional. Its value on every smooth \(z\) then represents the original form, and different choices of \(J\) give the same vector by nondegeneracy. The resulting linear map \(T\) commutes with \(G_n\). The admissible smooth Schur argument in Lemma 1.23l shows that it is scalar, say \(B_{w,u}(v,z)=C(w,u)H(v,z)\).

Right translation in the integral makes \(C(w,u)\) invariant under simultaneous translation of \(w,u\). It is linear in \(u\) and conjugate-linear in \(w\). The same compact-fixed representation argument gives \(C(w,u)=c_\rho H(u,w)\). Taking \(v=w=u=z\ne0\) makes the integral the squared absolute value of a coefficient, which is positive on a neighborhood of the identity and finite. Hence \(c_\rho>0\). This proves (1.39w) entirely within the actual smooth representation. \(\square\)

Put \(d_\rho=c_\rho^{-1}\), and define the relative coefficient kernels

\[ f_{vw}(g)=d_\rho H(v,\rho(g)w). \tag{1.39x} \]

They belong to \(\mathcal H_\omega(G_n)\); the inverse central weight follows from conjugate-linearity of \(H\)'s second variable. Equations (1.39u) and (1.39w) give exactly

\[ f_{vw}*f_{v'w'}=H(v',w)f_{vw'},\qquad \rho(f_{vw})u=H(u,w)v. \tag{1.39y} \]

For the first equality, use \(H(v',\rho(x^{-1}g)w')=H(\rho(x)v',\rho(g)w')\) inside the integral; (1.39w) then gives the scalar \(H(v',w)\). For the second, pair the vector integral with every smooth \(z\) and use (1.39w). All constants and conjugations are fixed by these substitutions.

The span of the \(f_{vw}\) is a two-sided coefficient ideal. For \(h\in\mathcal H_\omega(G_n)\),

\[ h*f_{vw}=f_{\rho(h)v,w},\qquad f_{vw}*h=f_{v,\rho(h^*)w},\qquad h^*(g)=\overline{h(g^{-1})}. \tag{1.39z} \]

These identities follow from (1.39u) by left translation and the substitution \(x=gy^{-1}\), respectively; the latter conjugation is necessary because \(w\mapsto f_{vw}\) is conjugate-linear. The unitary central character ensures \(h^*\in\mathcal H_\omega(G_n)\).

Lemma 1.23s (actual projectivity and embeddings). In the category of smooth modules with central character \(\omega\), the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{G_n}(\rho,-)\) is exact. Every irreducible subquotient isomorphic to this Jacquet-zero \(\rho\) of a module \(V\) gives an actual embedding \(\rho\hookrightarrow V\).

Proof. Choose \(w\) with \(H(w,w)=1\), and set \(e=f_{ww}\). Equation (1.39y) makes \(e\) an idempotent, whose action on \(\rho\) is the rank-one projection \(u\mapsto H(u,w)w\). The functor \(V\mapsto eV\) is exact: for an onto map, lift a vector and apply \(e\); for kernels, intersect with its image.

For \(u\in eV\), define

\[ T_u(v)=\pi_V(f_{vw})u. \tag{1.39aa} \]

Left translation gives \(L_a f_{vw}=f_{\rho(a)v,w}\), and (1.39v) gives \(\pi_V(a)\pi_V(f)=\pi_V(L_af)\). Thus \(T_u\) is a \(G_n\)-map. Moreover \(T_u(w)=eu=u\). Conversely, if \(T:\rho\to V\) is equivariant, \(Tw\in eV\) and \(T(v)=T(\rho(f_{vw})w)=\pi_V(f_{vw})Tw\). Consequently evaluation at \(w\) identifies

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_{G_n}(\rho,V)\simeq eV \tag{1.39ab} \]

naturally, proving exactness. If \(\rho\) is a subquotient of \(V\), exactness of \(e(-)\) makes \(eV\ne0\). A nonzero \(u\in eV\) gives the nonzero map \(T_u\), whose kernel is zero by irreducibility. This is the required embedding. \(\square\)

Corollary 1.23t. A proper parabolic induction of irreducible admissible Jacquet-zero blocks has no irreducible admissible Jacquet-zero subquotient.

Proof. Its center is the single smooth scalar character \(\omega=\prod_j\omega_{\rho_j}\). Twist the entire induction by \(\nu^s\), where \(s=\log|\omega(\varpi)|/(n\log q)\), so its central character becomes unitary. This simultaneously twists every inducing block by \(\nu^s\), preserving Jacquet vanishing and all subquotient relations. Any Jacquet-zero irreducible subquotient \(S\) now has this unitary center. Lemma 1.23l and Lemma 1.23s give an embedding of \(S\) into the full induction.

Normalized reciprocity for any block parabolic follows from exactly the written value-at-\(1\) proof: a \(G_n\)-map to \(I_P(\rho)\) evaluates to a map \(\delta_P^{-1/2}S_{U_P}\to\rho\), and conversely such a map \(T\) gives the section \(g\mapsto T(\pi(g)v)\). Its common right stabilizer is that of \(v\). Since \(P\) is proper and \(S\) is Jacquet-zero, this Hom space is zero. This contradicts the embedding. Untwisting proves the claim for the original induction. \(\square\)

Lemma 1.23u (the actual finite Jacquet filtration). Let \(I=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_t\) with each \(\rho_j\) irreducible admissible and Jacquet-zero, of rank \(n_j\). For \(1\le l<n\), the normalized \(P_{l,n-l}\)-Jacquet module has a finite filtration indexed by subsets \(A\subset\{1,\ldots,t\}\) with \(\sum_{j\in A}n_j=l\). The corresponding quotient is

\[ I_A\boxtimes I_{A^c},\qquad I_A=\mathop{\times}_{j\in A}\rho_j, \tag{1.39ac} \]

with the original relative order retained in both products.

Proof. The proof of Lemma 2.3p applies to arbitrary smooth inducing modules: the orbit decomposition, locally constant section restriction, exact additive unipotent coinvariants, fiber integration kernel, and density calculation use no irreducibility of an inducing module. Thus it applies when the second inducing module is itself an induction. Refine the partition \((n_1,\ldots,n_t)\) successively. At each step its finite orbit filtration assigns ranks \(i_j\) to the first Jacquet block. A rank \(0<i_j<n_j\) makes the corresponding Jacquet module of \(\rho_j\) zero. Hence a nonzero quotient assigns each whole block to one side, giving precisely the subsets in the statement.

Normalized induction is exact, as proved by the compact representative-value lifts, so it refines these successive filtrations. Induction in stages is the actual isomorphism (1.27v)–(1.27w), with its tensor section construction. The two negative half-moduli of the inducing Jacquet modules and the positive half-moduli of each new induction agree exactly with the exponents in (2.9ch); when a whole block is assigned, its own Jacquet half-modulus is one. No twist remains in (1.39ac). This proves the finite filtration and its precise ordered quotient modules, without a finite-length assertion about \(I\). \(\square\)

Theorem 1.23v (finite length, all ranks and both characteristics). Every induction of finitely many irreducible admissible Jacquet-zero blocks has finite length. If \(t\ge2\), its length is bounded by

\[ \ell(I)\le \sum_{l=1}^{n-1}\ell(r_{l,n-l}I) =\sum_{\varnothing\ne A\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,t\}} \ell(I_A)\ell(I_{A^c}). \tag{1.39ad} \]

The equality is the finite filtration length formula; the lower-rank lengths on its right are defined inductively. Parabolic induction preserves finite length for admissible data. Every Jacquet module of a finite-length admissible representation has finite length.

Proof. Induct on total rank \(n\). In rank one the only such induction is its irreducible block and has length one; the same holds in any rank when \(t=1\). Assume \(t\ge2\) and the theorem on cuspidal induction in all smaller ranks. Lemma 1.23u gives finite filtrations of each \(r_{l,n-l}I\) with quotients (1.39ac). Both factors have strictly smaller rank and therefore finite length. Tensoring their composition filtrations is exact over \(\mathbb C\); each successive outer tensor product of irreducible admissible factors is irreducible admissible by the tensor theorem used in Lemma 1.23d. Thus (1.39ac) has length \(\ell(I_A)\ell(I_{A^c})\), and the finite filtration gives the equality in (1.39ad). In particular all these Jacquet modules have finite length.

Every nonzero subquotient \(V\) of \(I\) has an irreducible subquotient: choose a nonzero vector, take its cyclic submodule, and apply the finite-generator Zorn argument to that cyclic module. Its simple quotient is admissible by compact averaging. Corollary 1.23t says it is not Jacquet-zero. Some proper standard two-block Jacquet module of that quotient is therefore nonzero. Exactness of that Jacquet functor implies \(r_{l,n-l}V\ne0\) for at least one \(l\).

For a submodule \(W\subset I\), let

\[ b(W)=\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}\ell(r_{l,n-l}W). \tag{1.39ae} \]

The terms are finite because they are submodules of the already finite-length \(r_{l,n-l}I\). If \(W\subsetneq W'\), the nonzero subquotient \(W'/W\) is detected by at least one of those Jacquet functors. Exactness and additivity of length give \(b(W')>b(W)\). Since \(0\le b(W)\le b(I)<\infty\), every strict chain of submodules has at most \(b(I)\) steps. This provides maximal proper submodules and termination of their descending recursion, hence a composition series of \(I\) and the inequality in (1.39ad). The rank induction is complete. This argument detects every subquotient by a finite collection of exact functors; it does not assert an unproved universal compact level.

For arbitrary irreducible admissible inducing blocks, Theorem 1.23e embeds each in an induction of Jacquet-zero irreducibles. Exactness and transitivity of induction and exactness of tensor products give an embedding of their whole induction into one of the cuspidal inductions just proved finite-length. A submodule of a finite-length module is finite-length, so induction from arbitrary irreducible admissible blocks is finite-length. For finite-length admissible inducing data, induce their finite composition filtrations and use exactness, reducing to the preceding assertion.

Finally, an irreducible admissible \(\pi\) embeds in a cuspidal induction \(I\). For a proper standard two-block parabolic, its Jacquet module embeds by exactness in the finite-length module furnished by Lemma 1.23u. Thus all such Jacquet modules of \(\pi\) are finite-length. Their simple factors are admissible representations of a product Levi and factor as actual outer tensor products by the tensor theorem. Iterating on the smaller ranks gives the same assertion for every standard multiblock Jacquet module. Coinvariants in stages follow directly by successively quotienting by the normal unipotent subgroups, with the product of their normalizing moduli. Flag conjugation gives every parabolic. An arbitrary finite-length admissible representation then follows by exactness along its finite composition series. \(\square\)

Multiblock Jacquet filtrations and intrinsic cuspidal support

Lemma 1.23w (multiblock whole-factor filtration). Let \(P\) have block ranks \(d_1,\ldots,d_s\), and let \(I=\sigma_1\times\cdots\times\sigma_t\), where each \(\sigma_j\) is Jacquet-cuspidal of rank \(m_j\). Its normalized \(P\)-Jacquet module has a finite filtration indexed by ordered partitions of the positions

\[ (A_1,\ldots,A_s),\qquad \coprod_{\alpha=1}^s A_\alpha=\{1,\ldots,t\},\qquad \sum_{j\in A_\alpha}m_j=d_\alpha. \tag{1.39af} \]

The corresponding quotient is

\[ I_{A_1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes I_{A_s}, \tag{1.39ag} \]

where each product retains the original relative order of its positions.

Proof. Cut the first \(d_1\) coordinates from the remaining coordinates. Lemma 1.23u gives the finite subset filtration, with the assigned factors and remaining factors. Apply the two-block Jacquet functor inside the second Levi block, then continue refining it. These functors are exact by compact averaging; they commute with tensor factors on which they act trivially, because the quotient relations are precisely the tensor product of the original relation subspace with that other factor. Thus they refine the finite filtration at each stage.

Coinvariants in stages are the actual successive quotient: the full refined upper radical is the product of the original normal radical and the new radical in its Levi, so quotienting successively imposes exactly all its relations. The normalizing moduli multiply, since their root-coordinate determinants multiply. This identifies the resulting normalized functor with \(r_P\), rather than with a twisted version. A nonzero term assigns each whole \(\sigma_j\) to one final block; a partial assignment would have a zero proper Jacquet module. The successive choices are exactly (1.39af), and transitive induction identifies their quotients with (1.39ag). As in Lemma 1.23u, the normalized density calculation cancels all intermediate half-moduli. This proves the stated finite filtration. \(\square\)

Theorem 1.23x (intrinsic cuspidal support). For every irreducible smooth admissible \(\pi\) of \(G_n\), there is a unique unordered multiset of actual Jacquet-cuspidal irreducible admissible representations such that \(\pi\) is a subquotient of their normalized induction. Multiplicities, ranks, representations and all norm twists are retained.

Proof. Theorem 1.23e gives an actual embedding

\[ \pi\hookrightarrow I_P(\rho_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\rho_s) \tag{1.39ah} \]

with Jacquet-cuspidal \(\rho_\alpha\) of ranks \(d_\alpha\). Normalized reciprocity sends this nonzero map to a nonzero map

\[ r_P\pi\longrightarrow \rho_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\rho_s. \tag{1.39ai} \]

The target is an actual irreducible admissible Levi representation by the tensor theorem, so this map is onto.

Suppose also that \(\pi\) is any actual subquotient of \(I=\sigma_1\times\cdots\times\sigma_t\) with Jacquet-cuspidal \(\sigma_j\). Exactness makes \(r_P\pi\) a subquotient of \(r_PI\). Consequently the tensor in (1.39ai) is an irreducible subquotient of that latter module.

An irreducible subquotient of a module with a finite filtration occurs as an actual subquotient of one of its successive quotients. Indeed, if \(C/D\) is the simple subquotient, intersect \(C\) with the filtration and take the first term having nonzero image in \(C/D\). That image is the whole simple module and the preceding term maps to zero. The intersection term modulo its preceding term embeds in the ambient successive quotient and maps onto \(C/D\). This proves the assertion without a virtual Grothendieck-group substitution.

Apply this fact to Lemma 1.23w. Each \(I_{A_\alpha}\) has finite length by Theorem 1.23v, so tensoring their actual composition series gives a finite filtration of (1.39ag) by simple outer tensor products. The same subquotient argument shows that the tensor of the \(\rho_\alpha\) is isomorphic to \(S_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes S_s\), where each \(S_\alpha\) is an irreducible constituent of \(I_{A_\alpha}\). Uniqueness of actual tensor factors gives \(S_\alpha\simeq\rho_\alpha\).

If \(|A_\alpha|\ge2\), that \(I_{A_\alpha}\) is a proper parabolic induction of Jacquet-cuspidal blocks, so Corollary 1.23t excludes its Jacquet-cuspidal constituent \(\rho_\alpha\). Every \(A_\alpha\) is nonempty because its assigned rank \(d_\alpha\) is positive. Hence each \(A_\alpha\) has exactly one position \(j\), and \(\rho_\alpha\simeq\sigma_j\) with the same rank. The disjoint partition covers all positions, proving \(s=t\) and equality of the unordered multisets including multiplicities and actual twists. This proves uniqueness and existence. \(\square\)

Corollary 1.23y (the full Jacquet supercuspidality criterion). For an irreducible smooth admissible representation, zero all proper Jacquet modules is equivalent to not occurring as a subquotient of any proper parabolic induction from irreducible admissible Levi data.

Proof. If a proper two-block Jacquet module is nonzero, the actual Lemma 1.23d constructs an embedding into a proper induction, hence a subquotient occurrence. Conversely, suppose a Jacquet-zero irreducible \(S\) occurred in a proper induction from arbitrary irreducible admissible blocks. Embed each inducing block in its actual cuspidal induction from Theorem 1.23e. Exactness, tensor injections and induction in stages embed the whole original induction in an induction from Jacquet-cuspidal blocks. Because the original parabolic was proper, the final list has at least two blocks. Transitivity of subquotient occurrence would put \(S\) in that proper cuspidal induction, contradicting Corollary 1.23t. Nonstandard parabolics are conjugated to standard ones by a flag basis, which transports induction and coinvariants by actual inner conjugation. \(\square\)

The arbitrary-algebra tensor results used here have complete earlier proofs in Restricted tensor products and the tensor product theorem, Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and Theorem 4.1. Their finite interpolation, simple-corner reconstruction and admissible tensor factorization apply to every product Levi in these arguments.

Direct positivity of the cuspidal matrix epsilon exponent

This proof treats every nonarchimedean local field and every rank \(n\geq2\). It uses the full matrix Fourier family and zero proper Jacquet modules. It does not construct an inducing type or assume a compact-induction realization.

Let \(k\) have integer ring \(\mathcal O\), uniformizer \(\varpi\), residue cardinality \(q\), and valuation \(v(\varpi)=1\). Put \[ G=\mathrm{GL}_n(k),\quad Z=k^\times I_n,\quad K=\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O),\quad j(g)=v(\det g),\quad X=q^{-s}. \tag{1.29a} \] The character \(\psi\) has annihilator \(\mathcal O\), and the matrix Fourier pairing is positive: \[ \widehat\Phi(Y)=\int_{M_n(k)}\Phi(A)\psi(\operatorname{tr}(AY))\,dA. \tag{1.29b} \] The additive measures give every integral coordinate lattice volume 1; they are self-dual. Multiplicative Haar measure gives \(K\) volume 1. Write \[ \alpha_n=\prod_{i=1}^n(1-q^{-i}),\qquad dg=\alpha_n^{-1}|\det g|^{-n}\,d_{\rm add}g. \tag{1.29c} \] Indeed additive matrix measure scaled by \(|\det g|^{-n}\) is left and right invariant: multiplication by \(a\) has additive Jacobian \(|\det a|^n\). The additive volume of \(K\) is the fraction of invertible matrices over the residue field, namely \(q^{-n^2}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^i)=\alpha_n\). This proves (1.29c) with the exact constant.

Proposition 1.3, Proposition 1.4, Corollary 1.4a, Theorem 1.17 and Lemma 1.20a are the preceding matrix proofs used here. They supply the entire rational matrix ideal, the scalar Fourier equation, the Laurent-unit epsilon factor, and compact-mod-center coefficient support from zero two-block Jacquet modules. In rank greater than one that support also gives \[ V^K=0,\qquad L_\pi=L_{\widetilde\pi}=1. \tag{1.29d} \] We also use the complete proofs of the unique extended absolute value and Newton factorization in Extensions of complete valued fields, Theorems 1.2 and 5.1. Those actual proofs explicitly include inseparable extensions and polynomials in positive characteristic.

Fix an irreducible smooth admissible \(\pi\) with \(V_{U_r}=0\) for every upper two-block radical \(U_r\), \(1\leq r<n\). Let \(c(g)=\ell(\pi(g)v)\). Both \(c\) and \(c^\vee(g)=c(g^{-1})\) have compact support modulo \(Z\).

Constant terms and compact determinant shells

If a locally constant function \(f\) has support in \(ZC\) for compact \(C\subset G\), its support on every shell \(j(g)=j\) is compact. In fact \(j(C)\) is a finite set, and \(j(zc)=nv(z)+j(c)\) confines \(v(z)\) to finitely many integers. The corresponding subsets \(\varpi^b\mathcal O^\times\) are compact, so their products with \(C\) are compact. In particular all integrals below on a fixed shell are absolutely convergent.

Lemma 1.24a (vanishing along the full unipotent fiber). For \(m=\operatorname{diag}(A,D)\), \(k_0\in K\), and \[ u(B)=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&B\\0&I_t\end{pmatrix}, \quad B\in M_{r,t}(k),\quad r+t=n, \] both \(f=c\) and \(f=c^\vee\) satisfy \[ \int_{M_{r,t}(k)} f(k_0u(B)m k_0^{-1})\,dB=0. \tag{1.29e} \] Moreover \[ \int_{j(g)=j}f(g)\,dg=0\qquad(j\in\mathbb Z). \tag{1.29f} \]

Proof. If a vector \(w\) has zero Jacquet class, write it as a finite sum of \((\pi(u_i)-1)w_i\). Any sufficiently large compact additive subgroup of \(U_r\) contains all \(u_i\); its probability average kills every summand by translation invariance. Thus its average kills \(w\).

The integrand in (1.29e) has compact support in \(B\). To check this from compact support modulo \(Z\), conjugation by \(k_0\) preserves compactness, so consider \(u(B)m=z h\) with \(h\) in a fixed compact subset of \(G\). The fixed invertible diagonal blocks \(A,D\) bound \(|z|\) below, using the bound on the entries of \(h\); the fixed diagonal blocks of the inverse bound \(|z|\) above, using the bound on the entries of \(h^{-1}\). The upper-right block \(BD\) is then bounded, hence so is \(B\). Closedness of the support and local compactness prove the assertion.

For \(c\), averaging the vector \(\pi(mk_0^{-1})v\) over a compact subgroup containing this support gives zero, proving (1.29e). For the inverse coefficient the integrand is \[ c^\vee(k_0u(B)m k_0^{-1}) =\ell\bigl(\pi(k_0m^{-1})\pi(u(-B))\pi(k_0^{-1})v\bigr). \] Averaging the vector \(\pi(k_0^{-1})v\) proves the same result. This does not require an unproved dual-Jacquet identity.

Finally use (1.29d). The shell is invariant under right \(K\) translation, and its integral for \(c\) equals the integral of the right \(K\)-average, which replaces \(v\) by \(e_Kv=0\). For \(c^\vee\), use left \(K\)-translation instead; it likewise replaces \(v\) by \(e_Kv=0\). Compact shell support and the compact \(K\)-orbit of each smooth vector justify Fubini. This proves (1.29f). \(\square\)

Splitting matrices according to root absolute values

Extend the absolute value uniquely to an algebraic closure of \(k\). For \(g\in G\), call its characteristic polynomial equal-valued if all its roots, counted with algebraic multiplicity, have the same absolute value. In that case their common valuation is \(j(g)/n\). Consequently \[ j(g)\geq0,\quad g\text{ equal-valued} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{tr}(g)\in\mathcal O. \tag{1.29g} \] Indeed the trace is the sum of those roots, all of absolute value at most 1, and belongs to \(k\).

If the roots are not equal-valued, let \(R\) be their largest absolute value, let \(r\) be the number of roots of that value, and put \(t=n-r>0\). Newton factorization, including polynomial multiplicities, gives coprime monic polynomials in \(k[T]\): \[ p_g=p_+p_-,\quad \deg p_+=r,\quad\deg p_-=t, \quad |\text{roots of }p_+|=R> |\text{each root of }p_-|. \tag{1.29h} \] There is a unique canonical \(r\)-dimensional subspace \[ W_g=\ker p_+(g). \tag{1.29i} \] For completeness, Bézout for \(p_+,p_-\), together with Cayley–Hamilton, splits \(k^n\) as \(\ker p_+(g)\oplus\ker p_-(g)\). The polynomial \(p_+\) kills the first summand and \(p_-\) the second. Over a splitting field an operator is upper triangularizable: choose an eigenvector, pass to its quotient, and induct on the dimension. Applying the annihilating polynomial to such a triangular form shows that its diagonal roots belong to the roots of that polynomial. The two summand characteristic polynomials therefore have disjoint root sets and multiply to \(p_g\); all the multiplicities of \(p_+\) must be in the first and all those of \(p_-\) in the second. They are \(p_+,p_-\) respectively. Their dimensions are therefore \(r,t\). The same reasoning shows that any invariant subspace carrying all \(r\) of the largest-value roots is killed by \(p_+(g)\), by Cayley–Hamilton on that subspace, and equals (1.29i). This proves uniqueness.

The Cayley–Hamilton identity used here also follows directly from \((TI-g)\operatorname{adj}(TI-g)=p_g(T)I= \operatorname{adj}(TI-g)(TI-g)\). The two identities show that each coefficient matrix of the adjugate commutes with \(g\); evaluating this polynomial matrix identity at \(T=g\) gives \(p_g(g)=0\). For the direct-sum assertion, a Bézout identity \(a p_++b p_-=1\) writes each vector as the sum of its \(b(g)p_-(g)\) image in \(\ker p_+(g)\) and its \(a(g)p_+(g)\) image in \(\ker p_-(g)\); their intersection is zero by the same identity.

The root-valuation multiset is locally constant as a function of an invertible matrix. Here is the needed topological detail. At a polynomial with nonzero leading and constant coefficients, the finitely many coefficient points defining its Newton polygon have fixed finite heights. A sufficiently small coefficient change keeps each nonzero coefficient's valuation fixed and puts every formerly zero coefficient strictly above that polygon. The polygon is unchanged. The preceding Newton theorem identifies its slopes and lengths with the root valuations and multiplicities. Characteristic coefficients are polynomial functions of matrix entries, so the assertion follows.

Write \(\Omega_r\) for matrices whose largest-value group has dimension \(r<n\). The \(\Omega_r\) are disjoint open sets covering the matrices that are not equal-valued. Define the open block domain \[ \mathcal D_r= \{(A,D)\in\mathrm{GL}_r(k)\times\mathrm{GL}_t(k): \text{all roots of }A\text{ have one absolute value, larger than every root absolute value of }D\}. \tag{1.29j} \]

We give finite integral charts for \(W_g\). Any \(r\)-subspace \(W\subset k^n\) has a saturated lattice \(\Lambda=W\cap\mathcal O^n\), and a basis of \(\Lambda\) extends to an integral basis of \(\mathcal O^n\). An explicit proof is to scale a nonzero vector in \(W\) until one coordinate is a unit, use integral elementary coordinate changes to send it to \(e_n\), and split \[ W=k e_n\oplus(W\cap k^{n-1}),\quad \Lambda=\mathcal O e_n\oplus(W\cap k^{n-1}\cap\mathcal O^{n-1}). \] Induction supplies the asserted integral basis.

Thus \(\Lambda/\varpi\Lambda\) determines an \(r\)-plane \(\overline W\) in the residue-field vector space. For each of the finitely many such planes choose \(k_{\overline W}\in K\) carrying the first coordinate \(r\)-plane to it on reduction. Every \(W\) with that reduction has a unique form \[ W=k_{\overline W} \{(x,Bx):x\in k^r\},\qquad B\in\varpi M_{t,r}(\mathcal O). \tag{1.29k} \] Indeed after \(k_{\overline W}^{-1}\), the projection of an integral basis of \(\Lambda\) to its first \(r\) coordinates is invertible modulo \(\varpi\), hence belongs to \(\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O)\). Normalizing that projection to the identity makes its lower block the unique \(B\), which is zero modulo \(\varpi\).

Put \(l(B)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I_r&0\\B&I_t\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(k_B=k_{\overline W}l(B)\in K\). The map \[ F_{\overline W}(B,A,C,D) =k_B\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix}k_B^{-1}, \quad B\in\varpi M_{t,r}(\mathcal O),\quad (A,D)\in\mathcal D_r,\quad C\in M_{r,t}(k), \tag{1.29l} \] is a bijection onto the part of \(\Omega_r\) with \(\overline{W_g}=\overline W\). Its canonical subspace is exactly \(k_B k^r\); uniqueness in (1.29i) determines \(B\), and reading the conjugated blocks determines \(A,C,D\). Conversely any \(g\) in that part preserves its canonical subspace, so this block reading gives (1.29l) and (1.29j). The charts are disjoint; no Weyl multiplicity or finite representative factor is omitted.

The measure calculation, including its analytic justification

Define the Sylvester map on the lower rectangular block: \[ S_{A,D}:M_{t,r}(k)\longrightarrow M_{t,r}(k), \qquad H\longmapsto HA-DH. \tag{1.29m} \] It is invertible on \(\mathcal D_r\). If \(HA=DH\), then \(Hp_A(A)=p_A(D)H=0\), where \(p_A\) is the characteristic polynomial of \(A\). Its coprimality with the characteristic polynomial of \(D\) makes \(p_A(D)\) invertible by Bézout. Hence \(H=0\), which proves invertibility in finite dimension.

The exact chart measure is \[ dg=\alpha_n^{-1}|\det A\,\det D|^{-n} |\det S_{A,D}|\,dB\,d_{\rm add}A\,dC\,d_{\rm add}D. \tag{1.29n} \] Most importantly its density is independent of \(B,C\). To calculate it, discard the fixed integral conjugation \(k_{\overline W}\), whose additive Jacobian is 1. Conjugation by \(l(B)\) also has additive Jacobian 1. Since \(l(B)^{-1}dl(B)= \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\dB&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the differential of (1.29l), after that conjugation, is \[ \begin{pmatrix} dA-C\,dB&dC\\ dB\,A-D\,dB&dD+dB\,C \end{pmatrix}. \tag{1.29o} \] As a linear map in \(dA,dC,dD,dB\), its determinant has absolute value \(|\det S_{A,D}|\): the lower output is \(S_{A,D}(dB)\), and the other three outputs have identity coefficients on \(dA,dC,dD\). Finally \(\det F_{\overline W}=\det A\,\det D\), and (1.29c) gives (1.29n).

Here the change of variables is valid in every characteristic. We include the finite-dimensional analytic fact being used, instead of importing it from a manual. If a polynomial map \(F:k^d\to k^d\) has invertible derivative \(L\) at \(x_0\), write \[ L^{-1}(F(x_0+h)-F(x_0))=h+R(h). \] The polynomial \(R\) has no constant or linear terms. On a sufficiently small ball \(\varpi^N\mathcal O^d\), its finitely many coefficients and the telescoping formula for a difference of monomials give \[ \|R(h)-R(h')\|\leq q^{-1}\|h-h'\|, \qquad R(\varpi^N\mathcal O^d)\subset \varpi^{N+1}\mathcal O^d. \tag{1.29p} \] For \(y\) in this ball, \(h\mapsto y-R(h)\) is a contraction of that complete ball. Successive iterates are Cauchy, with errors bounded by the geometric powers \(q^{-i}\); their limit is its unique fixed point. This proves a bijection of the ball under \(h\mapsto h+R(h)\), and proves continuity of its inverse. The same argument on every contained coset ball of radius \(q^{-a}\), \(a\geq N\), sends it onto the coset ball of the same radius around its image. It therefore preserves additive Haar measure: these coset balls form a basis, and locally constant compact tests are finite linear combinations of their indicators. Translation and the linear map \(L\) then supply the measure factor \(|\det L|\). The latter factor follows from integral row and column elimination and diagonal scalings.

The derivative determinant remains of that same absolute value on the sufficiently small ball. Thus this is the Jacobian change of variables there. A nonarchimedean local field has a countable basis of such coordinate balls: each quotient \(k/\varpi^a\mathcal O\) is countable. Partitioning an open domain into countably many sufficiently small disjoint balls proves the formula globally for nonnegative measurable functions, then for integrable functions. On (1.29l) its derivative is invertible everywhere, and the previously proved bijection removes all multiplicities. This proves (1.29n) and justifies its use for all the integrals below, without a separability or residual-characteristic restriction.

The nonnegative determinant Gauss integrals vanish

Lemma 1.24b. For \(f=c\) or \(f=c^\vee\), \[ \int_{j(g)=j}\psi(\operatorname{tr}g)f(g)\,dg=0 \qquad(j\geq0). \tag{1.29q} \]

Proof. By (1.29f) it suffices to integrate \[ h(g)f(g),\qquad h(g)=\psi(\operatorname{tr}g)-1. \] On the equal-valued matrices in this shell, (1.29g) and the conductor of \(\psi\) give \(h=0\). On each remaining \(\Omega_r\), use the finitely many disjoint charts (1.29l). The determinant and the trace are \(\det A\,\det D\) and \(\operatorname{tr}A+\operatorname{tr}D\). The shell condition, the root condition (1.29j), \(h\), and the measure density (1.29n) are consequently all independent of \(C\). The inner integral is \[ \int_C f\!\left(k_B \begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&D\end{pmatrix} k_B^{-1}\right)\,dC =|\det D|^r\int_Q f(k_Bu(Q)m k_B^{-1})\,dQ=0, \tag{1.29r} \] by \(C=QD\) and Lemma 1.24a. This proves the desired vanishing on each chart. Compact shell support, boundedness of \(h\), and (1.29n) justify the absolute Fubini rearrangement. Summing over the finite charts and \(1\leq r<n\) proves (1.29q). \(\square\)

The subtraction of 1 is essential: its shell integral is zero by the compact \(K\)-average, while the difference vanishes exactly where the trace is known to be integral. The argument does not identify a coefficient with a character distribution and does not infer scalar operator vanishing from a trace limit.

The Fourier equation now forces strict positivity

Theorem 1.24 (every Jacquet-cuspidal block). If \(n\geq2\) and \(\pi\) is irreducible smooth admissible with all proper two-block Jacquet modules zero, then its conductor-zero, positive-trace matrix epsilon factor has \[ \epsilon_\pi(s,\psi)=c_\pi X^{a_\pi},\qquad c_\pi\ne0,\qquad a_\pi>0. \tag{1.29s} \] This holds over every nonarchimedean local field.

Proof. The scalar Fourier equation and the Laurent-unit argument have already proved \(a_\pi\in\mathbb Z\). Choose \(v,\ell\) with \(\ell(v)=1\), and let \(J_N= 1+\varpi^N M_n(\mathcal O)\), \(N\geq1\), fix \(v,\ell\). Every deeper \(J_N\) does too. The actual test \[ \Phi_N=\operatorname{vol}_G(J_N)^{-1}1_{J_N} \] has \(Z_\pi(s,\Phi_N,c)=1\). Additive lattice orthogonality and (1.29c) give exactly \[ \widehat\Phi_N(Y)= \alpha_n\psi(\operatorname{tr}Y)\, 1_{\varpi^{-N}M_n(\mathcal O)}(Y). \tag{1.29t} \] There is no \(N\)-dependent scalar: the additive and multiplicative volumes of \(J_N\) have ratio \(\alpha_n\).

By (1.29d) gamma equals epsilon. Apply the whole-family Fourier equation to this test. Its exact Laurent expansion is \[ c_\pi X^{a_\pi} =\alpha_n\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z} q^{-j(n+1)/2}X^{-j} \int_{\substack{j(g)=j\\ g\in\varpi^{-N}M_n(\mathcal O)}} \psi(\operatorname{tr}g)c^\vee(g)\,dg. \tag{1.29u} \] For clarity this sum is finite. Its lower bound is \(j\geq-nN\), by the determinant expansion. For large positive \(j\), compact-mod-center support of \(c^\vee\) places its entire shell support in \(M_n(\mathcal O)\): write \(g=z h\), \(h\) in a fixed compact subset of \(G\); the finite values of \(j(h)\) force \(v(z)\to+\infty\) uniformly as \(j\to+\infty\). Its entries therefore tend uniformly to zero. The ball indicator is then 1 and \(\psi(\operatorname{tr}g)=1\); (1.29f) makes that shell coefficient zero. Thus (1.29u) is a genuine finite Laurent identity, obtained first in a convergence half-plane and then as the proved rational continuation.

Suppose \(a_\pi\leq0\), and put \(j_0=-a_\pi\geq0\). The support of \(c^\vee\) on that one shell is compact. Choose \(N\) sufficiently large that its support lies in \(\varpi^{-N}M_n(\mathcal O)\), retaining the fixed-vector condition. The coefficient of \(X^{a_\pi}=X^{-j_0}\) on the right of (1.29u) is then \[ \alpha_n q^{-j_0(n+1)/2} \int_{j(g)=j_0}\psi(\operatorname{tr}g)c^\vee(g)\,dg=0 \] by Lemma 1.24b. On the left it is the nonzero number \(c_\pi\). This contradiction proves \(a_\pi>0\). \(\square\)

Only one shell needs eventual containment. No uniform support bound over every vector, coefficient, test or determinant shell is assumed in this final extraction.

Every irreducible representation: nonnegative exponent and factor degree

Corollary 1.24c (universal nonnegative matrix exponent). Every irreducible smooth admissible \(\sigma\) embeds in normalized induction from terminal Jacquet-cuspidal blocks \(\rho_i\), by Theorem 1.23e. Its exact polynomial correction (1.27x)–(1.27y) gives \[ a_\sigma=\sum_i a_{\rho_i}+\deg R,\qquad R(0)=1, \quad R\in\mathbb C[X]. \tag{1.29v} \] Each block of rank greater than one has positive exponent by Theorem 1.24. Each rank-one block is a character and has nonnegative scalar Tate exponent by Proposition 1.16 in rank one. Since \(\deg R\geq0\), this proves \[ a_\sigma\geq0 \] for every smooth irreducible admissible \(\mathrm{GL}_n(k)\), in all ranks and all nonarchimedean characteristics. This proves the corollary. \(\square\)

This closes nonnegativity of the matrix epsilon exponent. It does not identify it with a generic minimal \(K_1\)-level or an Artin conductor, and does not assert existence of compact inducing data for every cuspidal representation. Those separate statements are unnecessary for the proof here.

Corollary 1.24d (degree bound and exponent zero). Write \(L_\sigma(s)=P_\sigma(q^{-s})^{-1}\), \(P_\sigma(0)=1\). For a cuspidal-support embedding as in Theorem 1.23e, let \(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_h\) be its unramified rank-one blocks, listed with multiplicity. Then \[ P_\sigma(X)R(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{h}(1-\chi_i(\varpi)X), \qquad \deg P_\sigma\leq h\leq n. \tag{1.29w} \] In particular \(L_\sigma=1\) if there are no such blocks. If \(a_\sigma=0\), every block has rank one and is unramified, \(h=n\), \(R=1\), and \[ P_\sigma(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-\chi_i(\varpi)X). \tag{1.29x} \]

Proof. Lemma 1.20a and Proposition 1.4 give factor 1 for each cuspidal block of higher rank. Proposition 1.16 in rank one gives factor 1 for a ramified character and \((1-\chi(\varpi)X)^{-1}\) for an unramified character. Substitution in (1.27x), followed by multiplication by \(P_\sigma\prod_i(1-\chi_i(\varpi)X)\), proves (1.29w). Degrees add in a product of nonzero polynomials, so its degree is \(h\), proving the bound. If \(h=0\), both polynomials have constant term 1 and their product is 1; hence both equal 1.

When \(a_\sigma=0\), (1.29v) is a sum of nonnegative integers. Every summand is therefore zero. Theorem 1.24 excludes a higher-rank block. The exact rank-one conductor in Proposition 1.16 makes every remaining character unramified. Thus \(h=n\). Also \(\deg R=0\) and \(R(0)=1\), so \(R=1\), proving (1.29x). \(\square\)

This is a conclusion about the cuspidal-support embedding and the matrix factor. A proof that \(\sigma\) itself has a \(K\)-fixed vector would require an additional argument. The algebraic compact-induction criteria in Lemmas 1.23f–1.23g retain \(n\geq2\) for strict positivity: an unramified rank-one character has exponent zero.

Further reading is Getz–Hahn, 22 April 2022 author draft, §8.7, Proposition 8.7.1, printed pages 207–208. The finite Newton charts, Sylvester Jacobian and full-fiber cancellation above provide the proof, including matrices that are not semisimple and fields of positive characteristic.

Matrix tests at a real or complex place

For \(F=\mathbb R\) use \(|x|_F=|x|\); for \(F=\mathbb C\) use \(|z|_F=z\bar z\). Put \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), \(\nu(g)=|\det g|_F\), and \(u_s=s+(n-1)/2\). On the additive matrix space use ordinary real Lebesgue measure, or the product of \(2\,d\Re z\,d\Im z\) at a complex place. Multiplicative Haar measure is \(dg=C_F\nu(g)^{-n}dX\), where \(C_F>0\) records the chosen normalization. This formula follows from the left and right additive Jacobians \(|\det h|_F^n\).

These arguments use smooth matrix coefficients of a specified smooth realization. Wherever differentiation of a zeta integral is used, the coefficients and the indicated Lie derivatives are assumed to have polynomial growth. No algebraic-to-smooth or Hilbert-to-smooth comparison theorem is inferred here. Polynomial growth here means a bound by \(C(1+\|g\|+\|g^{-1}\|)^N\), with a possibly different \(C,N\) for each of the finitely many derivatives used in an argument.

1. Polynomial multiplication and tests supported on the group

Proposition 1.5 (polynomial-module closure). Suppose a matrix coefficient \(c\) and its Lie derivatives have polynomial growth. In the initial domain of convergence, the complex span of its matrix zeta integrals, allowing all coefficient vectors and Schwartz tests, is stable under multiplication by \(s\). The same is true if the tests are Gaussian times polynomials and the coefficient vectors are bi-\(K\)-finite, where \(K=O(n)\) or \(U(n)\).

Choose a real Lie algebra element \(A\) with \[ \left.\frac{d}{dt}\log\nu(e^{tA})\right|_{t=0}=1: \quad A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,\ldots,0)\ \ (F=\mathbb R), \quad A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,0,\ldots,0)\ \ (F=\mathbb C). \] For functions on \(G\) or on the matrix space let \(R_Af(g)=\left.\frac d{dt}f(ge^{tA})\right|_{0}\). Right invariance of Haar measure and the substitution \(g\mapsto ge^{-tA}\) give \[ Z(s,R_A\Phi,c)+Z(s,\Phi,R_Ac) =-\left(s+\frac{n-1}{2}\right)Z(s,\Phi,c). \tag{1.8a} \] Polynomial growth of the coefficients and their derivatives, together with the Schwartz bounds, justifies differentiation in a sufficiently far right half-plane. Near singular matrices, the same determinant weight and polynomial bound in \(g^{-1}\) give a common integrable majorant after increasing \(\Re s\); for example Cartan polar coordinates, or the column Gram–Schmidt coordinates below, bound powers of \(g^{-1}\) by a power of \(\nu(g)^{-1}\) times a polynomial in the matrix entries. More explicitly, the adjugate identity gives \(\|g^{-1}\|\leq C\|g\|^{n-1}|\det g|_{\mathrm{ordinary}}^{-1}\); the Gram–Schmidt integral of a sufficiently large positive determinant power is finite. Both estimates are uniform when \(t\) ranges over a compact interval.

Equation (1.8a) expresses \(sZ\) as a sum of three actual integrals. Iterating proves the assertion for any polynomial in \(s\). Differentiating a polynomial times the basic Gaussian again gives a polynomial times that Gaussian. A Lie derivative of a \(K\)-finite vector remains \(K\)-finite: if its original \(K\)-span is \(W\), the span after differentiation lies in the image of the finite-dimensional space \(\operatorname{span}\{\operatorname{Ad}(k)A:k\in K\}\otimes W\). Apply the same observation to the dual vector. \(\square\)

Proposition 1.6 (an entire test nonzero at a prescribed parameter). For every \(s_0\in\mathbb C\) and a coefficient with \(c(1)=1\), there is a Schwartz test supported inside \(G\) for which \(Z(s_0,\Phi,c)\ne0\). Integrals with such compact support are entire in \(s\).

Take a nonzero nonnegative smooth function \(\eta\) supported in a sufficiently small compact neighborhood of 1 in \(G\), and set \[ \Phi(g)=\eta(g)\overline{c(g)}\,\nu(g)^{-s_0-(n-1)/2}. \] Extend it by zero to the matrix space. Its support stays away from the singular locus, so the extension is smooth and Schwartz. Then \[ Z(s_0,\Phi,c)=\int_G\eta(g)|c(g)|^2\,dg>0. \] On a compact subset of \(G\), the real function \(\log\nu(g)\) is bounded. This bounds every parameter derivative uniformly on compact sets of \(s\), proving entireness. \(\square\)

In particular, if a common meromorphic generator \(L\) has already been shown to divide every zeta integral with entire quotient, Proposition 1.6 proves that it has no zeros. The entire-quotient assertion is indispensable: nonvanishing of a compact-support integral does not prove that division theorem.

2. The Gaussian ideal for determinant characters in every rank

Let \(\pi(g)=\chi(\det g)\), with \[ \chi(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)^e|x|^a,\quad e\in\{0,1\}, \quad F=\mathbb R; \qquad \chi(z)=(z/|z|)^k|z|_F^a,\quad k\in\mathbb Z, \quad F=\mathbb C. \] All matrix coefficients are scalar multiples of this character. These formulas cover every smooth character of \(F^\times\): on positive radii the character, written in the logarithmic coordinate, satisfies \(h'(t)=h'(0)h(t)\) and is an exponential. Over \(\mathbb R\) its value at \(-1\) has square one. Over \(\mathbb C\), the same differential equation on the angular coordinate and period \(2\pi\) force the exponent to be \(ik\) with \(k\in\mathbb Z\); the radial exponent is written as \(2a\) because the normalized complex norm is the squared radius. Let \(\mathcal S_0\) be the polynomials times \(e^{-\pi\operatorname{tr}(XX^t)}\) over \(\mathbb R\), or the polynomials in \(X,\overline X\) times \(e^{-2\pi\operatorname{tr}(XX^*)}\) over \(\mathbb C\).

Proposition 1.7 (the Gaussian ideal for determinant characters). The span of the matrix zeta integrals with tests in \(\mathcal S_0\) is exactly \(L_\chi(s)\mathbb C[s]\), where a constant normalization independent of \(s\) is permitted and \[ L_\chi(s)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^n \Gamma_{\mathbb R}\!\left(s+a+e+j-\frac{n+1}{2}\right), &F=\mathbb R,\\[4pt] \displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^n \Gamma_{\mathbb C}\!\left(s+a+\frac{|k|}{2} +j-\frac{n+1}{2}\right), &F=\mathbb C. \end{cases} \tag{1.8b} \] Here \(\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(w)=\pi^{-w/2}\Gamma(w/2)\) and \(\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(w)=2(2\pi)^{-w}\Gamma(w)\). This is an assertion about every Gaussian-polynomial test, not just a calculation of one test.

Proof: averaging the polynomial. Replace a test by \[ \Phi^\chi(X)=\int_{K\times K}\chi(\det k_1)\chi(\det k_2) \Phi(k_1Xk_2)\,dk_1\,dk_2. \tag{1.8c} \] The measures here are probability measures. Change of variables in the absolutely convergent integral shows that its zeta integral is unchanged. The basic Gaussian is bi-\(K\)-invariant; averaging its polynomial factor gives another polynomial of the same degree bound. Write this factor as \(P_\chi\). It has the transformation law \[ P_\chi(h_1Xh_2)= \chi(\det h_1\det h_2)^{-1}P_\chi(X) \quad(h_1,h_2\in K). \tag{1.8d} \]

Over \(\mathbb R\), restrict to diagonal matrices with entries \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Changing the sign of an individual entry shows that its polynomial degree in that entry has parity \(e\). Conjugating by permutation matrices shows that \[ P_\chi(\operatorname{diag}(x_j)) =(x_1\cdots x_n)^e Q(x_1^2,\ldots,x_n^2) \] with \(Q\) symmetric. Over \(\mathbb C\), restrict to diagonal entries \(z_j\). An independent unitary phase in entry \(j\) shows that every surviving monomial has \(\deg z_j-\deg\bar z_j=-k\). Thus its restriction is \(\prod_j\bar z_j^k Q(|z_1|^2,\ldots,|z_n|^2)\) if \(k\geq0\), and \(\prod_jz_j^{-k}Q(|z_1|^2,\ldots,|z_n|^2)\) if \(k<0\), again with \(Q\) symmetric.

Every symmetric polynomial in \(n\) variables is a polynomial in their elementary symmetric functions. An elementary proof subtracts the product of elementary symmetric functions with the same highest lexicographic monomial, and repeats; each subtraction decreases that monomial and terminates at bounded degree. Apply this to \(Q\). Its value on the squared singular values is therefore a polynomial in the characteristic coefficients of \(X^*X\), or \(X^tX\). These coefficients are themselves polynomials in the matrix entries.

Every matrix admits a real or complex singular-value decomposition. To obtain it, diagonalize the positive symmetric or Hermitian matrix \(X^*X\): the maximum of its quadratic form on the unit sphere gives an eigenvector, its orthogonal complement is invariant, and induction gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. The positive-eigenvalue columns of \(X\), divided by their singular values, are orthonormal; complete them to an orthonormal basis. This gives the desired two compact factors, also for singular matrices. The transformation law (1.8d) therefore identifies the full polynomial as \[ P_\chi(X)= \begin{cases} (\det X)^e Q_{\mathrm{Gram}}(X^tX),&F=\mathbb R,\\ (\overline{\det X})^k Q_{\mathrm{Gram}}(X^*X),&F=\mathbb C,\ k\geq0,\\ (\det X)^{-k}Q_{\mathrm{Gram}}(X^*X),&F=\mathbb C,\ k<0. \end{cases} \tag{1.8e} \] The notation \(Q_{\mathrm{Gram}}\) means a polynomial in those characteristic coefficients. None of the displayed powers has a negative exponent.

Proof: all the Gaussian moments. The real Gaussian matrix measure and the complex Gaussian matrix measure just specified both have total mass one: the one-entry integrals are respectively \(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\pi x^2}dx=1\) and \(\int_{\mathbb C}e^{-2\pi|z|^2}2\,d\Re z\,d\Im z=1\). Perform Gram–Schmidt on the independent Gaussian columns and write \(X=UR\), with \(R\) upper triangular and positive real diagonal entries \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\). The singular set has measure zero: successively, a Gaussian column lies in the span of preceding columns with probability zero, since that is a proper linear subspace.

Conditional on the preceding columns, the next Gaussian column in any orthonormal frame has the same product Gaussian law. Its coordinates along those columns and its orthogonal component are independent, and their distributions do not depend on the preceding columns. Thus the upper entries of \(R\) are independent one-entry Gaussians, and \(r_j\) is the length of a Gaussian vector in dimension \(d=n-j+1\). The variables so obtained are independent. Radial integration shows that \(r_j^2\) has gamma density with shape \(d/2\) and rate \(\pi\) in the real case, or shape \(d\) and rate \(2\pi\) in the complex case. The normalizing constants follow by dividing the radial integral by its value at exponent zero. This uses only the one-dimensional gamma integral.

Consequently, for the test in (1.8e) with \(Q_{\mathrm{Gram}}=1\), put \[ \kappa=s+a+e-\frac{n+1}{2}\quad(F=\mathbb R),\qquad \beta=s+a+\frac{|k|}{2}-\frac{n+1}{2}\quad(F=\mathbb C). \] The sign or angular character cancels the determinant polynomial. Including the factor \(\nu(g)^{-n}\) in Haar measure, its integral is \[ \begin{split} Z_{\mathrm{base}}(s) &=C_{\mathbb R}\pi^{-n\kappa/2} \prod_{j=1}^n\frac{\Gamma((\kappa+j)/2)}{\Gamma(j/2)} &&(F=\mathbb R),\\ Z_{\mathrm{base}}(s) &=C_{\mathbb C}(2\pi)^{-n\beta} \prod_{j=1}^n\frac{\Gamma(\beta+j)}{\Gamma(j)} &&(F=\mathbb C). \end{split} \tag{1.8f} \] Initially these formulas hold respectively for \(\Re\kappa>-1\) and \(\Re\beta>-1\). Their ratios to (1.8b) are the positive constants \[ C_{\mathbb R} \frac{\pi^{\,n(n+1)/4}}{\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(j/2)}, \qquad C_{\mathbb C} \frac{(2\pi)^{\,n(n+1)/2}}{2^n\prod_{j=1}^n\Gamma(j)}. \tag{1.8g} \]

For a general \(Q_{\mathrm{Gram}}\), substitute \(X^*X=R^*R\) and integrate the polynomial in the strictly upper entries of \(R\). Their Gaussian moments are finite, so the result is a polynomial in the \(r_j\). It is a polynomial in the squares \(r_j^2\): in the real case, changing the sign of row \(j\) of \(R\) preserves \(R^tR\) and the Gaussian law of all its upper entries; in the complex case the analogous row phase preserves \(R^*R\) and forces equal holomorphic and antiholomorphic degrees in its diagonal variable. It is thus a finite sum of monomials \(\prod_jr_j^{2m_j}\), with \(m_j\geq0\).

The ratio of each corresponding real radial moment to the base moment is \(\pi^{-m_j}((\kappa+d)/2)_{m_j}\); the complex ratio is \((2\pi)^{-m_j}(\beta+d)_{m_j}\). The rising factorial \((w)_m=w(w+1)\cdots(w+m-1)\) follows by integrating the gamma integral by parts \(m\) times. These ratios are polynomials in \(s\). Hence every Gaussian-polynomial integral is a polynomial multiple of (1.8f), and continues meromorphically by that formula. The base test attains a nonzero constant times (1.8b). Proposition 1.5 then supplies every polynomial multiple. This proves the full asserted \(\mathbb C[s]\)-ideal. \(\square\)

The one-dimensional gamma integral, its recurrence and its absence of zeros are proved in the earlier Tate's local theory at the infinite places, the section “Mellin continuation without a functional equation” and Proposition 8.2. In particular (1.8b) is zero-free, its reciprocal is entire, and it has finitely many poles in any bounded vertical strip. Indeed the gamma poles form decreasing real arithmetic progressions after a fixed complex shift. The polynomial Gaussian calculation (1.8f) will now be extended to every Schwartz test in Theorem 1.18.

3. The full Schwartz family for determinant characters

Let \(F=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\), \(G=GL_n(F)\), and \(\nu(g)=|\det g|_F\). The complex absolute value is squared: \(|z|_F=z\bar z\). Use additive measure \(dX\) equal to real Lebesgue measure, or the product of \(2\,d\Re z\,d\Im z\) on complex entries, and write \[ dg=C_F\nu(g)^{-n}dX,\qquad C_F>0. \] Let \[ \chi(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)^e|x|^a \quad(F=\mathbb R,\ e=0,1),\qquad \chi(z)=(z/|z|)^k|z|_F^a \quad(F=\mathbb C,\ k\in\mathbb Z), \] where \(a\in\mathbb C\), and put \(\pi=\chi\circ\det\). Set \[ Z_\chi(s,\Phi)=\int_G\Phi(g)\chi(\det g)\nu(g)^{s+(n-1)/2}\,dg. \] The factor already obtained from all polynomial Gaussian tests is \[ L_\chi(s)= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^n \Gamma_{\mathbb R}\!\left(s+a+e+j-\frac{n+1}{2}\right),&F=\mathbb R,\\[3pt] \displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^n \Gamma_{\mathbb C}\!\left(s+a+\frac{|k|}{2}+j-\frac{n+1}{2}\right),&F=\mathbb C. \end{cases} \tag{1.22a} \] Here \(\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(w)=\pi^{-w/2}\Gamma(w/2)\) and \(\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(w)=2(2\pi)^{-w}\Gamma(w)\).

Theorem 1.18 (the full Schwartz family for determinant characters). In every rank, \(Z_\chi(s,\Phi)\) converges absolutely for every \(\Phi\in\mathcal S(M_n(F))\) when \(\Re(s+a)>(n-1)/2\). It continues meromorphically, and \[ \mathcal D_\chi(s)(\Phi)=Z_\chi(s,\Phi)/L_\chi(s) \tag{1.22b} \] is an entire family of tempered distributions.
