Lemma 2.3ab, applied to the character-last induction \(I\), expands each of these three scalars in its two blocks \(\pi,\eta\), regardless of the three fixed ranks. Rank-one multiplicativity gives \(\gamma(\sigma\times\eta) =\gamma(\sigma_a\times\eta)\gamma(\sigma_b\times\eta)\). Cancel these nonzero factors. This gives the scalar part of (2.14q).

For \(L\), choose \(\eta\) sufficiently ramified for \(\sigma,\sigma_a,\sigma_b\), using Proposition 2.3u. The induction hypothesis and Lemma 2.3ab give polynomials of constant term one: \[ \begin{split} L(\sigma\times I) &=L(\sigma_a\times I)L(\sigma_b\times I)P,\\ L(\sigma_i\times I)&=L(\sigma_i\times\pi)P_i,\\ L(\sigma\times I)&=L(\sigma\times\pi)P_3 . \end{split} \tag{2.14r} \] Lemma 2.3aa applies because \(r<t\); it includes the equality \(r+1=t\). It forces \(P_3=1\) by the same reciprocal-unit argument as in Lemma 2.3ab. The first two identities in (2.14r) prove (2.14q) with correction \(PP_aP_b\), of constant term one.

For multiple blocks, use actual transitivity of normalized induction, proved by the two inverse maps (1.27v)–(1.27w): the section laws on the two successive flag quotients multiply to the refined modulus, and the compact-level inverse gives the actual isomorphism. Group the last block and repeat the binary statement. No assertion reordering arbitrary inducing blocks is needed by this induction. This proves the theorem. \(\square\)

Actual generic irreducible subquotients

Corollary 2.3ad. Suppose an actual generic irreducible \(\tau\) is a specified subquotient \(U/V\) of one of these inductions. Its gamma is the same block product, and its \(L\)-factor divided by the block product is a polynomial of constant term one.

Here is the proof, without assuming finite length or a classification. Twisted \(N\)-coinvariants are exact by the compact Fourier averaging proof in the mirabolic spectral filtration above. The full induction has generic coinvariant dimension one by Lemma 2.3o, and \(\tau\) has dimension one by the actual Whittaker uniqueness provider. The two exact sequences imply \(\dim U_{N,\psi}=1\) and \(V_{N,\psi}=0\). Thus the full induction's functional restricts nontrivially to \(U\) and descends to \(U/V\). Its functions give a well-defined actual inclusion of the \(\tau\) Whittaker model in the induced function model: changing a lift by a vector of \(V\) gives zero under every translate. The full scalar equation restricts to this model; its reflected functions are the same actual inverse-transpose functions. Theorem 2.3h's uniqueness and a nonzero test therefore give the same gamma.

The inclusion of actual test families gives \(I(\tau\times\pi) \subset I(\operatorname{Ind}\times\pi)\). Writing their normalized generators as \(1/P_\tau,1/P_I\), finite test-data attainment gives \(P_\tau\mid P_I\) in \(\mathbf C[X]\); the quotient has constant term one. Hence \(L(\tau\times\pi)=L(\operatorname{Ind}\times\pi)(P_I/P_\tau)\). Combine with Theorem 2.3ac to get the claimed polynomial correction. This is an assertion about the supplied actual subquotient, not the existence or ordering of an unspecified decomposition.

The spherical value generates the whole local ideal

Theorem 2.3ae. Let \(\pi,\sigma\) be actual irreducible unramified generic representations of \(GL_n(k),GL_m(k)\), with Satake tuples \(\alpha=(\alpha_i)\), \(\beta=(\beta_j)\). With conductor-zero additive character and the measure normalization preceding (2.9a), \[ L(s,\pi\times\sigma)= \prod_{i=1}^n\prod_{j=1}^m(1-\alpha_i\beta_jq^{-s})^{-1}. \tag{2.15a} \] The spherical tests in the preceding Proposition 2.1c attain the normalized generator of the whole family. This includes repeated Satake eigenvalues and every residue characteristic.

Proof. The actual proof of The Satake isomorphism for unramified groups and unramified L-factors, Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.2 supplies \(\pi\) as an actual subquotient of normalized induction of the unramified characters \(\chi_i\), with \(\chi_i(\varpi)=\alpha_i\); it also supplies the analogous \(\eta_j(\varpi)=\beta_j\) data for \(\sigma\). It does not assume those principal series are irreducible. The hypotheses here supply the actual nonzero generic functionals. The complete spherical Whittaker proof in the preceding Proposition 2.1a shows evaluation at the spherical vector is injective on those functionals, so each may be normalized to have \(W(1)=1\).

Apply Theorem 2.3ac and Corollary 2.3ad to the supplied subquotients and then to all their rank-one inducing blocks. The full local factor has the form \[ L(s,\pi\times\sigma)=D(X)P(X),\qquad P\in\mathbf C[X],\quad P(0)=1, \quad D(X)=\prod_{i,j}(1-\alpha_i\beta_jX)^{-1}. \tag{2.15b} \] The rank-one factors are the actually proved unramified Tate factors. No direct equality of inducing and constituent factors was assumed.

The actual proofs of Lemma 2.1b and Proposition 2.1c give a pure spherical test with integral exactly \(D(X)\), using \(1_{\mathcal O^n}\) in equal rank and index zero in unequal rank. Since every actual test belongs to the full fractional ideal \(L(s,\pi\times\sigma)\mathbf C[X,X^{-1}]\), (2.15b) implies \(P(X)^{-1}\in\mathbf C[X,X^{-1}]\). Its constant term one makes a polynomial Laurent unit equal to one. Hence \(P=1\), proving (2.15a) and actual generator attainment. \(\square\)

For a different additive character, Proposition 2.3i proves that the entire normalized ideal is unchanged. Thus the factor (2.15a) is independent of that choice; the corresponding changed-character spherical tests are obtained by the explicitly proved diagonal scaling and measure factors in Proposition 2.3i.

Cuspidal pairs and their unramified self-twist factors

Here Jacquet-cuspidal means that all the ordinary Jacquet modules for proper standard parabolics are zero. This is an intrinsic property of the actual representation. No compact inducing construction or classification is assumed.

For \(z\in\mathbb C^\times\), let \(\chi_z\) be the unramified character of \(k^\times\) which is one on \(\mathcal O^\times\) and takes \(\varpi\) to \(z\). Define \[ T(\pi)=\{z:\pi\otimes(\chi_z\circ\det)\simeq\pi\}, \qquad t_\pi=|T(\pi)|. \tag{2.16a} \]

Theorem 2.3af. Suppose that the actual generic irreducible admissible representation \(\pi\) of \(G_n\) is Jacquet-cuspidal. If \(m<n\), then for every actual generic irreducible admissible \(\sigma\) of \(G_m\), \[ L(s,\pi\times\sigma)=1. \tag{2.16b} \] If \(m=n\), then the factor is one unless \(\sigma\simeq\widetilde\pi\otimes(\chi_{z_0}\circ\det)\) for an unramified character. In the latter case \[ L(s,\pi\times\sigma) =\frac{1}{1-z_0^{\,t_\pi}q^{-t_\pi s}}. \tag{2.16c} \] The set \(T(\pi)\) is a finite cyclic group of order dividing \(n\). Replacing \(z_0\) by any other character giving the same \(\sigma\) leaves (2.16c) unchanged. These conclusions hold in every residue and field characteristic.

Proof of compact Whittaker support and the unequal case. In Lemma 2.3 every polynomial \(p_i\), \(i<n\), can now be taken to be one. Its recurrence assertion says directly that a fixed torus restriction of \(W\) vanishes once any of its first \(n-1\) valuations is sufficiently large, with thresholds independent of the other coordinates. The lower support bounds from (2.9h) remain in force. There are only finitely many \(K_n\)-translates at the right level of \(W\). Their thresholds can consequently be combined. In Iwasawa ratio coordinates all the first \(n-1\) valuations are in finite intervals; the unit and compact coordinates form compact sets. Thus \[ \operatorname{supp}W \text{ is compact modulo }N_n Z_n. \tag{2.16d} \] This statement is about the support of the actual function, not the support of a matrix coefficient. When \(m<n\), the argument of (2.9n), including its final \(i=m\) coordinate, has no tail: \(p_{\pi,i}=1\) for every \(i\le m\). Its integrals are Laurent polynomials. Hence their ideal is contained in \(R\) and contains one by Proposition 2.3d, proving (2.16b).

Possible equal-rank poles and their invariant residues. In the equal case only the central denominator survives: \[ \mathcal I_{\pi,\sigma} \subset\frac{1}{1-\omega_\pi(\varpi) \omega_\sigma(\varpi)X^n}\,R. \tag{2.16e} \] It follows that the normalized reciprocal polynomial divides the displayed denominator. All its possible roots are nonzero and simple. Fix such a root \(X_0=q^{-s_0}\), choosing one complex \(s_0\). We show that any nonzero residue forces \[ \sigma\simeq\widetilde\pi\otimes|\det|^{-s_0}. \tag{2.16f} \]

Choose a smooth compact function \(\Phi\) with \(\Phi(0)=1\). Because of (2.16d), the noncentral ratio coordinates in the equal-rank integral lie in fixed compact sets. If a test \(\Phi_1\) is zero at zero, local constancy makes it zero on a neighbourhood of zero. The central coordinate is then bounded above and below on the support of \(W(g)W'(g)\Phi_1(e_ng)\). This integral has finitely many central valuation terms, and no residue at \(X_0\). Consequently the residue for an arbitrary test is \(\Phi_1(0)\) times the residue for the chosen \(\Phi\).

Let \(B_{s_0}(W,W')\) denote this residue, in the coordinate \(s\). The equivariance of the original integral under simultaneous right translation is \[ Z_s(R(h)W,R(h)W',R(h)\Phi) =|\det h|^{-s} Z_s(W,W',\Phi). \] The transformed test still has value one at zero. Taking residues gives \[ B_{s_0}(R(h)W,R(h)W') =|\det h|^{-s_0}B_{s_0}(W,W'). \tag{2.16g} \] For a fixed vector in \(\pi\), its functional on \(\sigma\) is smooth: a compact open group fixing that vector fixes the functional, since the norm character is one on that group. Thus a nonzero form (2.16g) gives a nonzero map \(\pi\to\widetilde\sigma\otimes|\det|^{-s_0}\). The smooth dual of an irreducible admissible module is irreducible. Here is the finite-dimensional argument, including its required extension. Compact-fixed duality identifies the \(J\)-fixed smooth dual with \((V^J)^*\), and identifies the double smooth dual with \(V\), for every compact open \(J\). If \(A\) is a nonzero submodule of the smooth dual, it is admissible. Every smooth functional on \(A\) extends to the ambient smooth dual: extend its restriction from \(A^J\) to the ambient \(J\)-fixed space, then compose with \(e_J\). Restriction is therefore a surjection \(V\to\widetilde A\) with nonzero target. Irreducibility makes it an isomorphism. At every \(J\), finite-dimensional duality gives \(\dim A^J=\dim\widetilde V^J\); hence \(A=\widetilde V\). This proves the assertion, and irreducibility turns the nonzero map into an isomorphism. Dualizing yields (2.16f). Since \(|\varpi|^{-s_0}=q^{s_0}=X_0^{-1}\), the character in (2.16f) is unramified with parameter \(X_0^{-1}\).

A genuine pole for a cuspidal dual pair. First suppose that \(\omega_\pi\) is unitary. The preceding matrix theory proves compactness modulo \(Z_n\) of all its smooth coefficients: Lemma 1.20a. This gives a unitary realization without a classification theorem. Indeed choose a nonzero smooth dual vector \(\ell\) and put \[ (v,w)=\int_{Z_n\backslash G_n} \ell(\pi(g)v)\overline{\ell(\pi(g)w)}\,dg. \tag{2.16h} \] Compact coefficient support makes this integral finite. Its integrand descends because the central character is unitary, and right invariance of Haar measure makes the form invariant. It is positive definite: if \(v\ne0\), irreducibility implies that the translates of \(v\) span the module, so some translate is detected by \(\ell\); local constancy then gives a positive integral. The completion is a unitary representation on which the given smooth module is embedded. The pairing sends the conjugate module into the smooth dual, because a vector fixed by a compact group defines a dual functional fixed by that same group. This map is nonzero and equivariant; irreducibility and compact-fixed duality make it an isomorphism. Therefore \(\overline W\) is an actual Whittaker function of \(\widetilde\pi\), with character \(\psi_n^{-1}\).

Take nonzero \(W\), \(W'=\overline W\), and a nonnegative lattice indicator \(\Phi\) which is one near zero. In the equal-rank Iwasawa formula the first \(n-1\) ratio coordinates are confined to the compact set of (2.16d). Their integration against \(|W|^2\) is finite and positive. For all sufficiently large central valuations \(\ell\), uniformly over these compact coordinates, \(\Phi(e_ng)=1\). The central characters in \(W\overline W\) cancel. Thus the tail of the integral is a transverse Laurent polynomial \(C(X)\), with \(C(1)>0\), times \[ \sum_{\ell\ge L}X^{n\ell} =\frac{X^{nL}}{1-X^n}. \tag{2.16i} \] The transverse polynomial comes from the finitely many noncentral determinant valuations; at \(s=0\) its integral is the positive integral of \(|W|^2\). At \(X=1\) the numerator of this tail has positive value. The remaining finitely many central terms cannot cancel its pole. Hence \(L(s,\pi\times\widetilde\pi)\) has a pole at \(X=1\).

For general \(\omega_\pi\), its absolute value on \(k^\times\) is \(|a|^c\) for one real \(c\). This follows directly by compactness of \(\mathcal O^\times\) and the valuation decomposition of \(k^\times\). Twisting \(\pi\) by \(|\det|^{-c/n}\) makes its central character unitary, and preserves its zero Jacquet modules. Its contragredient is twisted by the inverse norm character. Formula (2.9bh) leaves their paired factor unchanged. This proves the pole at \(X=1\) for every \(\pi,\widetilde\pi\).

All roots and the exact normalized factor. The set \(T(\pi)\) is a subgroup of \(\mathbb C^\times\). Central characters give \(z^n=1\) for every \(z\in T(\pi)\), so it is a subgroup of the \(n\)-th roots of unity. To check cyclicity and the precise order, write those roots as \(\exp(2\pi i j/n)\). The preimage of \(T(\pi)\) in \(\mathbf Z\) is an additive subgroup containing \(n\mathbf Z\). Its least positive element \(d\) generates it: division with remainder would otherwise give a smaller positive element. Thus \(d\mid n\), its order is \(t_\pi=n/d\), and its elements are exactly the \(t_\pi\)-th roots of unity. Each unramified \(\chi_z\) is a complex norm power. Twisting one factor and using (2.9bh) takes the genuine pole at \(X=1\) to \(X=z^{-1}\). If \(z\in T(\pi)\), the twisted dual representation is isomorphic to the original dual, so these are genuine poles of the same dual-pair factor. Conversely (2.16f) shows that every pole of the dual pair has this form with \(z\in T(\pi)\). Their product is \[ \prod_{z\in T(\pi)}(1-zX)=1-X^{t_\pi}. \] The polynomial normalization in Proposition 2.3d and simplicity from (2.16e) consequently give \(L(s,\pi\times\widetilde\pi) =(1-X^{t_\pi})^{-1}\). Twisting \(\sigma\) by \(\chi_{z_0}\) replaces \(X\) by \(z_0X\), proving (2.16c). The possible parameters \(z_0\) form a coset of \(T(\pi)\), so \(z_0^{t_\pi}\) is independent of the choice. If no such parameter exists, (2.16f) rules out every root of the normalized reciprocal polynomial; it is therefore one. \(\square\)

Coefficient-tempered factors and their pole half-plane

Call an actual irreducible admissible representation coefficient-tempered if its central character is unitary and every smooth matrix coefficient belongs to \(L^{2+\epsilon}(Z_r\backslash G_r)\) for every \(\epsilon>0\). This is the coefficient condition needed below. Neither a classification of tempered representations nor their genericity is inferred from it.

Lemma 2.3ag. For any supplied coefficient-tempered generic irreducibles \(\rho,\tau\), their entire Rankin--Selberg generators and those of their contragredients are holomorphic on \(\operatorname{Re}s>0\).

We prove the necessary Jacquet spectral estimate directly. Put \(a_i=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi I_i,I_{r-i})\) and \(J_d=1+\varpi^dM_r(\mathcal O)\), \(d\ge1\). Here \(J_d^+,J_d^0,J_d^-\) denote the upper-triangular, diagonal and lower-triangular parts. Elimination at unit pivots gives \(J_d=J_d^+J_d^0J_d^-\). For dominant diagonal \(a,b\), \(aJ_d^+a^{-1}\subset J_d^+\), \(b^{-1}J_d^-b\subset J_d^-\), and both commute with \(J_d^0\). Thus \(J_daJ_dbJ_d=J_dabJ_d\). The convolution of the two bi-\(J_d\)-invariant double-coset probability measures is the bi-\(J_d\)-invariant probability measure of \(J_dabJ_d\): its support is that double coset, and averaging over the transitive compact \(J_d\times J_d\) action proves uniqueness. Consequently, on \(E=V^{J_d}\), \[ T_i^h=e_{J_d}\rho(a_i^h)e_{J_d},\qquad T_i=e_{J_d}\rho(a_i)e_{J_d}. \tag{2.17a} \]

We verify the compact Jacquet lift used here rather than assume a tempered Jacquet criterion. For the upper radical \(U_i\), its opposite, and \(M_i\), block elimination gives the probability-average identity \(e_{J_d}=e_{J_d\cap U_i}e_{J_d\cap M_i}e_{J_d\cap U_i^-}\). The identity follows already in every finite congruence quotient by its unique upper-diagonal-lower block coordinates. If \(p:V\to V_{U_i}\) is the ordinary quotient, then \(E'=p(V^{J_d})\) is finite-dimensional. For \(v\in V^{J_d}\), \(\rho(a_i)v\) remains fixed by \(J_d\cap M_i\) and \(J_d\cap U_i^-\), so \(p(e_{J_d}\rho(a_i)v)=a_i p(v)\). Hence \(a_iE'\subset E'\); the action of \(a_i\) on the quotient is invertible, and finite dimension gives \(a_iE'=E'\). For \(y\in(V_{U_i})^{J_d\cap M_i}\), lift and average its lift over \(J_d\cap M_i\). A large positive power of \(a_i\) makes this lift fixed by \(J_d\cap U_i^-\): indeed \(a_i^{-h}U_i^-a_i^h\) contracts the lower entries into any prescribed stabilizer. Averaging over \(J_d\) therefore puts \(a_i^hy\) in \(E'\). Since \(a_i^{-h}E'=E'\), \(y\in E'\). Thus \[ p(V^{J_d})=(V_{U_i})^{J_d\cap M_i},\qquad pT_i=a_i p. \tag{2.17b} \] This proves admissibility of the Jacquet quotient as well. Its nonzero \(a_i\)-eigenvalues occur among the \(T_i\)-eigenvalues.

Let \(T_iv=\alpha v\), \(\alpha\ne0\), and choose a \(J_d\)-fixed smooth dual vector \(\ell\) with \(\ell(v)=1\). Extend a linear functional on the finite space \(V^{J_d}\) and compose with \(e_{J_d}\) to obtain such \(\ell\). The coefficient \(\ell(\rho(g)v)\) is exactly \(\alpha^h\) on \(J_da_i^hJ_d\), by (2.17a). For \(h\ge1\) these double cosets modulo the center are disjoint, because the gap between their two elementary-divisor levels is \(h\). Their quotient volumes are \(C_dq^{i(r-i)h}\), \(C_d>0\). To check this exact growth, the group volume is \(\operatorname{vol}(J_d)[J_d:J_d\cap a_i^hJ_da_i^{-h}]\). In block-elimination coordinates the intersection imposes exactly \(h\) extra powers of \(\varpi\) in its \(i(r-i)\) upper entries; the finite-coordinate index is \(q^{i(r-i)h}\). A scalar preserving the double coset has valuation zero and is one modulo \(\varpi^d\), by comparison of its two diagonal blocks. The central-fibre volume is therefore constant in \(h\). The term \(h=0\) is irrelevant to convergence. Integrability gives \[ \sum_{h\ge1}q^{i(r-i)h}|\alpha|^{(2+\epsilon)h}<\infty,\qquad |\alpha|\le q^{-i(r-i)/2}. \tag{2.17c} \]

For completeness the polynomial annihilator is global in the vector. One nonzero vector generates an irreducible representation. Iwasawa \(G_r=P_iK_r\) and its finite compact orbit therefore give finitely many \(M_i\)-generators of \(V_{U_i}\). Choose \(d\) fixing them. The characteristic polynomial of \(a_i\) on \((V_{U_i})^{J_d\cap M_i}\) has nonzero constant term and annihilates the entire Jacquet module, since \(a_i\) is central in \(M_i\). By (2.17b)--(2.17c), every root has the bound in (2.17c). The actual finite expression of this annihilation on a vector, \(\sum_hc_h\rho(a_i)^hv=\sum_l(\rho(u_l)-1)v_l\), gives the Whittaker recurrence whenever the ratio coordinate \(t_i\) has sufficiently large valuation: its characters are \(\psi(t_i(u_l)_{i,i+1})=1\). The threshold is independent of all other ratio coordinates. Right invariance gives a lower bound for each valuation. Solving a finite recurrence by its companion matrix gives finite sums of exponential-polynomial terms; finite Jordan blocks supply a uniform finite polynomial degree. Applying the recurrences one coordinate at a time gives the multivariable bound. This is the preceding uniform-recurrence argument; it proves the required Whittaker bound.

In equal ranks the Iwasawa density contributes \(q^{i(r-i)h}\), exactly cancelling the two root bounds \(q^{-i(r-i)h/2}\). The central characters have modulus one. In unequal ranks \(n>m\), for \(i<m\) the exponent after cancellation is \[ i(m-i)+i(n-m)/2-i(n-i)/2-i(m-i)/2=0, \] and for \(i=m\) it is \(m(n-m)/2-m(n-m)/2=0\). The embedded last identity coordinate bounds all ratio valuations below. The rectangular variables range through a fixed compact set: bottom-row wedges bound every rectangular entry by the uniformly bounded Iwasawa diagonal products, as in Proposition 2.3b. Smoothness then reduces their integral to finitely many index-zero right translates. All absolute-value integrals are thus bounded by finite sums of \[ \sum_{h_1,\ldots,h_d\ge0} \prod_i(1+h_i)^A q^{-i\operatorname{Re}(s)h_i}. \tag{2.17d} \] The geometric sums converge locally uniformly for \(\operatorname{Re}s>0\); derivatives in \(s\) insert only polynomial weights. Every integral is holomorphic there. Finite actual test-sum attainment makes the generator holomorphic there too. The actual inverse-transpose identification of the smooth dual preserves coefficient absolute-value integrability and the unitary central character, proving the dual assertion. \(\square\)

Thus for supplied \(\rho\nu^u,\tau\nu^v\), a pole can occur only when \(\operatorname{Re}(s+u+v)\le0\). This conclusion has a local proof; genericity, construction and classification of arbitrary tempered representations are separate matters.

A finite Fourier cutoff in every rectangular rank

Lemma 2.3ah. If \(W\) is any right-smooth Whittaker function on \(G_r\) and \(b<t<r\), there is a Whittaker vector \(W^0\) and compact-open neighbourhoods of zero for every lower entry and of one for every diagonal entry, such that for \[ q_t=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ x&h\end{pmatrix},\quad A\in G_b,\ x\in M_{t-b,b},\ h\in B^-_{t-b}, \] \[ W^0(\operatorname{diag}(q_t,I_{r-t})) =W(\operatorname{diag}(A,I_{r-b}))B(x,h), \tag{2.17e} \] where \(B\) is the product of the indicated indicators. Every neighbourhood can be chosen arbitrarily small.

Here is an explicit induction, including the cutoff left unspecified in JPSS §9.2. Suppose that the first \(u\) active coordinates have already been treated, with \(b\le u<t\). For a matrix \(Q\in G_{u+1}\), set \(q=\operatorname{diag}(Q,I)\) and write its last row as \(\beta\in k^{u+1}\). For \(y\in k^{u+1}\), put \(v(y)=1+\sum_{i\le u+1}y_iE_{i,u+2}\). The next identity coordinate exists because \(u+1\le t<r\). Direct multiplication gives \[ qv(y)=v(Qy)q,\qquad W_{\rm old}(qv(y))=\psi(\beta y)W_{\rm old}(q). \tag{2.17f} \] Only the simple root \((u+1,u+2)\) contributes to the character. Take \(p(\beta)\) to be the indicator of \(L^u\times S\), where \(L\) is small additive compact open and \(S\subset1+\mathfrak p^d\) is a small multiplicative unit neighbourhood. Let \(\xi\) be its inverse Fourier weight for the positive pairing in (2.17f). Define \(W_{\rm new}(g)=\int\xi(y)W_{\rm old}(gv(y))\,dy\). This is an actual vector: a Schwartz weight is compactly supported, and smoothness makes the averaging a finite sum of representation vectors. Fourier inversion gives \(W_{\rm new}(q)=p(\beta)W_{\rm old}(q)\).

If \(Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A_u&0\\z&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), then \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(A_u,1) \left(\begin{smallmatrix}I_u&0\\z&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Choose \(L,S\) so that the latter matrix embedded in \(G_r\) belongs to the right stabilizer of \(W_{\rm old}\). On the support of \(p\), its value is therefore \(W_{\rm old}(\operatorname{diag}(A_u,I))\); outside that support the new value is zero. This adds exactly one lower row. Induction from \(u=b\) through \(t-1\) proves (2.17e). Choosing every neighbourhood also inside any other fixed right stabilizer is allowed. There is no noncompact convergence or parameter continuation in this construction. The signs and unit Jacobians remain valid in characteristic two. \(\square\)

Trailing-block test ideals in every pair of ranks

Theorem 2.3ai. For supplied actual generic inducing blocks \(\rho_a,\tau_b\), let \(I=\operatorname{Ind}_{P_{a,b}}^{G_r}(\rho\otimes\tau)\), \(r=a+b\). For every fixed actual generic model \(\sigma_t\) in Lemma 2.3t's scope, \[ \mathcal I(\tau\times\sigma)\subset \mathcal I(I\times\sigma). \tag{2.17g} \] This statement also applies to a composite leading block, by actual transitivity of induction. It does not reorder inducing data.

Lemma 2.3o's full proof supplies, for every \(V\in\mathcal W(\tau)\) and \(\Phi\in\mathcal S(k^b)\), an actual vector with \[ W(\operatorname{diag}(A,I_a)) =V(A)\Phi(e_bA)\nu(A)^{a/2}. \tag{2.17h} \] To recall its exact test construction, take the upper open-cell section \(f(wu(Y))=\xi(Y)v_\rho\otimes v_\tau\), \(Y\in M_{b,a}\), \(\lambda_\rho(v_\rho)=1\). Its generic functional is \(\int(\lambda_\rho\otimes\lambda_\tau)f(wu(Y)) \psi(-Y_{b1})\,dY\). The identity \(wu(Y)\operatorname{diag}(A,I_a) =\operatorname{diag}(I_a,A)wu(A^{-1}Y)\) contributes \(\nu(A)^{-a/2}\); changing its \(a\) columns gives \(\nu(A)^a\). Choose the first-column Fourier weight of \(\Phi\) and a remaining-column Schwartz weight of integral one. Fourier inversion gives precisely (2.17h). The finite orbit filtration and exact twisted coinvariants in Lemma 2.3o identify this functional with the full induction's functional; no arbitrary-section Jacquet integral convergence is assumed.

If \(t=b\), (2.17h) cancels the unequal-rank shift \(a/2\) and includes every equal-rank old test, with its freely specified \(\Phi\). If \(t<b\), choose \(\Phi(e_b)=1\); the last row of \(\operatorname{diag}(g_t,I_{b-t})\) is \(e_b\), and the same cancellation includes every index-zero old test. Index independence in Corollary 2.3f proves the required ideal inclusion.

Suppose \(b<t<r\), and put \(c=t-b\). Start from an old index-zero test for \(\sigma_t\times\tau_b\). For this old larger-rank pair, choose base character \(\psi^{-1}\): \(\sigma_t\) uses \(\psi^{-1}\) and \(\tau_b\) uses \(\psi\), exactly matching the new \(I_r,\psi\) / \(\sigma_t,\psi^{-1}\) integral. Proposition 2.3i and Corollary 2.3j identify this old whole ideal with the original base-character ideal, so the choice changes no normalized \(L\)-factor. The support of \(V_\sigma(\operatorname{diag}(A,I_c))\) has \(e_bA\) in a fixed compact set. Indeed write \(A=nak\); finitely many compact translates give one Whittaker ratio bound, while the retained identity coordinates make the last large-rank diagonal absolute value one. The bottom-row wedge bounds every entry of \(e_bA\). Choose \(\Phi=1\) on that compact set in (2.17h), and apply Lemma 2.3ah. Choose its neighbourhoods so small that \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I_b&0\\x&h\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) fixes \(V_\sigma\). The values in (2.17e) then multiply exactly the old two Whittaker functions.

We give the quotient measure, not a suppressed Iwasawa constant. On the full-measure upper-lower Gauss chart of \(G_t\), quotient representatives are \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&0\\x&h\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(A\in N_b\backslash G_b\), \(h\in B_c^-\). If \(\alpha_j=\prod_{l=1}^j(1-q^{-l})\), their quotient measure is \[ C_{b,c}\nu(A)^{-c} \prod_{j=1}^c|h_{jj}|^{j-c}\, dA\,dx\prod_jd^\times h_{jj}\prod_{i>j}dh_{ij}, \quad C_{b,c}=\frac{\alpha_b(1-q^{-1})^c}{\alpha_t}. \tag{2.17i} \] For verification, write \(g=n(y) \left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&0\\x&H\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The additive Jacobian of \(y\mapsto yH\) is \(\nu(H)^b\). Use group density \(\alpha_t^{-1}|\det g|^{-t}d_{\rm add}g\) and \(d_{\rm add}A=\alpha_b\nu(A)^b\,dA\). Next write \(H=n_ch\). Elimination in the last column gives the additive Jacobian \(\prod_j|h_{jj}|^{j-1}\): the last pivot contributes \(|h_{cc}|^{c-1}\), and induction gives the earlier pivots. Replacing each additive diagonal measure by \((1-q^{-1})|h_{jj}|d^\times h_{jj}\) gives (2.17i). The upper coordinates being divided out have self-dual additive measure. The complement is a zero set of nonzero pivot polynomials and has measure zero: induction on the number of variables and Fubini reduce that assertion to the finite set of roots of a nonzero one-variable polynomial. Thus this chart computes the whole integral, not only a truncated test.

On the cutoff support every \(|h_{jj}|=1\), and the determinant power of \(A\) in the new index-zero integral is \[ s-(r-t)/2+a/2-c=s-(t-b)/2. \tag{2.17j} \] This is exactly the old exponent. The \(x,h\) integral is a positive constant independent of \(s,A\); scale \(W^0\) by its reciprocal, including \(C_{b,c}\), to make the new test equal the old test. The equality is first an absolutely convergent right half-plane equality, by Proposition 2.3b and Lemma 2.3t, and hence is an equality of the rational functions. This proves (2.17g) when \(t<r\).

Finally let \(t\ge r\). Prepend \(t+1-r\) sufficiently ramified characters to \(I\), obtaining \(I^+\) of rank \(t+1\) whose last block is still \(\tau\). For each character \(\eta\), Proposition 2.3u proves the entire factor \(L(\eta\times\sigma)=1\). The case just proved inserts \(\mathcal I(\tau\times\sigma)\) in \(\mathcal I(I^+\times\sigma)\). Theorem 2.3ac and actual transitivity give \(L(I^+\times\sigma)=L(I\times\sigma)A(X)\), with \(A\in\mathbf C[X]\), \(A(0)=1\). Consequently \[ \mathcal I(I^+\times\sigma) =L(I\times\sigma)A\mathscr R \subset L(I\times\sigma)\mathscr R . \] This proves (2.17g) also at equality and above. No equality of the auxiliary or inducing correction was needed. \(\square\)

Exact products for supplied ordered essentially tempered data

Theorem 2.3aj. Let \[ I=\tau_1\times\cdots\times\tau_m,\quad J=\sigma_1\times\cdots\times\sigma_n,\quad \tau_i=\tau_{i,0}\nu^{u_i},\ \sigma_j=\sigma_{j,0}\nu^{v_j}, \tag{2.17k} \] where the zero-index representations are supplied actual generic coefficient-tempered irreducibles, the real exponents satisfy \(u_1\ge\cdots\ge u_m\), \(v_1\ge\cdots\ge v_n\), and the products are upper normalized inductions. Then the entire faithful Whittaker-model generators satisfy \[ L(s,I\times J)= \prod_{i,j}L(s+u_i+v_j,\tau_{i,0}\times\sigma_{j,0}). \tag{2.17l} \] The exact polynomial correction relative to this product is one. Repeated exponents and repeated representations are included.

Put \(D=\prod_{i,j}L(s,\tau_i\times\sigma_j)\). Theorem 2.3ac gives \(L(I\times J)=D P(X)\), \(P(0)=1\). For the reversed dual inducing data, write \(I^{\mathrm{ref}}\) and \(J^{\mathrm{ref}}\). These denote the full inducing Whittaker models under inverse-transpose reflection, as constructed in the partial-transform comparison (2.11s)–(2.11u) and the reflected rectangular comparison (2.12p)–(2.12r); this does not identify the smooth dual of a reducible full induction. Write \[ L(1-s,I^{\mathrm{ref}}\times J^{\mathrm{ref}}) =D^\vee(1-s)P^\vee(q^{-1}X^{-1}). \] Gamma multiplicativity and the Laurent-unit epsilons give \[ \frac{P^\vee(q^{-1}X^{-1})}{P(X)} =\frac{\prod_{i,j}\epsilon_{ij}}{\epsilon_{I,J}} \in\mathscr R^\times. \tag{2.17m} \] Thus these two corrections have exactly the same nonzero zeros, with the same multiplicities. This follows from actual entire families; a scalar gamma identity alone would not have supplied the corrections.

Induct on \(m+n\), starting with \(m=n=1\). If \(m,n>1\), drop the first block of \(J\) using Theorem 2.3ai. The shorter ordered equality and inclusion say \[ \prod_{i,j\ge2}L_{ij}=D P Q,\quad Q\in\mathscr R. \] Therefore \(P Q\prod_i L_{i1}=1\): every zero of \(P\) is a pole of some \(L_{i1}\), including its multiplicity in the product. Apply Theorem 2.3ai to the reversed dual \(I^{\mathrm{ref}}\), dropping its first block \(\tau_m^\vee\). The shorter dual ordered equality and (2.17m) say that the same zero is a pole of some \(L(1-s,\tau_m^\vee\times\sigma_j^\vee)\). Choose \(s_0\) with \(q^{-s_0}=X_0\). By Lemma 2.3ag these two poles require \[ \operatorname{Re}s_0+u_i+v_1\le0,\qquad 1-\operatorname{Re}s_0-u_m-v_j\le0. \] Their sum is \(1+(u_i-u_m)+(v_1-v_j)\le0\), contradicting the order.

If \(n=1,m>1\), drop the first \(I\)-block in the direct and reversed dual inductions. The corresponding inequality is \(1+u_1-u_m\le0\). If \(m=1,n>1\), do this with \(J\) and obtain \(1+v_1-v_n\le0\). Each is impossible. For completeness, the root existence used here has an elementary local proof. A nonconstant complex polynomial \(p\) satisfies \(|p(z)|\to\infty\) as \(|z|\to\infty\), by comparison with its leading term; hence its absolute value attains a minimum. If the minimum at \(z_0\) were nonzero, write \(p(z_0+w)=p(z_0)+c_d w^d+O(|w|^{d+1})\), with the first nonzero coefficient \(c_d\). Choose the magnitude and angle of \(w\) so that \(c_dw^d=-\varepsilon p(z_0)\). The remaining finite polynomial terms are \(O(\varepsilon^{1+1/d})\), so for sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\) the absolute value decreases, a contradiction. Thus \(p\) has a root. In the present case \(P(0)=1\), so every such root is nonzero.

Therefore \(P=1\). This proves (2.17l). \(\square\)

This proves the factor identity for each actual ordered datum. Theorem 2.3cb below constructs the datum and whole quotient map for every irreducible admissible representation; generic targets are transferred by the next lemma.

Transfer through an actual generic quotient map

Lemma 2.3ak. Suppose \(q\colon I\twoheadrightarrow\pi\) is an actual surjective equivariant map and \(\pi\) is generic irreducible. Then \(\mathcal W(I)=\mathcal W(\pi)\) as actual function spaces, after a nonzero functional rescaling.

Indeed the nonzero functional \(\lambda_\pi q\) spans the one-dimensional generic functional space of \(I\), by Lemma 2.3o and Lemma 2.3t. For any \(f\in I\), \(\lambda_I(R(g)f)=c\lambda_\pi(\pi(g)qf)\). Surjectivity supplies every \(\pi\)-vector, and every \(I\)-vector gives one, proving equality of spaces in both directions. Consequently all the actual test families, their reflected functions, ideals and normalized factors are equal. No finite length, closed image, generic standard-module irreducibility or classification is used. \(\square\)

Applying this twice transfers (2.17l) to every supplied pair of generic surjective quotients of the ordered inductions. An arbitrary supplied subquotient is covered only by Corollary 2.3ad's inclusion and polynomial correction. A subquotient must not be renamed a quotient without an actual surjection.

Supplied segment factors and their polynomial correction

There is also an exact constituent computation that does not assume a Weil--Deligne factor identity. Let \(\rho_d,\zeta_e\) be supplied actual generic Jacquet-cuspidal irreducibles with unitary central characters. Suppose \(D_\ell(\rho)\) and \(D_k(\zeta)\) are supplied actual generic coefficient-tempered irreducible subquotients of the respective normalized inductions of \[ \rho\nu^{-(\ell-1)/2},\ldots,\rho\nu^{(\ell-1)/2}, \quad \zeta\nu^{-(k-1)/2},\ldots,\zeta\nu^{(k-1)/2}. \tag{2.17n} \] Theorems 2.3bd and 2.3bj below construct these subquotients and identify them as the square-integrable segment blocks. This factor computation uses their actual coefficient-tempered hypothesis.

Theorem 2.3al. For these actual subquotients, \[ L(s,D_\ell(\rho)\times D_k(\zeta)) =\prod_{h=0}^{\min(\ell,k)-1} L(s+(\ell+k-2)/2-h,\rho\times\zeta). \tag{2.17o} \] It is one unless \(d=e\) and \(\zeta\simeq\rho^\vee\otimes(\chi_z\circ\det)\). In the latter case, \(t=|T(\rho)|\) and the explicit value is \[ \prod_{h=0}^{\min(\ell,k)-1} \left(1-z^tq^{-t((\ell+k-2)/2-h)}X^t\right)^{-1}. \tag{2.17p} \] Here \(|z|=1\): comparison of the unitary central characters gives \(|z|^d=1\). Formula (2.17p) includes every ramified cuspidal and unramified self-twist group, and all field characteristics.

The proof of the cuspidal child factor is Theorem 2.3af, with its actual compact Whittaker support, equivariant-residue and positive dual-pair pole proofs; it is not imported from LLC. Corollary 2.3ad gives the full gamma product over the \(\ell k\) pairs in (2.17n), and a direct polynomial correction. If every child factor is one, the subquotient factor is a polynomial with constant term one and also the reciprocal of a polynomial with constant term one; hence it is one.

In the remaining case put \(A=(\ell+k-2)/2\), and let \(C(w)\) count pairs \(0\le a<\ell,0\le b<k\) with \(w=-A+a+b\). The entire cuspidal product denominator has factors \[ \prod_w(1-z^tq^{-tw}X^t)^{C(w)}. \tag{2.17q} \] The reflected dual denominator has its roots on the same unit phases at radii \(q^{w-1}\), whereas (2.17q) has radii \(q^w\). Thus the gamma divisor has zero multiplicity \(C(w)-C(w+1)\) at radius \(q^w\), interpreted negatively for a pole. Different real \(w\)'s have different radii, so no roots were mistakenly merged. Direct coefficient-tempered factors have no denominator roots with \(|X|<1\), by Lemma 2.3ag; reflected dual factors have no denominator roots with \(|X|>q^{-1}\). These two permitted regions are disjoint. Consequently on \(|X|\ge1\), every gamma zero must be a direct denominator root with the same multiplicity, and every such root is visible in gamma. There are no other direct roots.

Assume \(\ell\le k\). Counting the intervals \([0,\ell-1]\cap[w+A-k+1,w+A]\) shows \[ C(w)-C(w+1)=1 \quad\text{for }w=A,A-1,\ldots,A-\ell+1, \] is zero at all other nonnegative grid points, and is negative only at the reflected left tail. The same statement with \(\min(\ell,k)\) holds after interchanging the lengths. This determines the normalized direct reciprocal polynomial uniquely and gives (2.17o)--(2.17p).

In particular, relative to the full \(\ell k\) cuspidal product, the correction really is the possibly nonconstant polynomial \[ P_{\ell,k}(X)= \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{a=0}^{\ell-1}\prod_{b=0}^{k-1} \left(1-z^tq^{-t(-A+a+b)}X^t\right)} {\displaystyle\prod_{h=0}^{\min(\ell,k)-1} \left(1-z^tq^{-t(A-h)}X^t\right)}. \tag{2.17r} \] The denominator divides the numerator since each weight \(A-h\) occurs there; \(P_{\ell,k}(0)=1\). This computation preserves Corollary 2.3ad's correction. It sets it equal to one only for Theorem 2.3aj's ordered essentially tempered blocks, not for their individual cuspidal strings. For \(\ell=k=2,t=1,z=1\), (2.17r) is \((1-qX)(1-X)\), and (2.17p) is \(((1-q^{-1}X)(1-X))^{-1}\). \(\square\)

Twisting the two supplied segment subquotients by \(\nu^u,\nu^v\) replaces \(s\) by \(s+u+v\) in these exact formulas. Theorem 2.3aj then computes the product for any supplied ordered induction built from such blocks, and Lemma 2.3ak transfers it to its actual generic surjective quotient. The finite ideal construction guarantees finite actual test-sum attainment of each normalized factor.

Compact Jacquet kernels and exact coefficient integrability

Throughout the following finite-place arguments, \(k\) has either characteristic, \(G_n=GL_n(k)\), \(K_n=GL_n(\mathcal O)\), \(\nu=|\det|\), and \(Z_n=k^\times I_n\). The representations are actual complex smooth admissible modules. Compact probability averages, the congruence semigroup and Cartan volumes are proved in Proposition 1.3; compact Jacquet lifting is Lemma 1.17a. The arguments here derive the coefficient criteria directly from those finite operators.

For \(1\le i<n\) set \[ a_i=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi I_i,I_{n-i}),\quad J_d=1+\varpi^dM_n(\mathcal O),\quad E_d=V^{J_d}, \quad T_i=e_{J_d}\pi(a_i)e_{J_d}|_{E_d}. \tag{2.18a} \] Here \(e_C\) denotes probability averaging on a compact group \(C\). Let \(U_i\) be the upper radical of the parabolic of type \((i,n-i)\), \(M_i\) its Levi, \(U_i^-\) its opposite, and let \(p_i:V\to V_{U_i}\) be the unnormalized quotient.

Lemma 2.3am. The compact map \[ p_i:E_d\twoheadrightarrow F_{i,d}=(V_{U_i})^{J_d\cap M_i} \tag{2.18b} \] intertwines \(T_i\) with \(a_i\), and its kernel is \(T_i\)-nilpotent. The nonzero eigenvalues of \(T_i\), with algebraic multiplicities, are exactly the eigenvalues of \(a_i\) on \(F_{i,d}\).

Proof. Block elimination at unit pivots gives the unique upper–diagonal–lower factorization \[ J_d=(J_d\cap U_i)(J_d\cap M_i)(J_d\cap U_i^-), \quad e_{J_d}=e_{J_d\cap U_i}e_{J_d\cap M_i}e_{J_d\cap U_i^-}. \tag{2.18c} \] The second identity follows by the bijection of these coordinate sets in every finite congruence quotient; counting their probabilities and using smoothness proves the operator identity. The complete preceding compact lift proves (2.18b) and \(p_iT_i=a_ip_i\). For clarity, its finite-dimensional image is stable under \(a_i\), hence also \(a_i^{-1}\); a sufficiently large positive power of \(a_i\) makes a chosen Levi-fixed lift opposite-fixed, after which (2.18c) places its Jacquet class in that image.

The congruence semigroup gives \[ T_i^h=e_{J_d}\pi(a_i^h)e_{J_d}|_{E_d}\quad(h\ge0). \tag{2.18d} \] Indeed positive diagonal multiplication contracts the upper congruence group on the left and the lower one on the right, so \(J_daJ_dbJ_d=J_dabJ_d\). The bi-\(J_d\) probability measures on these double cosets multiply accordingly: a compact transitive \(J_d\times J_d\) action has exactly one invariant probability measure.

Let \(B=\ker(p_i|_{E_d})\). It is \(T_i\)-stable and finite-dimensional. Each of its basis vectors has a finite actual expression \[ v=\sum_\alpha(\pi(u_\alpha)-1)w_\alpha,\qquad u_\alpha\in U_i. \tag{2.18e} \] Choose one compact additive subgroup \(C\subset U_i\) containing every \(u_\alpha\) needed for that basis. Its probability average kills every basis vector by translation invariance. Every larger compact subgroup also kills them.

For \(v\in B\), the conjugate factorization of (2.18c) gives \[ \begin{split} e_{J_d}\pi(a_i^h)v &=\pi(a_i^h)e_{a_i^{-h}J_da_i^h}v\\ &=\pi(a_i^h)e_{a_i^{-h}(J_d\cap U_i)a_i^h}v. \end{split} \tag{2.18f} \] The Levi factor fixes \(v\), and the opposite factor is contracted inside its original stabilizer. The upper factor has entries in \(\varpi^{d-h}M_{i,n-i}(\mathcal O)\), so it contains \(C\) for all sufficiently large \(h\). Thus (2.18f) vanishes uniformly on the basis of \(B\). By (2.18d), \(T_i^hB=0\).

On the quotient \(E_d/B=F_{i,d}\), \(a_i\) is invertible. A basis adapted to \(B\) makes the characteristic polynomial of \(T_i\) the product of a power of \(T\) and the characteristic polynomial of the Jacquet action. This proves the spectral assertion. \(\square\)

The coefficient integrability criterion

Suppose that the center acts on \(V\) by a unitary scalar character. For \(i<n\), let \(\operatorname{Spec}_i(V)\) be the union of the eigenvalues of \(a_i\) on all the finite spaces \(F_{i,d}\). No global finite-length assumption is contained in this notation. All these eigenvalues are nonzero.

Theorem 2.3an. Every smooth coefficient of \(V\) is in \(L^2(Z_n\backslash G_n)\) if and only if \[ |\alpha|<q^{-i(n-i)/2} \quad\text{for every }i<n,\ \alpha\in\operatorname{Spec}_i(V). \tag{2.18g} \] Every smooth coefficient is in \(L^{2+\epsilon}(Z_n\backslash G_n)\) for every \(\epsilon>0\) if and only if \[ |\alpha|\le q^{-i(n-i)/2} \quad\text{for every }i<n,\ \alpha\in\operatorname{Spec}_i(V). \tag{2.18h} \] The absolute values of coefficients descend to the quotient because the scalar central character is unitary.

Necessity. Fix a Jacquet eigenvalue \(\alpha\) at level \(d\). Lemma 2.3am makes it an eigenvalue of \(T_i\); choose an eigenvector \(v\in E_d\) and a smooth \(J_d\)-fixed dual form \(\ell\) with \(\ell(v)=1\). The latter is a linear form on \(E_d\), extended to \(V\) by composition with \(e_{J_d}\). Then \[ \ell(\pi(g)v)=\alpha^h \quad(g\in J_da_i^hJ_d). \tag{2.18i} \] For \(h\ge1\) the images of these cosets modulo the center are disjoint: their two elementary-divisor levels differ by \(h\). Their exact quotient volumes are \(C_dq^{i(n-i)h}\), \(C_d>0\). Indeed \(J_d\cap a_i^hJ_da_i^{-h}\) imposes \(h\) additional congruence powers in each of \(i(n-i)\) upper entries. Block elimination in finite congruence quotients counts this index. A scalar preserving this double coset has valuation zero and is one modulo \(\varpi^d\), by comparison of its two diagonal blocks, so the central fibre volume is independent of \(h\). Consequently \(L^p\) integrability implies \[ \sum_{h\ge1}q^{i(n-i)h}|\alpha|^{ph}<\infty. \tag{2.18j} \] At \(p=2\) its ratio must be strictly less than one, giving (2.18g). For all \(p=2+\epsilon\), letting \(\epsilon\) decrease to zero gives (2.18h).

Sufficiency. Fix one smooth coefficient \(c(g)=\ell(\pi(g)v)\) and choose \(J_d\) fixing its vector and dual form. Since \(J_d\) is normal in \(K_n\), all their finitely many \(K_n\)-translates lie in the same finite fixed spaces. Write a dominant Cartan diagonal, modulo the center, as \[ a(h)=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}a_i^{h_i},\qquad h_i\ge0. \tag{2.18k} \] The preceding semigroup proof gives commuting \(T_i\)'s and \[ c(k_1a(h)k_2) =\ell_{k_1}\left(\prod_iT_i^{h_i}v_{k_2}\right). \tag{2.18l} \] Each finite matrix \(T_i\) has nonzero eigenvalues described by Lemma 2.3am and a nilpotent zero-primary part. Solving its finite recurrence, or using polynomial Bézout projections and finite differences, bounds its powers by exponential terms times fixed polynomials in \(h_i\).

Under (2.18g), choose \(r_i<q^{-i(n-i)/2}\) larger than the absolute values of every nonzero eigenvalue of \(T_i\). If all are zero, choose any such positive \(r_i\), absorbing the finitely many nonzero nilpotent powers into the constant. Hence \[ |c(k_1a(h)k_2)| \le C\prod_i(1+h_i)^A r_i^{h_i}. \tag{2.18m} \] The exact Cartan volume formula, proved by finite matrix counting, is a power \(q^{\sum_i i(n-i)h_i}\) times a ratio of products \(\prod_{j=1}^s(1-q^{-j})\) indexed by the equal-entry blocks. There are only finitely many block patterns, so that ratio is bounded uniformly above and below by positive constants. Normalize the central measure by giving \(\mathcal O^\times I_n\) volume one. For the representative with last valuation zero, the central fibre of \(K_na(h)K_n\) is precisely that unit group; its image in \(Z_n\backslash G_n\) has the same volume. Thus the absolute square integral is bounded by \[ C'\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \sum_{h_i\ge0}(1+h_i)^{2A} \left(q^{i(n-i)}r_i^2\right)^{h_i}<\infty. \tag{2.18n} \]

Under (2.18h), the same finite power argument gives (2.18m) with \(r_i=q^{-i(n-i)/2}\). For \(p=2+\epsilon\), the ratio after inserting the Cartan volume is \[ q^{i(n-i)}r_i^{2+\epsilon} =q^{-\epsilon i(n-i)/2}<1. \tag{2.18o} \] Polynomial factors remain summable. This proves every required \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) assertion. For \(n=1\) there are no proper ratios and the center quotient is a point, so both assertions hold directly. \(\square\)

For an irreducible admissible \(V\), the spectra are finite: a cyclic vector has finitely many compact \(K_n\)-orbit generators in each Jacquet module by \(G_n=P_iK_n\). The compact Jacquet lift puts them in one finite fixed space; its central characteristic polynomial annihilates all their Levi translates. This is the global Jacquet-polynomial argument in Lemma 2.3.

A real norm twist makes any smooth scalar central character unitary uniquely at the level of its absolute value. If \(|\omega_V(a)|=|a|^c\), the required twist is \(\nu^{-c/n}\). Thus Theorem 2.3an also gives an explicit necessary and sufficient test for essential square integrability after that central twist.

Coefficient-temperedness under actual parabolic induction

Theorem 2.3ao. Let \(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_s\) be actual irreducible admissible representations with unitary centers and all smooth coefficients in every \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) modulo their centers. Every smooth coefficient of their full normalized induction \(I\) is in every \(L^{2+\epsilon}(Z_n\backslash G_n)\). Every actual irreducible subquotient of \(I\) has the same property. This theorem asserts neither irreducibility nor exhaustiveness.

Proof. For two blocks of ranks \(a,b\), let \(l=i+j\) be a proper first-block Jacquet rank in their induction, \(n=a+b\). Lemma 2.3p gives a finite orbit filtration and the following raw central eigenvalues on its quotients: \[ q^{[i(a-i)+j(b-j)-l(n-l)]/2}\alpha\beta. \tag{2.18p} \] Here \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are actual raw partial-scalar Jacquet eigenvalues of the respective inducing blocks. At rank zero the corresponding scalar is one, and at full rank it is the unitary central scalar.

Theorem 2.3an bounds their absolute values by \(q^{-i(a-i)/2}\) and \(q^{-j(b-j)/2}\). Hence every root in (2.18p) has absolute value at most \(q^{-l(n-l)/2}\). Products of the quotient annihilators annihilate the full finite filtration; root collisions increase nilpotent multiplicities without changing this bound. The induction is admissible by the actual compact double-coset proof. Its center acts by the product of the inducing central characters, which is unitary. Theorem 2.3an therefore proves the assertion.

For several blocks, iterate the same finite orbit calculation. The actual transitivity maps evaluate functions on the two successive compact flag quotients and multiply their normalized section moduli. No intermediate irreducibility is needed: its global partial-scalar polynomials are the products just constructed along the finite filtration. Repeating (2.18p) cancels the intermediate normalization exponents. At a refined first-block rank \(l=\sum i_j\), the resulting root bound is \[ q^{[\sum_j i_j(n_j-i_j)-l(n-l)]/2} \prod_jq^{-i_j(n_j-i_j)/2} =q^{-l(n-l)/2}. \tag{2.18q} \] This proves the full induction assertion for every number of actual blocks.

Finally every coefficient of an actual subquotient is a coefficient of \(I\). For a submodule, extend a compact-fixed dual functional from its finite-dimensional fixed space to the ambient fixed space and compose with compact averaging. For a quotient, lift the vector and compose its dual functional with the quotient map. Apply these successively to a supplied subquotient. The scalar central action remains the same unitary character, so the coefficient bounds descend. \(\square\)

Constructing the generic constituent of a cuspidal string

For completeness, all iterated unipotent averages can be taken in explicit compact groups. In \(N_n\), put \[ C_B=\{u:v(u_{ij})\ge -B(j-i)\text{ for }i<j\},\qquad B\ge0. \] Matrix multiplication preserves the inequalities: a product through an intermediate index \(h\) has valuation at least \(-B(h-i)-B(j-h)=-B(j-i)\). The finite upper-triangular inverse expansion preserves them as well. These compact open subgroups exhaust \(N_n\). For a smooth character \(\chi\), probability averaging \(e_C^\chi v=\int_C\chi(c)^{-1}\pi(c)v\,dc\) is a finite sum, and \(e_C^\chi\pi(u)=\chi(u)e_C^\chi\) for \(u\in C\). A finite sum of twisted relations is therefore killed by one large average. Conversely a finite partition of its integrand gives \[ e_C^\chi v-v =\sum_j\mu_j\chi(c_j)^{-1} \bigl(\pi(c_j)v-\chi(c_j)v\bigr). \] If a vector in a submodule has zero twisted class in the ambient module, the killing average preserves that submodule and this formula expresses the vector using its own twisted relations. Lifting vectors and relations proves surjectivity for quotients. This proves the exactness used at every stage of the Fourier construction, in both field characteristics.

Let \(P_n\) be the mirabolic group and \[ A_n=\operatorname{c-Ind}_{N_n}^{P_n}\psi_n. \tag{2.18r} \] Induction in this paragraph is unnormalized. The Fourier construction (2.9p)–(2.9r) constructs naturally, in any smooth \(P_n\)-module \(V\), its bottom submodule \[ B(V)=A_n\otimes V_{N_n,\psi_n}, \tag{2.18s} \] and its inclusion induces the identity on the final generic coinvariant. The construction uses last-column frequencies successively. Every nonzero-frequency orbit is the full nonzero row orbit; its stabilizer is \(P_{n-1}\). The zero-frequency quotient at each stage has zero final generic coinvariant. The local-section maps and exact averages are proved in (2.9p)–(2.9r).

Lemma 2.3ap. \(A_n\) is irreducible as a \(P_n\)-module.

Proof. \(A_1=\mathbf C\). At the next last-column step, \(A_n\) is the compact section module on the nonzero row orbit with fibre \(A_{n-1}\). A \(P_n\)-submodule is stable under all compact Fourier idempotents. If nonzero, some row-frequency fibre is nonzero: the finite compact-open localization criterion detects a nonzero vector by a nonzero fibre. Transitivity transports that fibre to \(e_{n-1}\), where it is a nonzero \(P_{n-1}\)-submodule of \(A_{n-1}\), hence the entire fibre by induction. Every fibre is therefore the entire original fibre. The quotient has all fibres zero. A compact-open localization of each quotient vector is covered by finitely many zero-fibre neighborhoods, so that vector is zero. Thus the submodule is all of \(A_n\). \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3aq. Let \(V\) be an actual smooth admissible \(G_n\)-module with one-dimensional nonzero generic coinvariant. Its faithful Whittaker function quotient \[ Q=\{g\mapsto\lambda(\pi(g)v):v\in V\} \tag{2.18t} \] has an actual irreducible generic submodule \(S(V)\). It is contained in every nonzero \(G_n\)-submodule of \(Q\). It is the only irreducible generic subquotient of \(V\), up to isomorphism. This is not a claim that \(Q\) is irreducible.

Proof. The quotient \(Q\) is admissible, and evaluation at one is faithful under all its translates. Its generic coinvariant is one-dimensional: exactness gives a quotient of \(V_{N_n,\psi_n}\), and its nonzero evaluation functional prevents it from being zero. Let \(A=B(Q)\); it is a copy of \(A_n\) by (2.18s).

If \(M\subset Q\) is a nonzero \(G_n\)-submodule, choose a nonzero function in it and translate a nonzero value to one. Evaluation restricts nontrivially to \(M\). Exactness gives an injection \(M_{N_n,\psi_n}\hookrightarrow Q_{N_n,\psi_n}\); both dimensions are therefore one. Naturality of (2.18s) identifies \(B(M)\subset B(Q)\), and its map on the generic fibre is an isomorphism. By Lemma 2.3ap its nonzero image is exactly \(A\). Thus every such \(M\) contains \(A\).

Define \(S(V)\) to be the algebraic \(G_n\)-span of \(A\) inside \(Q\). It is nonzero, smooth and admissible. Any nonzero \(G_n\)-submodule of \(S(V)\), viewed inside \(Q\), contains \(A\), and hence its full \(G_n\)-span \(S(V)\). Thus \(S(V)\) is irreducible. Its evaluation functional is nonzero on \(A\), so it is generic.

For any actual generic irreducible subquotient \(U/W\) of \(V\), exactness and the one-dimensional full generic coinvariant imply \(\dim U_{N,\psi}=1\), \(W_{N,\psi}=0\). The functional on \(V\) restricts to \(U\), kills \(W\), and changing a lift by a vector of \(W\) kills every translated functional. Its actual Whittaker realization therefore embeds \(U/W\) in \(Q\). It is irreducible, so the preceding essential-submodule assertion makes it equal to \(S(V)\). This proves uniqueness without assuming a Jordan–Hölder series. \(\square\)

Corollary 2.3ar. Every actual Jacquet-cuspidal irreducible admissible representation \(\rho\) of \(G_d\) is generic. If its central character is unitary, it is coefficient square-integrable and coefficient-tempered.

Proof. For \(d>1\), all its proper ordinary Jacquet modules vanish. In the mirabolic orbit-depth filtration (2.9z), every proper derivative is \[ (V_{U_{d-i,i}})_{N_i,\psi_i}=0\quad(i<d). \tag{2.18u} \] Only the bottom layer (2.18s) remains. The restriction to \(P_d\) is nonzero, so \(V_{N_d,\psi_d}\ne0\). Theorem 2.0 makes its dimension one. For \(d=1\), irreducibility and admissibility for the abelian group give a character and the same conclusion directly. The spectra in (2.18g) and (2.18h) are empty. Both coefficient assertions follow from Theorem 2.3an. \(\square\)

Let \(\rho\) now have unitary center, and form the actual increasing centered cuspidal string \[ I_\ell(\rho)= \rho\nu^{-(\ell-1)/2}\times \rho\nu^{-(\ell-3)/2}\times\cdots\times \rho\nu^{(\ell-1)/2}. \tag{2.18v} \] Corollary 2.3ar makes all its inducing blocks generic. Lemma 2.3o gives its generic coinvariant dimension one. Theorem 2.3aq therefore constructs \[ S_\ell(\rho)=S(I_\ell(\rho)) \tag{2.18w} \] as an actual irreducible generic subquotient, unique among actual generic irreducible subquotients of this string. Its central character is \(\omega_\rho^\ell\), since the real inducing exponents sum to zero. This proves construction, irreducibility and genericity. It has not yet proved square integrability or identified this subquotient as a quotient of the whole string.

Lemma 2.3as (actual cuspidal-string Jacquet restrictions). For \(n=d\ell\), the ordinary Jacquet module of \(S_\ell(\rho)\) is zero at every proper cut not divisible by \(d\). At a cut \(i=ad\), its raw central spectrum is contained in the finite set \[ \left\{ \omega_\rho(\varpi)^a q^{-d^2a(\ell-a)/2-d\sum_{t\in A}t}: A\subset\{-(\ell-1)/2,\ldots,(\ell-1)/2\},\ |A|=a \right\}. \tag{2.18wa} \] The exponents in this set are separated by integral multiples of \(d\). This lemma does not select which of them occur.

Proof. Iterate the actual two-parabolic orbit filtration of Theorem 2.3ao through the \(\ell\) inducing blocks in (2.18v). Every quotient is indexed by the first-block ranks assigned to those cuspidal factors. A rank strictly between zero and \(d\) makes that factor's ordinary Jacquet module zero. Thus a nonzero quotient assigns each whole factor to one of the two blocks. Its first-block rank is a multiple of \(d\); at rank \(ad\), its assignments are precisely the \(a\)-element subsets \(A\) in (2.18wa). This proves the vanishing for the whole induction, and exactness proves the same vanishing for its actual subquotient \(S_\ell\).

The corresponding normalized orbit quotient is induction on \(G_{ad}\times G_{d(\ell-a)}\) from those assigned whole cuspidal factors, with their actual twists. The first central scalar \(\varpi I_{ad}\) therefore acts by \(\omega_\rho(\varpi)^a q^{-d\sum_{t\in A}t}\). The inducing modulus on this central element is one. Returning to the raw Jacquet module multiplies the scalar by \(q^{-ad\,d(\ell-a)/2}\), giving (2.18wa). The product, over the finite assignment filtration, of these scalar linear annihilators annihilates the whole raw Jacquet module. It survives every actual subquotient. Hence its spectrum contains no other root. Two subsets of the same cardinality have exponent sums differing by an integer, since the common half-integer offset cancels. This proves the separation. \(\square\)

The segment Jacquet formula and its coefficient consequence

Lemma 2.3as already proves the vanishing at cuts not divisible by \(d\). The segment Jacquet formula is explicit: at \(i=ad\), \(0<a<\ell\), it identifies the normalized Jacquet module of (2.18w) as \[ r_{ad,d(\ell-a)}S_\ell(\rho) \simeq S_a(\rho)\nu^{(\ell-a)/2}\boxtimes S_{\ell-a}(\rho)\nu^{-a/2}. \tag{2.18x} \] Theorem 2.3bd below proves this identity. The next proposition records its coefficient consequence; the later proof selects the descending tuple using actual adjacent kernel submodules.

Proposition 2.3at (coefficient consequence of the segment Jacquet formula). Formula (2.18x), proved in Theorem 2.3bd for \(S_\ell(\rho)\), implies that \(S_\ell(\rho)\) is square-integrable modulo its unitary center.

Proof. On the first normalized block, the scalar \(\varpi I_{ad}\) has eigenvalue \[ \omega_\rho(\varpi)^a q^{-ad(\ell-a)/2}. \tag{2.18y} \] This uses the actual central character in (2.18w), not a square-integrability assertion about shorter blocks. Returning from the normalized to the raw Jacquet module multiplies it by \(q^{-ad\cdot d(\ell-a)/2}\). Its absolute value is therefore \[ q^{-ad\cdot d(\ell-a)/2} q^{-ad(\ell-a)/2} <q^{-ad\cdot d(\ell-a)/2}. \tag{2.18z} \] At every other cut the spectrum is empty. Theorem 2.3an gives square integrability. The extra gap exponent \(ad(\ell-a)/2\) is strictly positive at every proper divisible cut, including ramified \(\rho\) and either field characteristic. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3bd proves the exact selection (2.18x), so this square-integrability conclusion applies to every constructed segment. Lemma 2.3as supplies its finite candidate set; the later adjacent-kernel argument selects the descending tuple.

Further reading is Zelevinsky’s freely accessible NUMDAM paper, §§1.11 and 9.1–9.8. The coefficient criteria and constituent construction used here are proved above.

From cuspidal strings to the universal finite-place classification

The next proofs supply three concrete pieces of data: the descending Jacquet tuple of a segment, the uniquely reconstructed discrete blocks of a tempered representation, and the unique decreasing quotient datum of an arbitrary irreducible admissible representation. The maps are normalized upper-parabolic induction maps, with right translation. Here \(k\) is any nondiscrete nonarchimedean local field, of either characteristic. All representations are complex smooth admissible modules; repeated factors and ramified cuspidals are allowed.

Use finite length from Theorem 1.23v, intrinsic support from Theorem 1.23x, and cuspidal exclusion from Corollary 1.23t. The exact induction, adjunction and ordinary-dual formulas are Lemmas 1.23a–1.23f and Lemma 1.23j. The two-parabolic section, coinvariant-kernel and density proof is Lemma 2.3p; its iterated version is Lemma 1.23w. The Fourier sequence and raw pairing kernel are (2.9p)–(2.9r) and Proposition 2.3g. Whittaker uniqueness and inverse-transpose contragredience are proved in Theorem 2.0, and generic induction in Lemma 2.3o. The arbitrary-algebra tensor and finite-interpolation proofs linked after Corollary 1.23y apply to all product Levis here.

Write \(A\times B\) for full normalized induction. For the next arguments \(P_n\) denotes the mirabolic group; a parabolic carrying a partition is denoted \(P_{a,b}\) or \(P\) with that partition specified. The raw and normalized Jacquet functors remain distinct.

Cuspidal support and reversal of composition factors

Call an irreducible admissible representation cuspidal if every proper ordinary Jacquet module is zero. Let \(I=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_t\) be normalized induction of cuspidal irreducibles, of ranks \(n_j\).

Lemma 2.3au. Every irreducible subquotient \(V\) of \(I\) has the actual cuspidal-support multiset \(\{\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_t\}\). This multiset is independent of the supplied induction or the cuspidal embedding used to obtain it.

Proof. The written cuspidal embedding gives \(V\hookrightarrow\sigma_1\times\cdots\times\sigma_s\) with cuspidal irreducibles \(\sigma_j\). Value-at-one reciprocity gives a nonzero map from the normalized Jacquet module of \(V\) for that block partition onto \(\boxtimes_j\sigma_j\). The tensor product is irreducible by the actual admissible tensor theorem; the map is therefore onto.

Exact Jacquet functors make it an actual subquotient of the corresponding Jacquet module of \(I\). Iterate the full two-parabolic orbit calculation. A nonzero quotient assigns each original whole cuspidal block to one target block: an internal split makes that cuspidal block's proper Jacquet module zero. The target-block quotient is normalized induction of the assigned original blocks, with their original relative order and no extra twist. This is the repeated cancellation of the half moduli and positive additive quotient Jacobian in the written two-parabolic calculation.

All these modules have finite length by Theorem 1.23v. Their finite composition filtrations and exact tensor products show that \(\sigma_j\) is an actual subquotient of the induction assigned to target block \(j\). If it has two or more assigned blocks, Corollary 1.23t excludes that cuspidal subquotient. Thus each target block contains exactly one original block. None is empty, and each original block is assigned once. Consequently \(s=t\), with the same multiset of actual representations. This also proves independence of the original supplied induction. \(\square\)

In particular the full ordered cuspidal Jacquet functors detect every nonzero subquotient of \(I\): choose a simple subquotient and the embedding just used; its full cuspidal Jacquet module is nonzero, and exactness lifts that detection. When all ranks are the same \(d\), the one functor \(r_{d,\ldots,d}\) suffices.

We need reversal of composition factors, not an identification of the ordinary dual of a reducible induction with its reversal. Put \(\theta_n(g)=w_n\,{}^tg^{-1}w_n\). The written contragredient theorem gives \(X\circ\theta_n\simeq X^\vee\) for each irreducible admissible \(X\). Changing variables in the section covariance gives the actual module isomorphism \[ (A\times B)\circ\theta_{a+b} \simeq (B\circ\theta_b)\times(A\circ\theta_a). \tag{2.19a} \] Indeed \(\theta\) sends the upper block parabolic to the upper parabolic with reversed block sizes and sends its block entries to reversed inverse transposes. Its half modulus transforms into the half modulus of that reversed parabolic. The inverse section map uses the same automorphism, so this is an actual isomorphism, valid before irreducibility.

Ordinary smooth duality, in contrast, gives \((A\times B)^\vee=A^\vee\times B^\vee\), on the same upper parabolic and in the same order. Applying these two exact functors to a finite composition series, and using the contragredient theorem only on its irreducible factors, shows that \(A\times B\) and \(B\times A\) have the same composition multiset when \(A,B\) are irreducible admissible. Finite composition filtrations give the same conclusion for finite-length admissible blocks. Exact induction makes adjacent block exchanges preserve composition multisets in any longer product. This assertion supplies no invertible exchange map at a reducibility point.

Normalized derivatives and their actual product filtration

Use the unnormalized Fourier functors of the Fourier construction (2.9p)–(2.9r) proof: \(D\) is the nonzero last-column character fibre, \(E\) the ordinary last-column quotient, \(D^+\) compact section induction from that nonzero orbit, and \(E^+\) inflation. Define \[ \Phi^-T=DT\otimes\nu^{-1/2},\quad \Psi^-T=ET\otimes\nu^{-1/2},\qquad \Phi^+T=D^+T\otimes\nu^{1/2},\quad \Psi^+A=E^+A\otimes\nu^{1/2}. \tag{2.19b} \] The determinant on a mirabolic subgroup means the determinant of its upper-left block. Twists pass through the fibres because they are trivial on every unipotent group. The raw Fourier sequence therefore becomes, with actual natural maps, \[ 0\to\Phi^+\Phi^-T\to T\to\Psi^+\Psi^-T\to0. \tag{2.19c} \] All these functors are exact by the written compact weighted averaging and compact-open section proofs.

For a \(G_n\)-module \(V\), write \[ \partial_i V=\Psi^-(\Phi^-)^{i-1}(V|_{P_n}) =\bigl((V_{U_{n-i,i}})_{N_i,\psi_i}\bigr)\nu^{-i/2}, \quad 1\le i\le n, \qquad \partial_0V=V. \tag{2.19d} \] This equality follows by ordering the actual last-column twisted differences as in Proposition 2.3g. It identifies \(\partial_iV\) with the trailing generic coinvariant of the normalized Jacquet module \(r_{n-i,i}V\). On the remaining \(G_{n-i}\), the negative half modulus is precisely \(\nu^{-i/2}\); on the trailing \(N_i\), every determinant factor is one. Thus no normalization is implicit in (2.19d).

Lemma 2.3av. For finite-length admissible \(A,B\), \(\partial_k(A\times B)\) has a finite filtration whose quotients are \[ \partial_iA\times\partial_jB, \qquad i+j=k. \tag{2.19e} \] All derivatives of a finite-length admissible \(G\)-module are finite-length admissible on their remaining \(G\)-group.

Proof. Apply the actual two-parabolic Jacquet filtration at the cut \((a+b-k,k)\). An orbit assigns removed ranks \(i,j\) to the trailing block. Its normalized quotient is induction from \(r_{a-i,i}A\) and \(r_{b-j,j}B\), with first factors assigned to the remaining block and second factors to the trailing one. Take the trailing generic coinvariant. The same pivot-word filtration used in the actual generic induction proof kills every word except the open reversed block word: an adjacent forward cross-block root acts trivially on the fibre but has nontrivial prescribed character. Integration in the surviving additive coordinates leaves the two actual trailing generic coinvariants. Its first-block section space is their normalized product. Exactness gives the resulting finite filtration (2.19e).

The normalized root factor for this calculation is already fixed by the quotient density. In raw notation, returning to a derivative contributes \(\nu^{k/2}\), while each child raw derivative contributes \(\nu^{i/2}\) or \(\nu^{j/2}\). The parent twist in (2.19d) cancels the parent factor; hence the section calculation leaves exactly (2.19e), not additional real twists.

For finiteness, Theorem 1.23v makes \(r_{n-i,i}V\) finite-length admissible. Its simple factors are actual outer tensor products. The finite Whittaker uniqueness proof makes the trailing generic coinvariant of each irreducible factor zero or one dimensional. Exactness then yields a finite filtration of \(\partial_iV\) by admissible irreducibles of the remaining group. \(\square\)

For a cuspidal \(\rho\) of rank \(d\), Corollary 2.3ar and (2.19d) give \(\partial_i\rho=0\) for \(0<i<d\), and \(\partial_d\rho=\mathbf C\). Its mirabolic restriction is the simple compact Whittaker section module \(A_d=c\operatorname{-Ind}_{N_d}^{P_d}\psi_d\): its only orbit-depth layer is the bottom one, and its generic fibre has dimension one. The Fourier proof of irreducibility of that compact section module is Lemma 2.3ap.

For a cuspidal product \(I\), (2.19e) therefore gives \(\partial_nI=\mathbf C\). A derivative of order \(i<n\) has quotients consisting of products of the remaining whole cuspidal blocks; its simple factors have support contained in the original list, by Lemma 2.3au.

The highest-derivative pairing, including its density

Use inverse generic characters on paired modules. The raw layer of orbit depth \(i\) is \[ \mathcal I_i(C)= c\operatorname{-Ind}_{H_{n,i}}^{P_n}(C\otimes\psi_i), \quad H_{n,i}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}h&x\\0&u\end{pmatrix}: h\in G_{n-i},\ u\in N_i\right\}. \tag{2.19f} \] Its normalized version is \(\widehat{\mathcal I}_i(C) =(\Phi^+)^{i-1}\Psi^+C =\mathcal I_i(C\nu^{i/2})\). The equality follows by successively restricting the \(i\) half-determinant twists to the final stabilizer.

Proposition 2.3g kernel proof supplies the following actual statements. Two different depths have zero bilinear pairing. At the same depth, an invariant raw pairing gives the fibre law \[ \lambda(hv,hw)=\nu(h)^{i-1}\lambda(v,w). \tag{2.19g} \] Here is the density and kernel mechanism. Last-column Fourier actions on the two factors are multiplication by opposite characters. A compact Fourier idempotent separates two unequal frequency boxes and kills their pairing; finite compact-open partitions reduce every off-diagonal support to such boxes. Restriction to the diagonal has no jets. Local sections of the nonzero row orbit then pull the remaining pairing to its stabilizer fibre. Additive row measure scales by \(\nu(h)\). Repeating \(i-1\) rows gives (2.19g). Equivalently \(\Delta(H_{n,i})/\Delta(P_n)=\nu^{i-1}\). Compact coset indicators show that the integration kernel on each fibre is exactly the span of its actual translation differences; finite local partitions give the global kernel. Thus this is an identification of actual forms, not a formal comparison of characters.

It follows, after inserting the two \(\nu^{i/2}\) fibre twists, that a pairing on normalized depth-\(i\) layers transforming by \(\nu\) on \(P_n\) induces an invariant pairing on the two \(G_{n-i}\) fibres. In fact the required raw exponent is now \(i\): twisting the first module by \(\nu^{-1}\) makes the pairing invariant and changes \(i-1\) to \(i\). The two fibre twists contribute exactly that \(i\), and cancel.

Lemma 2.3aw. Suppose that \(M\) is a \(P_n\)-submodule of a finite-length admissible \(G_n\)-module \(V\), and \(\partial_iM\) is its highest nonzero derivative. There is an invariant bilinear pairing \[ \partial_iM\ \times\ \partial_i(\nu V^\vee) \longrightarrow\mathbf C \tag{2.19h} \] nondegenerate in the first factor.

Proof. The actual smooth dual separates every vector of \(V\). Its perfect pairing, with the second representation twisted by \(\nu\), has the covariance \(B(pv,pw)=\nu(p)B(v,w)\). It is nondegenerate on \(M\) in its first factor.

Because depths larger than \(i\) vanish for \(M\), its bottom layer is \(L=\widehat{\mathcal I}_i(\partial_iM)\). In the second module, first quotient its filtration by all depths larger than \(i\). Pairings of \(L\) with those depths vanish by the Fourier separation just proved, so the form descends. Restrict the second variable to its depth-\(i\) submodule. This restriction is nondegenerate in the first variable: its radical \(R\subset L\) is a submodule of the single-depth section module and therefore itself has depth \(i\). If that radical were nonzero, its pairing with the remaining lower-depth quotient would also vanish, again by Fourier separation along its finite filtration. It would then be a radical of the original nondegenerate pairing, a contradiction.

The equal-depth stabilizer identification and the exact normalization cancellation above now give (2.19h). Nondegeneracy passes to fibres: a nonzero fibre vector localized in one compact-open section can be paired with the corresponding inverse-character section; conversely a fibre radical would induce a section radical. This proves the claimed nondegeneracy. \(\square\)

For \(V=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_t\), every irreducible submodule \(\sigma\subset\partial_iM\), \(i<n\), consequently has support both in \[ \{\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_t\} \quad\text{and in}\quad \{\rho_1\nu^{-1},\ldots,\rho_t\nu^{-1}\}. \tag{2.19i} \] For the first statement use exact derivatives and Lemma 2.3av. For the second, (2.19h) gives an embedding of \(\sigma\) in the ordinary smooth dual of the finite-length admissible second derivative. Its factors, by Lemma 2.3av and exact ordinary duality, are products of \(\rho_j\nu^{-1}\). The map is smooth: a fixed vector in \(\sigma\) makes its functional on the second module fixed by the same compact group. Lemma 2.3au identifies its support. Since the remaining rank is positive, this support is nonempty.

The two mirabolic orbits and the support assertion needed for them

We give the matrix models to control the one-sided statement. For \(R\) on \(G_a\) and \(T\) on \(P_b\), define \(R\star T\) on \(P_{a+b}\) by compact section induction from \[ H_c=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A&X\\0&D\end{pmatrix}: A\in G_a,\ D\in P_b\right\}, \qquad |\det A|^{b/2}|\det D|^{-a/2}R(A)\otimes T(D). \tag{2.19j} \] Its quotient is compact, so compact section induction is the full smooth section space here. For \(T\) on \(P_a\) and \(R\) on \(G_b\), use coordinates \((a-1,b,1)\) and define \(T\star R\) by compact section induction from \[ H_o=\left\{ \begin{pmatrix}h&X&u\\0&g&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix} :h\in G_{a-1},\ g\in G_b\right\}, \qquad |\det h|^{b/2}|\det g|^{-a/2} T\left(\begin{smallmatrix}h&u\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right) \otimes R(g). \tag{2.19k} \] Zero-size blocks mean omission. All the displayed characters are the original full normalized-induction half modulus, restricted to the indicated stabilizer. In (2.19k), the additive \(X\)-radical has modulus \(|\det h|^b|\det g|^{-(a-1)}\); its square root is accompanied by the explicit extra \(|\det g|^{-1/2}\).

Lemma 2.3ax. There are actual natural maps giving \[ 0\to (R|_{P_a})\star S \to (R\times S)|_{P_{a+b}} \to R\star(S|_{P_b})\to0. \tag{2.19l} \] Moreover \[ \begin{aligned} \Psi^-(R\star T)&=R\times\Psi^-T,& \Phi^-(R\star T)&=R\star\Phi^-T,\\ \Psi^-(T\star R)&=\Psi^-T\times R,& 0\to(\Phi^-T)\star R&\to\Phi^-(T\star R) \to(\Psi^-T)\star(R|_{P_b})\to0. \end{aligned} \tag{2.19m} \] Every nonzero \(P_{a+b}\)-submodule of \(T\star R\), with \(b>0\), has nonzero \(\Phi^-\).

Proof of (2.19l). The block flag quotient of \(P_{a,b}\backslash G_{a+b}\) has two mirabolic orbits, according as the represented first block lies in the hyperplane \(e_{a+b}=0\) or not. Eliminate its first nonzero last coordinate on the open stratum and the ordinary block pivots on the closed one. These operations give the identity representative for the closed stratum and the permutation with coordinate order \((1,\ldots,a-1,a+1,\ldots,a+b,a)\) for the open stratum. Their stabilizers are exactly \(H_c\) and \(H_o\), and restriction of the original covariance gives (2.19j) and (2.19k). The closed condition is a vanishing minor condition. Restrictions of smooth sections to it extend from a finite compact-open coordinate partition. A section restricting to zero vanishes near its compact support on that stratum and is a compact section on the open orbit. This proves both the kernel and surjectivity in (2.19l).

Proof of (2.19m), with the normalization. In (2.19j), the first \(a\) coordinates of the final column belong to the inducing radical and act trivially on its fibre. The other final-column action is that on \(T\). For the ordinary fibre, the remaining \(G_{a+b-1}\) acts transitively on the closed flag space, giving the ordinary fibre of \(T\). For a nonzero fixed frequency, its stabilizer has two flag orbits, according as the first block lies in the frequency's kernel. If it does not, a final-column entry in the trivial cross radical has nontrivial prescribed character and kills that orbit's fibre. If it does, ordinary block pivots give precisely the nonzero fibre of \(T\). For \(b=1\) the frequency kernel has dimension \(a-1\) and cannot contain the first \(a\)-block, so that fibre is zero. The compact averaging argument proves these orbit vanishings for actual section quotients. The new negative half determinant changes the first exponent \(b/2\) to \((b-1)/2\), exactly the modulus for a product with the remaining \(b-1\) block; the second negative half determinant is already in \(\Phi^-T\) or \(\Psi^-T\). This proves the first row.

For (2.19k), the final-column quotient left free by \(H_o\) is the additive middle coordinate \(y\in k^b\). Take its ordinary or character-weighted integral. Its translation kernel is exact: at a common compact lattice, the kernel of the integral is a finite sum of coset indicators minus their translates; fibre relations are killed by a common compact weighted average. Local compact-open partitions make these actual fixed group translations throughout each piece, and give the global kernel. Under \(g\in G_b\), the coordinate is \(y\mapsto gy\), so the positive integration Jacobian is \(|\det g|\). Combining it with (2.19k) and the new \(\nu^{-1/2}\) normalization leaves the exponents \[ \begin{array}{c|cc} &h&g\\\hline \text{initial}&b/2&-a/2\\ \text{integration}&0&1\\ \text{new negative half determinant}&-1/2&-1/2\\\hline \text{result}&(b-1)/2&-(a-1)/2. \end{array} \tag{2.19n} \] For the ordinary quotient these are exactly those of \(\Psi^-T\times R\).

For the nonzero fibre, write the final-column frequency as \((\xi,\eta)\) on the first \(a-1\) and middle \(b\) coordinates. The cross block \(X\) sends it to \((\xi,\eta-\xi X)\). On \(\xi\ne0\), eliminate \(\eta\) and put a nonzero coordinate of \(\xi\) into its last position; the stabilizer gives \((\Phi^-T)\star R\). On \(\xi=0,\eta\ne0\), the first module has its ordinary fibre and the stabilizer of \(\eta\) in \(G_b\) is \(P_b\), giving \((\Psi^-T)\star(R|_{P_b})\). These are a closed–open two-stratum decomposition within the nonzero frequencies. The Fourier local-section proof gives their exact section sequence. Table (2.19n) agrees with both claimed target covariances: in the first, the \(\Phi^-T\) factor contributes \(-1/2\) on \(h\) to the \((a-1,b)\) open product; in the second the \(\Psi^-T\) factor contributes the same to its closed product.
