Every nonzero pivot division has a continuous local section, and the preceding translation-kernel argument applies on each compact-open chart. This proves all maps and the exact last sequence in (2.19m).

Finally if \(\Phi^-M=0\), Fourier sequence (2.19c) says the final additive column acts trivially on \(M\). Take a nonzero section of \(M\) and translate a nonzero value to one. Its values on the whole final column are then that same nonzero value. Its support contains \(H_oU_{a+b}/H_o\simeq k^b\), a closed noncompact subset of \(H_o\backslash P_{a+b}\). It is closed because \(H_oU_{a+b}\) is the closed matrix-pattern subgroup obtained by adding the middle final column to (2.19k). This contradicts compact support modulo \(H_o\). Thus every such nonzero submodule has nonzero \(\Phi^-\). \(\square\)

One-sided mirabolic homogeneity and increasing generic heads

Theorem 2.3ay. If the cuspidal list satisfies \[ \rho_j\not\simeq\rho_i\nu\qquad(i<j), \tag{2.19o} \] then \(I=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_t\) has no nonzero mirabolic submodule with zero final generic coinvariant.

Proof. Induct on \(t\). At \(t=1\), the restriction is the simple \(A_d\), so the statement holds. Write \(I=\rho_1\times I'\), with \(d=\operatorname{rank}\rho_1\). Use (2.19l), with open submodule \(C=A_d\star I'\) and closed quotient \(C'=\rho_1\star(I'|_P)\).

If a nonzero nongeneric submodule \(M\) meets \(C\), replace it by that nonzero intersection. Repeated (2.19m) gives \((\Phi^-)^jC=A_{d-j}\star I'\) for \(j<d\), and \((\Phi^-)^dC=I'|_P\). At every step the support assertion in Lemma 2.3ax makes the image of a nonzero submodule nonzero. The image of \(M\) after these \(d\) steps is therefore a nonzero nongeneric submodule of \(I'|_P\), contradicting induction. Its nongenericity follows from (2.19d) and exactness: the final generic functor is the remaining generic functor after these steps.

Otherwise \(M\) embeds in \(C'\). Its highest derivative \(\partial_iM\), \(i<n\), is nonzero; some derivative must be nonzero by the finite orbit-depth filtration. It is a submodule of a finite-length derivative of \(I\), so choose an irreducible submodule \(\sigma\) in it. The first row of (2.19m) gives \(\partial_iC'=\rho_1\times\partial_iI'\) and zero beyond the rank of \(I'\). By Lemma 2.3av and Lemma 2.3au, the support of every simple constituent of this module contains \(\rho_1\). But (2.19i) also puts that support among the \(\rho_j\nu^{-1}\). Thus \(\rho_1\simeq\rho_j\nu^{-1}\) for some \(j\). It cannot be \(j=1\), since a nonzero real norm twist changes the absolute value of the central uniformizer character. For \(j>1\) it contradicts (2.19o). This proves the theorem. \(\square\)

Consequently any list increasing in the real cuspidal exponents has a simple generic head, of multiplicity one. Indeed its ordinary dual has decreasing exponents and satisfies (2.19o). Every irreducible quotient of the original induction dualizes to an irreducible submodule of that homogeneous dual, and is generic: inverse-transpose contragredience preserves genericity with inverse character. The finite semisimple head exists by finite length, and the full generic coinvariant has dimension one. Thus the head has exactly one simple generic summand and multiplicity one. This is an actual whole-induction surjection.

Nonadjacent cuspidal irreducibility and actual exchange

Theorem 2.3az. If \(\rho_j\not\simeq\rho_i\nu\) for all \(i,j\), the full cuspidal product is irreducible.

Proof. Theorem 2.3ay applies to it and to its ordinary dual, since the same two-sided condition is preserved by contragredience. Choose a simple submodule \(S\) by finite length. It is generic. Its full generic dimension is one, equal to that of the whole product. If the quotient by \(S\) were nonzero, it would have an irreducible nongeneric quotient. Its dual would be a nongeneric submodule of the dual product, contrary to Theorem 2.3ay. Hence the original product equals \(S\). \(\square\)

For \(\rho_a=\rho\nu^a\), \(\rho_b=\rho\nu^b\), with \(a\ne b\) and \(|a-b|\ne1\), this also constructs the actual exchange map. The normalized \((d,d)\)-Jacquet module has its two orbit factors \(\rho_a\boxtimes\rho_b\) and \(\rho_b\boxtimes\rho_a\). The first block central uniformizer has distinct absolute eigenvalues on them, so polynomial Bézout projections split it as their actual direct sum. Projection onto the second factor, followed by normalized value-at-one reciprocity, gives \[ \mathcal A_{a,b}:\rho_a\times\rho_b \longrightarrow\rho_b\times\rho_a, \quad v\longmapsto[g\mapsto p_{b,a}([\pi(g)v])]. \tag{2.19p} \] Its inverse section construction and its smooth right stabilizer are the actual reciprocity proof. It is nonzero; both modules are irreducible by Theorem 2.3az, so it is an isomorphism. The same reciprocity shows its Hom space has dimension one. At any nonzero real difference, including difference one, the projection still defines this nonzero map; irreducibility and invertibility at difference one are not assumed.

Adjacent reducibility from finite Hermitian corners

We prove the remaining rank-two reducibility without quoting an analytic intertwiner theorem or an invariant-form theorem. Normalize \(\rho\) to unitary center. Lemma 1.23l supplies its compatible unitary form. Put \[ I(s)=\rho\nu^{-s/2}\times\rho\nu^{s/2}, \qquad s\in\mathbb R. \tag{2.19q} \] Both proper Jacquet orbit factors occur, and all other proper two-block cuts vanish, by cuspidality.

Lemma 2.3ba. It is impossible that every \(I(s)\) is irreducible.

Proof. Suppose otherwise. At \(s\ne0\), (2.19p) is an isomorphism \(I(s)\to I(-s)\); its construction needs only the distinct central eigenvalues and the supposed irreducibility of its ends. At zero use the identity. The compact-picture pairing between \(I(s)\) and \(I(-s)\), obtained from the unitary form on \(\rho\), is perfect and invariant. Its two real inducing twists cancel in the pairing; the two half moduli multiply to the quotient integration modulus, exactly as in the written normalized-induction duality proof. Compose with the isomorphism to obtain a nondegenerate invariant sesquilinear form on \(I(s)\).

Its conjugate transpose is another such form. The space of these forms is a complex line by irreducibility, admissibility and Schur's lemma. If the transpose is \(c\) times the form, \(|c|=1\); multiplying by a suitable phase makes it Hermitian. Denote any such nonzero Hermitian form by \(B_s\).

All \(I(s)\) have the same compact-picture space \(\mathcal E\) and the same \(K_{2d}\)-action, since norm characters are one on the inducing compact subgroup. Fix a congruence group \(J\) with \(\mathcal E^J\ne0\). This finite space and its basis can be chosen independent of \(s\). For each compact bi-\(J\) Hecke test \(h\), the matrix \(A_s(h)\) on it has real-analytic entries. To verify this, partition the compact integration support and compact flag representatives into finitely many Iwasawa charts at a common vector level. The inducing vector actions are fixed on each piece and every norm factor is a fixed power of \(q^{-s/2}\). The integrals are finite sums of those powers with constant coefficients.

The restriction of \(B_s\) to \(\mathcal E^J\) is nondegenerate: averaging is self-adjoint for an invariant Hermitian form, so a fixed vector orthogonal to the fixed space is orthogonal to the entire smooth module. At a fixed \(s_0\), the simple Hecke corner on \(\mathcal E^J\) has image the full matrix algebra, by the earlier finite interpolation proof. Choose finitely many tests whose images span it, and include their involutions \(h^*(g)=\overline{h(g^{-1})}\). For a Hermitian matrix \(H\), impose the finite equations \[ A_s(h)^*H=H A_s(h^*). \tag{2.19r} \] At \(s_0\), their real solution space is one dimensional. Indeed comparison with the known invertible matrix of \(B_{s_0}\) makes the ratio commute with the full corner, so it is a real scalar.

A nonzero maximal minor of this finite real-linear system remains nonzero near \(s_0\). Its kernel therefore has dimension at most one nearby; the actual nonzero restrictions of \(B_s\) make it exactly one. Gaussian elimination, with one nonzero real coordinate normalized, produces a local real-analytic Hermitian solution \(H_s\). It is a nonzero scalar multiple of the actual restriction and is invertible for every nearby \(s\). Its signature is constant there. Here is a finite-dimensional proof of this assertion. A Hermitian matrix has an orthogonal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues: maximize its real Rayleigh quotient on the compact unit sphere, use first variation to obtain an eigenvector, and repeat on its orthogonal complement. At an invertible matrix, the positive and negative eigenspaces have positive minimum absolute Rayleigh values on their unit spheres. A sufficiently small perturbation preserves those two signs on those two spaces. Their dimensions already sum to the full dimension, so both dimensions remain unchanged.

At zero the normalized unitary compact-picture form is positive. The property that this line of forms is definite is locally constant on the connected real parameter line, so it is definite at every \(s\), for each nonzero fixed space. Fix one nonzero vector and make \(B_s\) positive on it. Any other vector and this one lie in a common fixed space; its definite form then makes \(B_s\) positive on that entire space. Thus the actual global form \(B_s\) is positive definite. Every \(I(s)\) is unitarizable.

This contradicts a finite compressed operator. The first raw \((d,d)\)-Jacquet root of \(I(s)\) has absolute value \[ q^{-d^2/2+ds/2}. \tag{2.19s} \] Here the raw half modulus contributes \(q^{-d^2/2}\) and the scalar in \(\rho\nu^{-s/2}\) contributes \(q^{ds/2}\). A nonzero orbit quotient makes this an actual eigenvalue on some finite Jacquet fixed space; the compact Jacquet lift and Lemma 2.3am transfer it to \(e_J\pi(a_d)e_J\) on the original fixed space. In a positive invariant form, \(\pi(a_d)\) is an isometry and \(e_J\) an orthogonal projection, so that compression has norm at most one. Taking \(s>d\) makes (2.19s) greater than one, impossible. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3bb. The adjacent products \(\rho\nu^{-1/2}\times\rho\nu^{1/2}\) and their reversal are reducible, each of length two.

Proof. Theorem 2.3az gives irreducibility for every real \(s\) other than \(\pm1\). If one adjacent product were irreducible, its nonzero map (2.19p) to the reversal would be an embedding. Its full \((d,d)\)-Jacquet module already has both simple orbit factors. The reversal has only those two factors, so the cokernel has zero full cuspidal Jacquet module. Lemma 2.3au detects every nonzero subquotient of this proper cuspidal induction, and forces the cokernel to be zero. The reversal would also be irreducible. All real \(I(s)\) would then be irreducible, contrary to Lemma 2.3ba. Hence both are reducible.

Their full cuspidal Jacquet modules have length two and detect every nonzero subquotient. Exactness bounds their lengths by two. Reducibility makes those lengths exactly two. Twisting the entire construction proves the same assertion for any adjacent \(\rho\nu^a,\rho\nu^{a+1}\), without a unitary-center restriction on the original \(\rho\). \(\square\)

The adjacent map's actual image, kernel and direction

Put \(L=\rho\nu^a\), \(H=\rho\nu^{a+1}\). The decreasing product \(H\times L\) satisfies (2.19o), so every nonzero mirabolic submodule is generic. Its length is two, its simple socle is generic, and its quotient is nongeneric. The increasing product \(L\times H\) has a simple generic head by Theorem 2.3ay and a nongeneric simple kernel.

The map \(\mathcal A_{a,a+1}\) in (2.19p) has nonzero image in \(H\times L\), hence generic image. Its kernel and image cannot both be nonzero generic modules because the original generic dimension is one. If the image had length two it would be onto, and equal finite lengths would make it invertible; that would put the nongeneric kernel submodule of \(L\times H\) into the homogeneous decreasing product, a contradiction. The image therefore has length one. It is the generic socle of \(H\times L\) and the generic head of \(L\times H\). Denote it by \(S([a,a+1]_\rho)\).

Reciprocity makes the projection onto \(H\boxtimes L\) of the image's normalized Jacquet module nonzero. Since this image has length one, its full cuspidal Jacquet module has that single factor: the nongeneric kernel has a nonzero factor by Lemma 2.3au and the whole module has only two. Distinct central eigenvalues give actual direct sums. Thus \[ \begin{gathered} r_{d,d}S([a,a+1]_\rho)=H\boxtimes L,\\ 0\to T([a,a+1]_\rho)\to L\times H \twoheadrightarrow S([a,a+1]_\rho)\to0,\\ r_{d,d}T([a,a+1]_\rho)=L\boxtimes H,\qquad T([a,a+1]_\rho)_{N,\psi}=0. \end{gathered} \tag{2.19t} \] All cuts not divisible by \(d\) are zero. These are actual map and module statements at the reducibility point. No reversed induced module is being identified with an ordinary smooth dual.

The reverse map \(\mathcal A_{a+1,a}:H\times L\to L\times H\) has image \(T([a,a+1]_\rho)\) and kernel \(S([a,a+1]_\rho)\). It cannot have length-two image, since that would give the same impossible isomorphism. Reciprocity makes its projection onto the ascending Jacquet tensor nonzero. Its simple image is therefore the nongeneric kernel of the increasing product, and exactness identifies its generic kernel. In particular both composites of these two actual maps are zero. The forward map may be normalized by making its induced map on the one-dimensional generic fibres the identity; the reverse map has zero generic-fibre map and is fixed only up to a nonzero scalar. No analytic dependence of these chosen normalizations is used in Lemma 2.3ba.

The full string Jacquet selection and whole surjection

Let \[ \rho_j=\rho\nu^{j-(\ell+1)/2},\quad 1\le j\le\ell, \qquad I_\ell=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_\ell. \tag{2.19u} \] Here \(\rho\) has unitary center. Its cuspidal twists are distinct, since their central absolute values are distinct. Theorem 2.3ay already supplies a simple generic head of the whole increasing induction.

Lemma 2.3bc. The full normalized cuspidal Jacquet module of \(I_\ell\) is the actual direct sum \[ r_{d,\ldots,d}I_\ell =\bigoplus_{\sigma\in S_\ell} \rho_{\sigma(1)}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\rho_{\sigma(\ell)}, \tag{2.19v} \] with each summand occurring once. The functor detects every nonzero subquotient of \(I_\ell\).

Proof. Iterate the actual orbit Jacquet filtration. Cuspidality allows each original block only to be assigned whole to one of the target \(d\)-blocks. Its nonzero quotients are precisely the permutations in (2.19v), once each. The normalization is that of the actual multiblock refinement of the two-parabolic density, so its quotients have the stated representations.

On these finitely many quotients, the commuting block central uniformizers have pairwise distinct tuples of scalar eigenvalues. A product of their finite scalar annihilators kills the full filtration. Polynomial Bézout projections separate its finitely many joint generalized characters. Each projected space has only one quotient in that filtration, and that quotient is an irreducible tensor product. The projected space is therefore that quotient itself. This proves the actual direct sum, including absence of nilpotent central extensions. Detection was proved in Lemma 2.3au. \(\square\)

For adjacent original positions \(j,j+1\), insert the nongeneric kernel \(T([j,j+1])\) of (2.19t) into those two slots and induce with the other cuspidal factors. Exact induction gives an actual submodule \(K_j\subset I_\ell\). Its generic fibre is zero: the same generic flag quotient calculation multiplies the block generic fibres, and the middle one is zero. This argument also applies to a nongeneric middle block; it needs no nonzero Whittaker functional there.

Its full cuspidal Jacquet module consists exactly of the summands in (2.19v) in which \(j\) precedes \(j+1\). Here is the module calculation. In the refined orbit filtration, the two-rank block \(T\) must occupy two target \(d\)-blocks: all other proper cuts of \(T\) are zero, and its \((d,d)\)-Jacquet module is the single ascending tensor in (2.19t). Those two occupied target positions have that internal order. All other blocks are arbitrary whole assignments to the remaining positions, once each. This gives precisely the stated summands. Exactness embeds them into (2.19v), and its distinct-character decomposition makes the assertion an actual equality of submodules.

Put \(K=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}K_j\). Its generic fibre is zero, by exactness applied to the onto map from their finite direct sum. It is proper since the generic fibre of \(I_\ell\) is one dimensional. The full cuspidal Jacquet module of \(I_\ell/K\) has only the permutation in which every \(j+1\) precedes \(j\), namely the descending tuple. Detection in Lemma 2.3bc shows that this quotient has length one: a longer composition series would give at least two nonzero simple factors in its exact full Jacquet module, whose length is one. Thus \[ I_\ell\twoheadrightarrow G_\ell:=I_\ell/K, \qquad r_{d,\ldots,d}G_\ell =\rho_\ell\boxtimes\rho_{\ell-1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes\rho_1. \tag{2.19w} \] This is an actual whole increasing-string surjection onto an irreducible generic representation. Since the whole induction has generic dimension one and finite length, it has only one generic irreducible composition factor. Thus \(G_\ell\) is the earlier actually constructed \(S_\ell(\rho)\), without assuming that identification as a premise. The head calculation also proves that every irreducible quotient of the string is this one, with head multiplicity one.

Theorem 2.3bd (the exact segment Jacquet formula). All cuts not divisible by \(d\) vanish. For \(0<a<\ell\), \[ r_{ad,d(\ell-a)}S_\ell(\rho) \simeq S_a(\rho)\nu^{(\ell-a)/2} \boxtimes S_{\ell-a}(\rho)\nu^{-a/2}. \tag{2.19x} \]

Proof. Vanishing at other cuts follows from the whole cuspidal induction and exactness, as already proved in Lemma 2.3as. At a divisible cut let \(R\) be the normalized Jacquet module. Its further full cuspidal Jacquet module is the one descending tuple in (2.19w), by actual coinvariants in stages and multiplication of the normalizing half moduli.

The orbit filtration of \(r_{ad,d(\ell-a)}I_\ell\) has quotients \(I_A\boxtimes I_{A^c}\), for \(|A|=a\), retaining the original relative order. Every nonzero subquotient of such a quotient is detected by full cuspidal Jacquet functors on its two Levi factors: finite composition factors are outer tensor products, and Lemma 2.3au detects each factor. Exactness along the finite orbit filtration gives the same detection for every nonzero subquotient of this Jacquet module, hence of \(R\). Its full cuspidal Jacquet module has length one, so \(R\) is irreducible.

Write it as \(V_1\boxtimes V_2\), by the actual admissible tensor theorem. Its cuspidal data are, respectively, the top \(a\) and bottom \(\ell-a\) factors of (2.19u), forced by its one full tuple and Lemma 2.3au. Consequently it can occur only in the orbit quotient for that subset \(A\), and \(V_1,V_2\) are actual subquotients of those two increasing strings. Their full cuspidal Jacquet tuples are descending. In each shorter string, (2.19v) has multiplicity one for every tuple, and (2.19w) constructs a simple factor with that descending tuple. Exactness makes different simple factors' tuple sets disjoint. Therefore \(V_1,V_2\) are those already constructed shorter generic heads.

The top original exponents are a centered \(a\)-string shifted by \((\ell-a)/2\), and the bottom ones are a centered \((\ell-a)\)-string shifted by \(-a/2\). This proves exactly (2.19x), as an actual normalized module identity. \(\square\)

Proposition 2.3at now proves square integrability locally, rather than conditionally: the first raw Jacquet eigenvalue at this cut has absolute value \[ q^{-d^2a(\ell-a)/2}\,q^{-da(\ell-a)/2} <q^{-d^2a(\ell-a)/2}. \tag{2.19y} \] The first factor is the raw half modulus; the second is the strictly positive extra decay gap from (2.19x). The unitary central character is \(\omega_\rho^\ell\). This proves construction, irreducibility, genericity, whole-string surjection and coefficient square integrability for every cuspidal segment.

Segment derivatives and contragredience

For a segment \(\Delta=[u,v]_\rho=\{\rho\nu^u,\rho\nu^{u+1},\ldots,\rho\nu^v\}\), \(v-u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), denote its constructed generic head by \(S(\Delta)\). It is the appropriate real twist of the centered construction. Formula (2.19x) gives the exact normalized derivatives \[ \partial_{rd}S([u,v]_\rho) =S([u+r,v]_\rho),\quad 0\le r\le v-u+1, \tag{2.19z} \] where an empty segment is the trivial \(G_0\)-module; other derivative ranks are zero. Indeed the trailing factor in (2.19x) is generic of dimension one, and (2.19d) is exactly its normalized generic coinvariant. The remaining first-factor twists identify the terminal subsegment \([u+r,v]\), without an additional half determinant. This checks both the rank and twist in (2.19z).

Also \[ S([u,v]_\rho)^\vee \simeq S([-v,-u]_{\rho^\vee}). \tag{2.19aa} \] To prove it, ordinary duality makes the left side an irreducible generic subquotient of the decreasing dual cuspidal string. Genericity follows from the actual inverse-transpose theorem. The composition reversal argument of Lemma 2.3au puts it in the increasing dual string's composition multiset. That string has exactly one generic irreducible factor, namely its constructed head. This gives (2.19aa); it does not identify the ordinary dual of the whole increasing induction with its reflected reversal.

Unlinked segment induction is irreducible

Two segments on the same integral cuspidal line are linked if neither contains the other and their union is a segment. Segments on distinct integral lines are unlinked. A line here is an actual orbit under the integral twists \(\nu^{\mathbb Z}\); nonzero real twists never stabilize a cuspidal representation.

Lemma 2.3be (finite interval mechanism). Let a finite multiset of integer intervals be pairwise unlinked. For each interval \(\Delta\), choose a terminal subinterval \(U_\Delta\) and an initial subinterval \(L_\Delta\), allowing either to be empty. If \[ \sum_\Delta U_\Delta =\sum_\Delta(L_\Delta-1) \tag{2.19ab} \] as multisets of integers, all chosen subintervals are empty.

Proof. Distinct maximal intervals are disjoint and separated by at least one missing integer: otherwise their union is an interval and they are linked. Every other interval is contained in a maximal one. Fix a maximal \([a,b]\), including all its copies. If one of its terminal choices is nonempty, the left side contains \(b\). A shifted initial choice from an interval contained in this maximal interval has endpoint at most \(b-1\). Choices from a disjoint maximal interval to the right start at least at \(b+1\) after shifting; those to the left end earlier. None contains \(b\). Thus every terminal choice for this maximal interval is empty. Similarly a nonempty initial choice for it puts \(a-1\) on the right, while all terminal choices in its component start at least at \(a\), and disjoint components cannot contain \(a-1\). All its initial choices are empty too. Remove every copy of the maximal intervals and repeat. The remaining family is still pairwise unlinked; finite induction proves the lemma. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3bf. Normalized induction of a finite pairwise unlinked multiset \(S(\Delta_1),\ldots,S(\Delta_t)\) is irreducible and generic, in any order.

Proof. Its generic coinvariant is one dimensional and its length is finite by the actual flag calculation and Theorem 1.23v. Suppose that its mirabolic restriction had a nonzero nongeneric submodule \(M\). Let \(\partial_iM\), \(i<n\), be its highest nonzero derivative, and choose a simple submodule \(\sigma\) there. Lemma 2.3av and (2.19z) show that its support is the multiset of terminal subsegments of the original segments, with positive total remaining rank. For completeness, each quotient derivative product is itself a quotient of the cuspidal induction of those terminal segments; Lemma 2.3au therefore identifies each simple constituent's support exactly.

The pairing (2.19h), ordinary duality, and (2.19aa) also identify the same support as a multiset of initial subsegments of the original segments shifted by \(-1\). The two derivative allocations may be different, which is why (2.19ab) permits independent choices on its two sides. Resolve their equality separately on each integral cuspidal line. Lemma 2.3be makes every remaining segment empty, contradicting the positive remaining rank. Thus there is no such mirabolic submodule.

The dual family remains pairwise unlinked by (2.19aa), so the dual induction has the same homogeneity. The finite-length argument of Theorem 2.3az now applies: a generic simple submodule consumes the full generic fibre, and any nonzero remaining quotient would give a nongeneric submodule of the homogeneous dual. Hence the original induction is irreducible and generic. \(\square\)

Exhaustion and uniqueness of generic representations

Given a finite cuspidal multiset, separate its actual integral lines. On one line, let \(m(j)\) be the multiplicity of its \(j\)-th twist. For each positive integer \(h\), take the connected integer intervals in \(\{j:m(j)\ge h\}\). These finitely many intervals, over all levels and lines, form a pairwise unlinked segment multiset: components at one level are separated by a missing integer, and components at higher levels are contained in components at lower levels. Their total cuspidal multiset is the given one.

This is the unique pairwise unlinked segment multiset with those multiplicities. To verify uniqueness, maximal intervals in any such family are disjoint with a gap, and each other interval lies in one of them. Thus the maximal intervals are exactly the level-one connected components. Remove one copy of each. The resulting support multiplicities are \(m-1\) on each original component, and the remaining family is still unlinked. Repeat the argument at the next level. It reconstructs precisely the level components just described, including repeated intervals.

Theorem 2.3bg. Every irreducible admissible generic representation is the normalized induction of this unique pairwise unlinked multiset of constructed cuspidal segments. Conversely all those inductions are irreducible generic representations.

Proof. The actual unordered cuspidal quotient Theorem 1.23k supplies a cuspidal multiset for the representation. Alternatively its actual embedding supplies the same multiset by Lemma 2.3au. Its full cuspidal induction has generic dimension one and finite length, so exactly one of its irreducible composition factors is generic. Composition multisets are preserved under arbitrary cuspidal reorderings by Lemma 2.3au.

Induce the level-component segments just constructed. Theorem 2.3bf makes that actual induction irreducible generic. Each segment is an actual quotient of its whole increasing cuspidal string; exactness and induction in stages make the segment induction an actual quotient of a cuspidal induction with the given multiset. It is therefore the unique generic composition factor, equal to the original representation. This proves exhaustion. Its support determines the unique level components, proving uniqueness. The converse was Theorem 2.3bf. \(\square\)

Every coefficient-tempered irreducible is generic

This analytic-to-generic step does not assume the classification just proved.

Lemma 2.3bh. Let \(V\) be a finite-length admissible module with unitary scalar center, whose every smooth coefficient belongs to every \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) modulo the center. Its mirabolic restriction has no nonzero nongeneric submodule.

Proof. Ordinary smooth dual coefficients are the original coefficients composed with inversion, by smooth biduality; quotient Haar measure is invariant under inversion. Thus \(V^\vee\) has the same property. By the proved Theorem 2.3an criterion, every raw Jacquet root at the cut \((m,i)\), \(m=n-i\), has absolute value at most \(q^{-mi/2}\). The normalized module \(r_{m,i}V\) multiplies its first-block central scalar by \(q^{mi/2}\). Consequently every central root on \(\partial_iV\), the trailing generic coinvariant of that normalized Jacquet module, has absolute value at most one. This is an actual finite module assertion, using Lemma 2.3av and the compact Jacquet lift. The same bound holds for \(\partial_iV^\vee\).

If \(M\subset V|_P\) were nonzero and nongeneric, let \(\partial_iM\), \(i<n\), be highest, and take an irreducible submodule \(\sigma\). Its central uniformizer scalar has absolute value at most one, since it is a subquotient of \(\partial_iV\). The pairing (2.19h) embeds \(\sigma\) in \((\partial_i(\nu V^\vee))^\vee\). Every central root of \(\partial_i(\nu V^\vee)\) has absolute value at most \(q^{-m}\), because the remaining rank is \(m>0\). Its ordinary dual roots are their inverses, of absolute value at least \(q^m>1\). This contradicts the first bound on the actual central scalar of \(\sigma\). No support or segment hypothesis entered this contradiction. \(\square\)

Taking \(M=V|_P\) shows that every nonzero such module has a nonzero generic coinvariant. In particular every irreducible coefficient-tempered representation with unitary center is generic.

Actual tempered induction classification, including ties

Theorem 2.3bi. An irreducible admissible representation with unitary center is coefficient-tempered if and only if it is normalized induction of a uniquely determined unordered multiset of unitary-centered cuspidal-segment square-integrable blocks. Every such induction is irreducible and generic. In particular equal real exponents can be combined into an actual irreducible coefficient-tempered block.

Proof. In the forward direction Lemma 2.3bh gives genericity and Theorem 2.3bg gives an induction of a unique unlinked segment multiset. Write its factors as \(D_j\nu^{e_j}\), where \(D_j\) is the unitary-centered constructed segment and \(e_j\in\mathbb R\). All the \(D_j\) are square-integrable by (2.19y), and \(\sum_j n_je_j=0\) because the full central character is unitary.

For each \(j\), place this segment first. Reordering the unlinked segment factors gives another irreducible generic induction by Theorem 2.3bf and the same composition multiset by Lemma 2.3au; thus it is actually isomorphic to the original irreducible representation. Its normalized Jacquet module at rank \(n_j\) has the identity-orbit quotient consisting of that first whole segment and the remaining induction. The first central scalar on this nonzero quotient has absolute value \(q^{-n_je_j}\). The normalized Theorem 2.3an bound is at most one, so \(e_j\ge0\).

Place the same segment last and use the first rank \(n-n_j\). Its identity-orbit quotient has first central absolute value \(q^{-\sum_{k\ne j}n_ke_k}=q^{n_je_j}\), so \(e_j\le0\). If there is just one segment, the unitary central character itself gives \(e_j=0\). Thus every segment is unitary-centered. The quotients and eigenvalues here are actual: they are the closed identity stratum in the section filtration, and compact fixed-vector exactness transfers their scalar to the finite Jacquet spectra. No formal factor product is used.

Conversely unitary-centered segments are pairwise unlinked. On the same integral line their intervals are centered at the same point and hence nested; opposite half-integer parities lie on different integral lines. Different unitary cuspidal bases cannot be nontrivial real integral twists of each other, since that changes the central absolute value. Theorem 2.3bf therefore makes their induction irreducible generic. Theorem 2.3ao gives its coefficient-temperedness. Uniqueness of the segment multiset was Theorem 2.3bg.

An alternative check of irreducibility, useful for ties, is Lemma 2.3bh applied to the full induction and its dual, together with its generic dimension one and finite length. This gives the same simple-module argument as Theorem 2.3az, without a general unitary equivalence assumption. Twisting an equal-exponent induction by the inverse common real norm reduces it to exactly the unitary-centered case just proved. \(\square\)

These tempered blocks also have compatible unitary realizations. For a square-integrable irreducible segment, choose a nonzero smooth dual functional and integrate the product of its coefficients over \(Z\backslash G\), as in Lemma 1.23l. Finiteness follows from Cauchy-Schwarz and the proved coefficient L2 property; positivity, invariant kernel, and irreducibility make it a positive definite invariant form. Right invariance gives its invariance. The completion has exactly the finite-dimensional smooth fixed spaces, by compact orthogonal averaging and admissibility, so it is compatible. Normalized induction of finitely many such Hilbert blocks has the positive compact-picture inner product. The exact quotient integration law proves invariance. Compact averaging again identifies its smooth fixed spaces with those of the actual admissible induction. Its irreducibility was proved above, so this is its compatible irreducible unitary realization. No unitarity criterion is being quoted.

Exhaustion of essentially square-integrable blocks

Theorem 2.3bj. Every irreducible admissible essentially coefficient-square-integrable representation is a real norm twist of one constructed cuspidal segment, uniquely up to the isomorphism of its cuspidal data. Conversely each such twist is essentially square-integrable, irreducible and generic.

Proof. Unitarize the absolute value of the scalar central character by its unique real determinant twist, as in Theorem 2.3an or Lemma 1.23l. The strict Theorem 2.3an inequalities for L2 imply its non-strict inequalities for all \(L^{2+\epsilon}\), so Theorem 2.3bi expresses this representation as induction of unitary-centered segments.

If there are at least two segments, put one first and take the corresponding proper Jacquet cut. The identity-orbit normalized quotient has first central scalar of absolute value one. Returning to the raw module gives a root of absolute value exactly \(q^{-n_j(n-n_j)/2}\). It occurs in an actual finite Jacquet fixed space. The strict Theorem 2.3an L2 criterion forbids this equality. Thus there is only one segment, proving exhaustion. The real twist is uniquely fixed by the central absolute value, and Theorem 2.3bg uniquely reconstructs its segment and cuspidal base. The converse, irreducibility and genericity were the construction and (2.19y). \(\square\)

Positive realizations without a classification premise

The preceding segment construction gives positive realizations directly. The following alternative rank induction proves compatible unitarity from the coefficient criterion alone. A compatible realization means that the smooth vectors of the completed Hilbert representation are exactly the original admissible module.

The actual zero-exponent splitting

Lemma 2.3bk. If a coefficient-tempered irreducible \(V\) of rank \(d>1\) is not \(L^2\), it embeds in \(W_1\times W_2\), where \(W_1,W_2\) are coefficient-tempered irreducibles of positive smaller ranks.

Proof. The strict Theorem 2.3an criterion for \(L^2\) fails, while its weak tempered criterion holds. Some raw Jacquet root at a proper cut \((p,d-p)\) therefore has absolute value exactly \(q^{-p(d-p)/2}\). On the normalized Jacquet module this root is \(\beta\), of absolute value one. This is an actual root on a finite compact fixed space, not a limiting spectral value.

Theorem 1.23v gives finite length of this normalized Jacquet module. Its first-block central uniformizer \(T\) has a global annihilating polynomial, obtained by multiplying its scalar annihilators along a composition series. Polynomial Bézout projections select its nonzero \(\beta\)-primary summand. Select an actual simple quotient of that summand. The tensor theorem writes it as \(W_1\boxtimes W_2\). Its first scalar is \(\beta\), so the center of \(W_1\) is unitary. The full scalar of \(V\) is unitary and the parabolic modulus is one on it, so the center of \(W_2\) is unitary as well. A smooth character on \(\mathcal O^\times\) has finite image; its absolute value is one. Consequently the uniformizer calculation proves unitarity on the entire centers.

We check all proper normalized Jacquet roots of both \(W_j\), rather than inferring temperedness just from their central characters. Refine \(W_1\) at a cut \((h,p-h)\). Exactness and normalized coinvariants in stages make its Jacquet module tensored with \(W_2\) an actual quotient of \(r_{h,p-h,d-p}V\). Group its last two blocks. The first rank-\(h\) scalar is a scalar of \(r_{h,d-h}V\), whose absolute value is at most one by Theorem 2.3an. Its value survives the subsequent refinement because the refinement modulus is one on the scalar of the first coarse block. Thus every normalized first-central root of every proper Jacquet module of \(W_1\) has absolute value at most one.

For a proper cut \((h,d-p-h)\) of \(W_2\), use \(r_{p,h,d-p-h}V\), and group its first two blocks. The rank-\(p+h\) coarse scalar is the product of the full scalar of \(W_1\) and the first rank-\(h\) scalar of \(W_2\). The former has absolute value one. Theorem 2.3an bounds the product by one. The normalized modulus of refinement inside that coarse first block is one on its full scalar, so no extra factor enters. Thus every normalized first-central root of \(W_2\) also has absolute value at most one.

These statements concern every actual root: finite-length annihilators pass through exact Jacquet refinements and actual quotient modules; taking the product with a nonzero other tensor factor loses none of their roots. Undoing normalization gives precisely the raw Theorem 2.3an bounds for \(W_1,W_2\). They are coefficient-tempered. The simple tensor is a quotient of \(r_{p,d-p}V\); actual adjunction supplies a nonzero map \(V\to W_1\times W_2\), which is injective. \(\square\)

Positive forms, completions and smooth vectors

Lemma 2.3bl. An \(L^2\) irreducible has a compatible irreducible unitary realization.

Proof. Choose a nonzero smooth dual functional \(\ell\), and define

\[ H(v,w)=\int_{Z_d\backslash G_d} \ell(V(g)v)\,\overline{\ell(V(g)w)}\,d\bar g . \tag{2.20a} \]

The integrand is well-defined on the quotient because the scalar center is unitary; finiteness follows from the coefficient \(L^2\) hypothesis and Cauchy–Schwarz. The quotient integration and bi-invariant measure are the actual construction in Lemma 1.23h. Right invariance proves \(G_d\)-invariance of \(H\). It is positive semidefinite. It is nonzero since some \(\ell(v)\ne0\) and that coefficient is constant and nonzero on an identity compact open neighborhood. Its kernel is an invariant subspace, so irreducibility makes it zero.

Complete this positive space. Each group operator extends isometrically. Strong continuity follows by density from the fact that each smooth vector is fixed by a compact open subgroup. For any compact open \(J\), orthogonal averaging \(E_J\) is continuous, and \[ \mathcal H^J=\overline{E_JV}=\overline{V^J}=V^J, \tag{2.20b} \] the last equality because \(V^J\) is finite-dimensional. Thus the smooth vectors of the completion are exactly the original actual module \(V\). Any closed invariant Hilbert subspace has an orthogonal projection commuting with the group. Its restriction preserves the spaces in (2.20b) and hence gives an invariant direct summand of \(V\). Irreducibility of \(V\) makes the Hilbert representation irreducible. \(\square\)

Lemma 2.3bm. Normalized induction of finitely many compatible unitary admissible blocks has a compatible unitary realization. Every actual submodule of its smooth module splits.

Proof. Tensor the positive invariant forms of its actual blocks. In the compact section picture define \[ H_I(f,f')=\int_{K_d}H_M(f(k),f'(k))\,dk,\qquad \operatorname{vol}(K_d)=1 . \tag{2.20c} \] A nonzero section is nonzero on a compact open set, so this form is positive definite. Its scalar-valued integrand transforms by the parabolic modulus, because the section covariance contains its positive half modulus and the inducing form is invariant. The actual quotient integration law of Lemma 1.23a consequently proves right-\(G_d\) invariance of (2.20c). This checks the normalization needed here: the product of the two half moduli is precisely that quotient density.

Its completion is strongly continuous by the same dense smooth-vector argument. Induction is admissible by the written finite compact double-coset proof. Orthogonal compact averaging therefore gives \(\mathcal H_I^J=I^J\) as in (2.20b); the smooth core is the actual full induction.

Let \(W\subset I\) be any actual invariant submodule, and let \(\mathcal H_W\) be its Hilbert closure. Averaging on that closure gives \[ \mathcal H_W^J=\overline{W^J}=W^J. \tag{2.20d} \] Indeed \(W^J\subset I^J\) is finite-dimensional. The orthogonal projection onto \(\mathcal H_W\) commutes with the group and maps \(I^J\) into \(W^J\). Every vector of \(I\) lies in some \(I^J\), so this projection restricts to an actual smooth \(G_d\)-equivariant projection \(I\to W\). Thus every submodule splits. If \(I\) has finite length, it is a finite semisimple smooth module, by splitting a simple submodule and inducting on length. \(\square\)

Exhaustion by actual \(L^2\) inductions and unitarity

Theorem 2.3bn. Every coefficient-tempered irreducible has a compatible irreducible unitary realization. It embeds in, and is an actual quotient of, a normalized induction of actual unitary \(L^2\) irreducibles. That full induction is finite-length semisimple.

Proof. Induct on rank. At rank one the unitary scalar character already has its one-dimensional unitary realization and is \(L^2\) modulo its center. At any rank an \(L^2\) irreducible is handled by Lemma 2.3bl. Otherwise Lemma 2.3bk embeds \(V\) in an induction from smaller-rank coefficient-tempered irreducibles. By rank induction those blocks have compatible unitary realizations, so Lemma 2.3bm makes their induction unitary. Restrict its positive form to the actual embedded \(V\), and repeat the completion and admissibility argument of Lemma 2.3bl. This gives a compatible irreducible unitary realization of \(V\).

The same rank induction refines every non-\(L^2\) block by Lemma 2.3bk until only \(L^2\) blocks remain. Exact induction and actual induction in stages preserve the embedding at each step. Every split lowers the ranks of both children; this finite recursion ends after at most \(d-1\) proper splits. Its final induction is unitary by Lemma 2.3bm and finite-length by Theorem 1.23v. It is therefore semisimple by Lemma 2.3bm. The embedded simple \(V\) is a direct summand and hence an actual quotient as well. This is an existence theorem for the actual discrete blocks, without a claim that their multiset has yet been reconstructed uniquely. \(\square\)

For a real twist \(V\nu^a\), this theorem gives the compatible essentially unitary realization after removing that exact real exponent. No exchange, segment construction or a classification stated in a reference is used.

Finite real profiles and the decreasing quotient

For an irreducible rank-\(d\) block set \[ e(V)=-\frac{\log|\omega_V(\varpi)|}{d\log q}. \tag{2.21a} \] Then \(V\nu^{-e(V)}\) has unitary center. Its smooth scalar character has finite image on \(\mathcal O^\times\), and \(\nu(\varpi I_d)=q^{-d}\) gives the sign and denominator. Throughout this construction coefficient-tempered means unitary center and all smooth coefficients in every \(L^{2+\epsilon}(Z\backslash G)\). The positive-realization proofs above make these blocks compatibly unitary. Pooling consecutive blocks preserves an actual embedding by the finite-filtration argument below.

Finite real profiles and actual finite-filtration selection

Lemma 2.3bo. Fix an irreducible admissible \(\pi\) of \(G_n\). Its actual embeddings into normalized induction from irreducible admissible blocks have only finitely many central real profiles, including the sole block \(\pi\). A profile has value \(e_j\) on a block of length \(d_j\), and

\[ \|\lambda\|^2=\sum_jd_je_j^2. \tag{2.21b} \]

Proof. For an embedding into blocks \(\mu_j\), refine each block by its actual cuspidal embedding. Exact induction, tensor injections and induction in stages give an actual embedding of \(\pi\) into induction from their combined cuspidal lists. Intrinsic cuspidal-support uniqueness Theorem 1.23x identifies that combined list with the fixed finite multiset \(S(\pi)\). Central action on each full induction is the product of its inducing central characters, since its modulus is one on a scalar matrix; the same is true on every subquotient. Therefore each \(e(\mu_j)\) is the rank-weighted average of the real exponents of its assigned submultiset of \(S(\pi)\). There are finitely many ordered partitions of the finite set of positions of that multiset. They give all possible ranks and profiles. Multiplicities are represented by distinct positions, so repetitions introduce no finiteness assumption. The identity embedding supplies the sole block. \(\square\)

Lemma 2.3bp (actual selection under coarsening). Suppose simple admissible \(\pi\) embeds in induction from a list of actual irreducible admissible blocks. Partition that list into consecutive groups. Then \(\pi\) embeds in induction from one actual irreducible constituent of the full induction inside each group. The chosen constituent's central real exponent is that group's rank-weighted average.

Proof. Let \(J_a\) be the full normalized induction in each consecutive group. It is finite-length admissible by Theorem 1.23v. Induction in stages gives an actual isomorphism between the original ambient induction and \(I_Q(J_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes J_s)\). Tensor their finite composition filtrations; every successive factor is an actual simple outer tensor product by the proved tensor theorem. Induction is exact, so these give a finite filtration of the ambient \(G_n\)-module.

Intersect this filtration with the embedded simple image of \(\pi\). Every intersection is either zero or that whole image. At the first nonzero intersection, the preceding intersection is zero, so projection to that successive quotient remains injective on \(\pi\). That quotient is exactly induction from an actual simple constituent in each \(J_a\). This proves the selected embedding, through actual submodules and quotient maps, rather than virtual composition factors. The center of \(J_a\) is the product of its original block characters, and remains so on its selected constituent. Formula (2.21a) gives the claimed weighted average. \(\square\)

The exact weighted pooling lemma

Consider finitely many entries \(z_j\), with positive integer weights \(d_j\), and inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_jd_jx_jy_j\). Let \(C=\{y_1\le\cdots\le y_m\}\).

Lemma 2.3bq. Repeatedly pool adjacent blocks whose weighted averages are in the wrong order, replacing each pooled block by its weighted average. This terminates in the orthogonal projection \(y\) of \(z\) onto \(C\). Equal adjacent final averages may be combined.

Proof. Start with singleton blocks. Maintain the assertion that in every current block its residual \(z\) minus the block average has nonnegative weighted prefix sums and total sum zero. It holds initially. Suppose averages \(c_1>c_2\) are pooled to \(c\). A prefix within the first block gains \((c_1-c)\) times its weight, hence remains nonnegative. A prefix extending into the second has residual

\[ (c_1-c)D_1+(c_2-c)D'_2+R'_2, \tag{2.21c} \]

where \(0\le D'_2\le D_2\), \(R'_2\ge0\), and \((c_1-c)D_1+(c_2-c)D_2=0\). Since \(c_2-c\le0\), the displayed expression is nonnegative. Its total residual is zero. Pooling reduces the number of blocks, so it terminates.

For the final \(y\), let \(R_j=d_j(z_j-y_j)\). Its total sum is zero, every prefix sum is nonnegative, and its sum within each constant block of \(y\) is zero. Summation by parts yields

\[ \langle z-y,u\rangle =-\sum_{j<m}\left(\sum_{a\le j}R_a\right)(u_{j+1}-u_j) \le0\quad(u\in C),\qquad \langle z-y,y\rangle=0. \tag{2.21d} \]

Consequently \(\langle z-y,u-y\rangle\le0\), and expansion of \(\|z-u\|^2\) shows it is at least \(\|z-y\|^2+\|u-y\|^2\). This is the required unique orthogonal projection. Combining equal final averages does not alter \(y\) or these identities. \(\square\)

Lemma 2.3br (strict norm gain). Let \(x\) be constant on consecutive blocks with strictly increasing block values. Split one block into two positive lengths with new values \(a<c<b\), where \(c\) was the old value and the split has the same weighted average \(c\). Write \(z=x+\delta\) on the refined coordinates. Its pooled profile \(y\) satisfies \(\|y\|>\|x\|\).

Proof. The split gives \(\delta\ne0\), supported in the old block, with weighted sum zero. Thus \(\langle x,\delta\rangle=0\). For a sufficiently small \(0<\epsilon\le1\), \(u=x+\epsilon\delta\) is nondecreasing: the split is internally increasing, and the old inter-block gaps were strict. By (2.21d),

\[ \langle z,u\rangle\le\langle y,u\rangle\le\|y\|\|u\|. \tag{2.21e} \]

Put \(A=\|x\|^2\ge0\), \(B=\|\delta\|^2>0\). The numerator is \(A+\epsilon B\), and \(\|u\|^2=A+\epsilon^2B>0\). Therefore

\[ \|y\|^2\ge\frac{(A+\epsilon B)^2}{A+\epsilon^2B}>A, \tag{2.21f} \]

because the difference of its numerator from \(A(A+\epsilon^2B)\) is \(\epsilon B[2A+\epsilon(B-A)]>0\) for \(0<\epsilon\le1\). This includes \(A=0\). \(\square\)

Increasing coefficient-tempered embedding existence

Lemma 2.3bs (a non-tempered block splits in the required direction). Let irreducible admissible \(V\) have central real exponent \(c\). If \(V\nu^{-c}\) is not coefficient-tempered, then \(V\) embeds in a proper two-block induction from irreducible admissible \(V_1,V_2\), of ranks \(p,d-p\), with

\[ e(V_1)=a<c<b=e(V_2),\qquad pa+(d-p)b=dc. \tag{2.21g} \]

Proof. Apply the proved Theorem 2.3an criterion to the unitary-central \(V\nu^{-c}\). Some raw proper Jacquet eigenvalue \(\alpha\) satisfies \(|\alpha|>q^{-p(d-p)/2}\). The normalized first-central action has eigenvalue \(\beta=q^{p(d-p)/2}\alpha\), with \(|\beta|>1\).

This normalized Jacquet module is finite-length admissible by Theorem 1.23v. Its first scalar \(T=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi I_p,I_{d-p})\) acts centrally. Its finite composition series has scalar eigenvalues \(\beta_a\) on its simple factors; the product \(\prod_a(T-\beta_a)\) annihilates the whole module, by successive application along that series. Polynomial Bézout identities split the module into invariant generalized-root summands. The \(\beta\)-summand is nonzero because the specified fixed-space eigenvector lies in it. It has an actual simple quotient; on that quotient \(T\) acts by \(\beta\). The actual tensor theorem writes it as \(W_1\boxtimes W_2\).

Formula (2.21a) gives \(e(W_1)=-\log|\beta|/(p\log q)<0\). The total central character of the normalized Jacquet module is that of \(V\nu^{-c}\), because the parabolic modulus is one on the full scalar. Hence \(pe(W_1)+(d-p)e(W_2)=0\), and \(e(W_2)>0\). Untwisting produces a simple quotient \(V_1\boxtimes V_2\) of \(r_{p,d-p}V\) with (2.21g). Actual normalized reciprocity supplies a nonzero map \(V\to V_1\times V_2\), whose kernel is zero by irreducibility. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3bt. Every irreducible admissible \(\pi\) has an actual embedding

\[ \pi\hookrightarrow I_P((\tau_1\nu^{e_1})\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes(\tau_r\nu^{e_r})), \qquad e_1<\cdots<e_r, \tag{2.21h} \]

with actual irreducible coefficient-tempered \(\tau_j\).

Proof. Among the finitely many strictly increasing realized profiles of Lemma 2.3bo choose one of maximal squared norm. Such a datum exists, since the sole block is allowed. If some normalized block were non-tempered, Lemma 2.3bs and exact induction would refine the actual embedding by a split \(a<c<b\). Pool this refined real profile by Lemma 2.3bq, combining all equal final averages. Each pool is a consecutive group of the refined actual irreducible blocks. Lemma 2.3bp selects actual irreducible constituents preserving an embedding of \(\pi\); their exponents are exactly the strictly increasing pooled averages. Lemma 2.3br makes its squared norm larger, contradicting maximality. Therefore all normalized blocks are coefficient-tempered. No permutation or adjacent-exchange operator is used. \(\square\)

The general geometric matrix and its exact weights

Lemma 2.3bu. Let \(P\) have ordered ranks \(d_i\), and \(Q\) ranks \(d'_j\). For actual irreducible admissible inducing blocks \(V_i\), every irreducible constituent \(M_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes M_s\) of \(r_QI_P(V_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes V_r)\) comes from a nonnegative integer dimension matrix \(p_{ji}\), with column sums \(d_i\) and row sums \(d'_j\), and actual irreducible factors \(W_{ji}\), of rank \(p_{ji}\), such that:

  1. For every column \(i\), the tensor of its nonzero \(W_{ji}\), in increasing row order, is an actual irreducible constituent of the normalized Jacquet module of \(V_i\) for those ranks.
  2. For every row \(j\), \(M_j\) is an actual irreducible constituent of the normalized induction of its \(W_{ji}\), in increasing column order.
  3. Its central real exponents satisfy
\[ d'_j e(M_j)=\sum_i p_{ji}e(W_{ji}). \tag{2.21i} \]

The diagonal whole-block matrix, when \(P=Q\), supplies the inducing tensor exactly once in the geometric filtration.

Proof. Apply the complete two-parabolic calculation to the first cut of \(Q\), refining the ordered inducing list by induction in stages. The proof of that calculation applies also when the remaining inducing factor is a full induction: its orbit sections, fiber relations, coinvariants and density do not require irreducibility. Each quotient assigns rank \(p_{1i}\) of each \(V_i\) to the first row and leaves rank \(d_i-p_{1i}\) to the remaining rows. Its normalized fiber is the tensor of the corresponding two-block Jacquet modules, with the normalized row inductions specified by the exact density table (2.9ch).

All these Jacquet modules and inductions have finite length by Theorem 1.23v. Refine their actual composition filtrations into simple outer tensors, using the actual tensor theorem. Exact Jacquet functors in the remaining rows refine this filtration further; coinvariants in stages impose exactly the full refined radical's relations, and their normalizing moduli multiply. Continue through all rows. Its dimension choices are precisely the matrices \(p_{ji}\).

Successive row refinement keeps the pieces in their original column order. Exactness also shows that the final column tensor is an actual constituent of the original multiblock Jacquet module of \(V_i\), rather than a label on virtual constituents. Every ambient irreducible constituent occurs in a successive quotient of this finite filtration: intersect its submodule preimage with the filtration and take the first nonzero simple image, as in Theorem 1.23x. Further actual composition filtrations of the row inductions give items 1–2.

The normalization at every binary step is the two negative half-moduli on the inducing Jacquet fibers plus the positive half-moduli on the row inductions, exactly as computed in (2.9ch). Transitivity multiplies these same densities. Thus no character remains beyond the normalized column Jacquet modules and normalized row inductions. A scalar in a row has modulus one for that row's inducing parabolic, so its central character is the product of the \(W_{ji}\) central characters. Formula (2.21a) gives (2.21i).

If the dimension choices send each whole \(V_i\) to its matching row and nothing elsewhere, every binary orbit choice is forced, the column Jacquet operation is the identity on \(V_i\), and each row induction has one block. Thus this geometric term is exactly \(\boxtimes_iV_i\) once. This last count concerns the actual filtration; further composition filtrations do not add multiplicity because that term is already simple. \(\square\)

Lemma 2.3bv (tempered column prefixes). In Lemma 2.3bu, suppose \(V_i=\tau_i\nu^{e_i}\), where \(\tau_i\) is coefficient-tempered. Put \(b_{ji}=e(W_{ji})-e_i\), with zero entries omitted. Then

\[ \sum_j p_{ji}b_{ji}=0,\qquad \sum_{j\le a}p_{ji}b_{ji}\ge0 \quad(1\le a<s). \tag{2.21j} \]

Proof. Untwist the column by \(\nu^{-e_i}\). Its total normalized-Jacquet central character remains the unitary character of \(\tau_i\); hence the total sum is zero. For a proper prefix of positive rank \(h<d_i\), group that prefix into one block. Coinvariants in stages show that its central scalar eigenvalue is a root of the normalized two-block Jacquet module of \(\tau_i\): first take that two-block module, then refine within the two Levi factors. A first scalar central in that coarse Levi retains its eigenvalue on all such refined subquotients. Alternatively, a polynomial annihilator of that scalar on the finite-length coarse module descends to every refinement. Its normalized absolute value is at most \(1\) by Theorem 2.3an, since the raw bound is \(q^{-h(d_i-h)/2}\) and normalization multiplies by \(q^{h(d_i-h)/2}\).

On the supplied column tensor the same scalar has absolute value \(q^{-\sum_{j\le a}p_{ji}b_{ji}}\). This proves the prefix inequality. Prefix rank zero gives sum zero; prefix rank \(d_i\) gives the already proved total zero. Empty matrix entries cause no new condition. \(\square\)

The norm inequality and the identity orbit

Lemma 2.3bw. In the situation of Lemma 2.3bu–Lemma 2.3bv, let the source exponents \(e_i\) be strictly increasing, and let the target constituent profile \(f_j=e(M_j)\) be nondecreasing. Then

\[ \|f\|^2=\sum_jd'_jf_j^2\le\sum_id_ie_i^2=\|e\|^2. \tag{2.21k} \]

If both profiles are strictly increasing and their norms agree, their ordered block ranks and real exponents agree, the only possible dimension matrix is the diagonal whole-block matrix, and the target constituent is the original inducing tensor.

Proof. Equations (2.21i)–(2.21j) and summation by parts give

\[ \begin{aligned} \|f\|^2 &=\sum_{j,i}p_{ji}f_j(e_i+b_{ji})\\ &\le\sum_{j,i}p_{ji}f_je_i\\ &\le \left(\sum_{j,i}p_{ji}f_j^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{j,i}p_{ji}e_i^2\right)^{1/2} =\|f\|\|e\|. \end{aligned} \tag{2.21l} \]

The first inequality has the sign shown because every column's weighted offset prefixes are nonnegative, its total is zero, and \(f_j\) is nondecreasing. The next inequality is the ordinary real weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with zero matrix entries ignored. If \(\|f\|=0\), (2.21k) is immediate; otherwise divide by \(\|f\|\).

If equal norms are positive, equality in Cauchy–Schwarz forces \(f_j=e_i\) for every positive \(p_{ji}\), since the two vectors have the same norm and positive proportionality factor one. If both norms are zero, that same conclusion holds directly. Every row and column has positive total rank. Strict increasing order therefore pairs their distinct values bijectively in order, so their counts coincide and each column's entire rank goes to its matching row. Their ranks coincide as well. No column is split, so its Jacquet operation is the identity, and no row has more than one inducing block. Lemma 2.3bu therefore identifies the target as \(\boxtimes_iV_i\), with the diagonal orbit's single occurrence. \(\square\)

Unique socle, unique decreasing head and canonical grouped data

Theorem 2.3bx (increasing unique socle). If \(V_i=\tau_i\nu^{e_i}\) with coefficient-tempered irreducible \(\tau_i\) and \(e_1<\cdots<e_r\), the full normalized induction \(I_P(V_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes V_r)\) has a unique irreducible subrepresentation, of socle multiplicity one.

Proof. It is a nonzero finite-length admissible module by Theorem 1.23v, so it has an irreducible submodule. Its normalized \(P\)-Jacquet module contains \(V_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes V_r\) as a geometric constituent exactly once: applying Lemma 2.3bw at this profile excludes every nondiagonal matrix, while Lemma 2.3bu gives the diagonal term once.

For any irreducible submodule \(S\hookrightarrow I_P\), actual reciprocity gives a nonzero map \(r_PS\to\boxtimes_iV_i\), hence an onto map to this simple tensor. If two distinct irreducible submodules existed, their intersection would be zero, giving an injection of their direct sum into \(I_P\). Exact Jacquet and finite-length additivity would then make the inducing tensor occur at least twice in \(r_PI_P\), a contradiction. The same proves socle multiplicity one: two independent embeddings of the same simple module either have different images, just excluded, or the same simple image and differ by a scalar by admissible Schur. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3by (canonical increasing data). If the same irreducible admissible \(\pi\) embeds into two inductions as in Theorem 2.3bx, their parabolics, ordered real exponents and actual normalized coefficient-tempered blocks are equal up to isomorphism.

Proof. Let one profile be \(e\), the other \(f\). Reciprocity makes the second inducing tensor an actual quotient of \(r_Q\pi\). Exactness makes \(r_Q\pi\) a submodule of the Jacquet module of the first ambient induction, so this inducing tensor is an actual constituent there. Lemma 2.3bw gives \(\|f\|\le\|e\|\). Reverse the two embeddings to obtain \(\|e\|\le\|f\|\). Equality forces the diagonal whole-block situation and identifies the actual inducing tensors. The tensor-factor uniqueness theorem then identifies each block representation. Formula (2.21a) already identifies each real exponent, and removing it identifies each \(\tau_i\). No Euler factors or central characters alone are used to identify those actual representations. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3bz (grouped decreasing coefficient-tempered quotient classification). Every irreducible smooth admissible representation \(\pi\) of every \(G_n(k)\) has a unique canonical datum

\[ (d_1,\ldots,d_r;\ \tau_1,\ldots,\tau_r;\ a_1>\cdots>a_r), \qquad \sum_id_i=n, \tag{2.21m} \]

where \(\tau_i\) are actual irreducible coefficient-tempered representations of \(G_{d_i}(k)\), such that \(\pi\) is the unique irreducible quotient of

\[ I_P((\tau_1\nu^{a_1})\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes(\tau_r\nu^{a_r})). \tag{2.21n} \]

This quotient has head multiplicity one. Every supplied strictly decreasing datum has such a unique quotient, and two such data have isomorphic quotients only when their actual blocks, ranks and real exponents agree.

Proof. Apply Theorem 2.3bt to \(\pi^\vee\). Ordinary smooth duality is exact on these admissible modules, uses the same upper parabolic and block order, and reverses real twists. The resulting onto map to \(\pi\) has strictly decreasing exponents \(a_i=-e_i\).

The contragredient of a coefficient-tempered irreducible is coefficient-tempered: every smooth coefficient of its dual is a coefficient of the original composed with inversion, by actual smooth biduality; inversion preserves the bi-invariant quotient measure and the unitary central modulus. Thus these are actual blocks of the required class. Theorem 2.3bx, dualized, proves uniqueness of the head and its multiplicity one, for the constructed datum and for every supplied strictly decreasing datum. Theorem 2.3by, applied to the two dual embeddings, proves canonical data uniqueness. Nonzero full induction has finite length, so its unique irreducible quotient exists. The same arguments work in rank one, where the datum is its unitary character and unique real exponent. \(\square\)

Irreducibility and independence of order at a tied exponent

Theorem 2.3ca. For any finite list of coefficient-tempered irreducibles \(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_t\), including repetitions, their full normalized induction is an actual irreducible coefficient-tempered representation with a compatible unitary realization. Its isomorphism class is independent of the order of the blocks.

Proof. Theorem 2.3bn supplies compatible unitary realizations of the actual \(\tau_j\). Lemma 2.3bm makes their full induction unitary. Theorem 1.23v makes it finite-length, and Lemma 2.3bm therefore makes it semisimple. Theorem 2.3ao gives coefficient-temperedness of the full induction and of every actual irreducible constituent.

Each \(\tau_j\) is generic by Lemma 2.3bh. The full earlier generic-induction section proof identifies the full generic coinvariant with the tensor product of their generic coinvariants. It is one-dimensional by the all-rank Whittaker uniqueness proof. On the other hand every irreducible constituent is generic by Lemma 2.3bh and has a one-dimensional generic coinvariant. Exactness of generic coinvariants, applied to a finite composition series (or to the actual semisimple decomposition), says that this one-dimensional space has dimension equal to the total length, with repetitions counted. That length is one. Thus the actual full induction is irreducible.

For order independence we need only an actual equality of composition multisets for adjacent exchanges, which has a short written proof. The full earlier contragredient theorem says \(X\circ\theta_d\simeq X^\vee\) for every irreducible admissible \(X\), where \(\theta_d(g)=w_d\,{}^tg^{-1}w_d\). Changing variables in normalized sections gives \[ (A\times B)\circ\theta_{a+b} \simeq (B\circ\theta_b)\times(A\circ\theta_a). \tag{2.22g} \] The upper parabolic is sent to the upper parabolic with reversed block sizes, and its half modulus to the reversed half modulus. Ordinary smooth duality instead gives \((A\times B)^\vee=A^\vee\times B^\vee\) in the same order. Apply these two exact functors to an actual finite composition series, and use inverse-transpose contragredience only on its irreducible factors. It follows that \(A\times B\) and \(B\times A\) have the same actual composition multiset for irreducible admissible \(A,B\). Composition filtrations give the same assertion for finite-length blocks. Exact induction then gives it for an adjacent exchange in a longer list. Any permutation is a finite succession of adjacent exchanges. Both original and permuted tempered inductions have length one by the preceding argument, so equality of their composition multisets is an actual isomorphism. No invertible exchange map at a reducibility point is assumed. \(\square\)

In particular, for any common \(a\in\mathbf R\), the full induction of \(\tau_j\nu^a\) is the real twist \((\tau_1\times\cdots\times\tau_t)\nu^a\) of this actual irreducible tempered block. Repeated or equal blocks cause no extra multiplicity.

The full weakly decreasing statement and canonical data

Theorem 2.3cb. Every irreducible admissible representation of every \(G_n(k)\) is the unique irreducible quotient, of head multiplicity one, of an induction of actual essentially tempered blocks in decreasing real order. Every supplied weakly decreasing list \[ \tau_1\nu^{a_1},\ldots,\tau_s\nu^{a_s}, \qquad a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_s, \tag{2.22h} \] has a unique irreducible quotient. Its canonical datum consists of the distinct decreasing real exponents and, at each exponent, the actual irreducible normalized induction of the supplied coefficient-tempered factors there. This grouped datum is unique for each quotient, and identifies its actual block representations, ranks and real exponents.

Proof. The strictly grouped Theorem 2.3bz classification constructs the datum and unique head for every irreducible, with canonical-data reconstruction Theorem 2.3by. Theorem 2.3bn proves that each of its coefficient-tempered blocks is genuinely compatible unitary tempered; therefore these are essentially tempered blocks in the stated sense.

For a supplied weakly decreasing list, gather consecutive equal exponents. By Theorem 2.3ca the full induction inside each group is an actual irreducible coefficient-tempered representation, independent of internal ordering. Normalized induction in stages identifies the whole supplied induction with the induction of those actual grouped blocks at the strictly decreasing distinct exponents. Theorem 2.3bx–Theorem 2.3bz therefore prove its unique irreducible quotient and head multiplicity one. Theorem 2.3by reconstructs and identifies these grouped blocks and exponents whenever two such quotients are isomorphic.

This is the canonical statement with ties: an ungrouped datum can replace one tempered block by an induction of smaller unitary tempered blocks and still describe the same induced module. Ungrouped lists are therefore not asserted to be unique. The actual block at each distinct real exponent is unique, as are its rank and real exponent. Repeated data and all finite nilpotent Jacquet root multiplicities were allowed in Lemma 2.3bo–Theorem 2.3bz and Lemma 2.3aw–Theorem 2.3ca. Nothing in these arguments uses the characteristic of \(k\) beyond finite residue field, additive Fourier inversion and the written compact matrix counts, valid in both cases. \(\square\)

Reconstructing the actual discrete blocks from Jacquet matrices

Theorem 2.3cc. Every coefficient-tempered irreducible is the actual full normalized induction of a uniquely determined unordered multiset of actual unitary \(L^2\) irreducibles. Every supplied such induction is irreducible, coefficient-tempered and compatibly unitary. Its decomposition is unique with repetitions counted.

Proof. Theorem 2.3bn embeds every coefficient-tempered irreducible into a normalized induction of actual unitary \(L^2\) irreducibles. Those blocks are coefficient-tempered by the strict and weak Theorem 2.3an criteria. Theorem 2.3ca makes their full induction irreducible. The nonzero embedding is therefore an actual isomorphism. The assertion for every supplied induction is precisely Theorem 2.3ca and Lemma 2.3bm.

For uniqueness, suppose the same actual irreducible is realized as \[ \pi\simeq D_1\times\cdots\times D_r \simeq E_1\times\cdots\times E_s, \tag{2.23a} \] where all \(D_i,E_j\) are unitary \(L^2\) irreducibles. Write their ranks as \(d_i,h_j\). The second realization and actual adjunction give an onto map \[ r_{h_1,\ldots,h_s}\pi\longrightarrow E_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes E_s . \tag{2.23b} \] Thus this tensor is an actual constituent of the Jacquet module of the first full induction. Apply the fully written dimension-matrix selection Lemma 2.3bu. It supplies a nonnegative matrix \(p_{ji}\), row sums \(h_j\), column sums \(d_i\), and actual normalized-Jacquet column constituents \(W_{ji}\), with row constituents \(E_j\). Put \(b_{ji}=e(W_{ji})\), since \(e(D_i)=0\).

Every column has total weighted exponent zero. For any proper positive prefix of rank \(a\) in column \(i\), the strict \(L^2\) Theorem 2.3an root bound, after normalization, is strictly less than one. As in Lemma 2.3bv, grouping that column's prefix produces an actual normalized Jacquet root of \(D_i\), whose absolute value is \[ q^{-\sum_{j\le t}p_{ji}b_{ji}}<1 . \tag{2.23c} \] Hence that column prefix sum is strictly positive. A zero-rank prefix or a whole-column prefix has sum zero. All column prefix sums are therefore nonnegative, and are strictly positive exactly when the cut divides that column into two nonempty pieces.

Each \(E_j\) has unitary center, so its real exponent is zero. The row equation in Lemma 2.3bu gives \[ \sum_i p_{ji}b_{ji}=h_j e(E_j)=0 . \tag{2.23d} \] Summing (2.23d) over any initial set of rows gives zero. It is also the sum of the nonnegative column prefix sums just described. None of those sums can be positive. Consequently no column can have entries in two different rows: a cut between two such rows would have a proper positive prefix in that column. Every column is sent whole to one row, and its actual Jacquet operation is the identity on \(D_i\).

Each row \(j\) is now assigned whole actual \(D_i\)'s, and \(E_j\) is a constituent of their normalized induction. Theorem 2.3ca makes this full induction irreducible, so it is \(E_j\) itself. A row cannot contain two or more columns. Indeed, partition such a row's inducing list after its first column. The actual identity orbit in the two-parabolic Jacquet filtration supplies a nonzero constituent whose first-block central uniformizer has absolute value one: the first whole \(D_i\) and all remaining blocks have unitary centers. Its scalar is an actual normalized Jacquet root, since finite-length annihilators and compact lifts identify these constituent scalars with roots. The strict Theorem 2.3an \(L^2\) bound would require absolute value less than one at that proper cut. This contradicts the \(L^2\) property of \(E_j\).

Thus every row contains exactly one whole column. The matrix is a permutation of whole blocks. Its row constituent is the assigned \(D_i\), with equal rank. Therefore the actual representations \(\{E_j\}\) and \(\{D_i\}\) agree as unordered multisets. Repeated isomorphic blocks remain separate columns and are counted separately. Theorem 2.3ca proves independence of the original block order. This proves the theorem. \(\square\)

Exact finite-place factors for every generic pair

Corollary 2.3cd. Let \(\pi,\sigma\) be any irreducible smooth admissible generic representations of positive ranks over \(k\). Their unique unlinked segment data give actual isomorphisms \[ \pi\simeq\mathop{\times}_i S_{\ell_i}(\rho_i)\nu^{u_i}, \qquad \sigma\simeq\mathop{\times}_j S_{k_j}(\zeta_j)\nu^{v_j}, \tag{2.24a} \] with unitary-centered cuspidals \(\rho_i,\zeta_j\). Then \[ L(s,\pi\times\sigma)= \prod_{i,j}\prod_{h=0}^{\min(\ell_i,k_j)-1} L\!\left(s+u_i+v_j+\frac{\ell_i+k_j-2}{2}-h,\, \rho_i\times\zeta_j\right). \tag{2.24b} \] Every cuspidal child factor is the explicit factor of Theorem 2.3af: it is one unless the ranks agree and \(\zeta_j\simeq\rho_i^\vee\otimes(\chi_z\circ\det)\). In that case it is \((1-z^tq^{-tw}X^t)^{-1}\) at shift \(w\), where \(t=|T(\rho_i)|\) and \(X=q^{-s}\). Repetitions contribute their full multiplicities. The normalized generator is attained by a finite sum of actual tests.

Proof. Theorem 2.3bg constructs (2.24a) for every generic irreducible and proves its uniqueness and irreducibility. Normalize each segment's central real character to obtain the displayed unitary-centered base and real twist. Permuting its unlinked factors still gives an irreducible induction by Theorem 2.3bf. The composition-multiset reversal proved after Lemma 2.3au identifies these irreducibles, so order them by decreasing \(u_i\) and \(v_j\). Theorem 2.3bd supplies the whole increasing-string map and exact Jacquet identity, and Proposition 2.3at proves square integrability of each base. Thus each displayed block is an actual generic essentially coefficient-tempered irreducible. Theorem 2.3aj applies to their whole ordered inductions and gives the product of block factors. Theorem 2.3al identifies each block-pair factor, giving (2.24b). The cuspidal factors are Theorem 2.3af with the direct norm substitution. Finally Proposition 2.3d proves finite actual test-sum attainment of the normalized ideal generator. All identifications here concern the Rankin–Selberg integral definition; comparison with separately chosen standard parameters and conductor labels requires those additional identification proofs. \(\square\)

Theorem 2.3cb gives a whole ordered quotient map for every irreducible admissible representation, including nongeneric ones. For a generic target, Lemma 2.3ak also transfers the full ordered Whittaker test space and its factor through that actual surjection. The more explicit unlinked presentation above supplies the stated cuspidal product.

Further reading is Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the freely accessible 1977 NUMDAM paper, §§3.7–4.15 and 7.1–7.3 and the 1980 sequel cited above. The derivative maps, adjacent reducibility, selected Jacquet modules and classification used here are proved in this lesson.

Which cuspidal strings contribute to a generic standard factor?

Only selected cuspidal strings contribute an Euler denominator. The integral definition determines their endpoint shifts and counts the contributing strings without assigning cuspidal Weil parameters.

Corollary 2.3ce. Let \(\pi\) be an irreducible smooth admissible generic representation of \(G_n(k)\), with the unique unlinked data of (2.24a). Write \(d_i\) for the rank of \(\rho_i\), so that \(\sum_i d_i\ell_i=n\), and let \(\chi\) be any smooth character of \(k^\times\). Define \[ J_\chi=\{i:d_i=1,\quad (\rho_i\chi)|_{\mathcal O^\times}=1\},\qquad b_i=(\rho_i\chi)(\varpi)\, q^{-u_i-(\ell_i-1)/2}\quad(i\in J_\chi). \tag{2.25a} \] Here a rank-one cuspidal \(\rho_i\) is an actual character of \(k^\times\). Then \[ L_{\mathrm{mat}}\bigl(s,\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det)\bigr) =\prod_{i\in J_\chi}(1-b_iq^{-s})^{-1}. \tag{2.25b} \] Its reciprocal polynomial in \(X=q^{-s}\) has degree exactly \(|J_\chi|\), with repetitions counted. In particular its degree is at most \(n\), and is \(n\) exactly when every string has length one and rank-one cuspidal base, and every \(\rho_i\chi\) is unramified. If \(\pi\) is coefficient-tempered and \(\chi\) is unitary, every pole has real part at most zero.

Proof. Theorem 2.3l identifies the left side of (2.25b) with \(L_{\mathrm{RS}}(s,\pi\times\chi)\), including equality of the complete test ideals. A character is the length-one, rank-one segment \(S_1(\zeta)\nu^v\), where \(\zeta\) is unitary and \(\chi=\zeta|\cdot|^v\), \(v\in\mathbb R\). To obtain this decomposition, observe that the absolute value of a smooth character is one on the compact unit group: its image there is a compact subgroup of the positive real numbers, and such a subgroup is trivial since the powers of any element other than one are unbounded in one direction. Its value on \(\varpi\) then determines \(v\). Corollary 2.3cd has \(\min(\ell_i,1)=1\); therefore it gives \[ L_{\mathrm{RS}}(s,\pi\times\chi) =\prod_i L_{\mathrm{RS}} \left(s+u_i+\frac{\ell_i-1}{2},\,\rho_i\times\chi\right). \tag{2.25c} \] The real norm \(v\) has been absorbed into the actual character \(\chi\) by the direct norm-substitution identity (2.9bh).

If \(d_i>1\), the unequal-rank assertion of Theorem 2.3af makes that factor one. For \(d_i=1\), its equal-rank assertion gives a nontrivial factor exactly when \(\chi=\rho_i^{-1}\chi_z\) for some unramified character \(\chi_z\). This is exactly the condition \((\rho_i\chi)|_{\mathcal O^\times}=1\); in that case \(z=(\rho_i\chi)(\varpi)\). A character has no nontrivial unramified self-twist, since cancellation in \(\rho_i\chi_z=\rho_i\) forces \(\chi_z=1\). Thus \(t_{\rho_i}=1\) in (2.16c), which gives precisely the linear factor in (2.25b).

Every \(b_i\) is nonzero. The product of the normalized linear polynomials \(1-b_iX\) has constant term one and degree \(|J_\chi|\): its leading coefficient is \((-1)^{|J_\chi|}\prod_i b_i\ne0\). The numerator of the factor is one, so neither coincidence of roots nor repetition cancels a denominator. Since \[ |J_\chi|\le\#\{i\}\le\sum_i d_i\ell_i=n, \tag{2.25d} \] equality with \(n\) forces every \(i\) to belong to \(J_\chi\) and every positive integer \(d_i\ell_i\) to be one. Conversely those conditions give equality.

For coefficient-tempered \(\pi\), Theorems 2.3bi and 2.3cc express it using unitary-centered strings with all \(u_i=0\). Each rank-one \(\rho_i\) is unitary; hence a unitary \(\chi\) gives \(|b_i|=q^{-(\ell_i-1)/2}\). A root \(1-b_iq^{-s}=0\) has \(q^{-\operatorname{Re}s}=|b_i|^{-1}\), so that \(\operatorname{Re}s=-(\ell_i-1)/2\le0\). This proves the final assertion. \(\square\)

For example, the centered length-\(n\) string with base the trivial character has matrix factor \((1-q^{-s-(n-1)/2})^{-1}\). Its reciprocal degree is one although the representation has rank \(n\).
