A higher-rank cuspidal string contributes no standard Euler denominator, even after a character twist. The degree counts the contributing strings. The monodromy calculation below gives the corresponding count for supplied parameters; Corollary 2.3cn states the precise compatibility hypotheses.

The exact epsilon exponent of a cuspidal string

Fix an additive character \(\psi\) whose annihilator of \(\mathcal O\) is \(\mathcal O\), and retain the self-dual measures. For any irreducible admissible representation \(\tau\), write its matrix epsilon factor, as proved in Theorem 1.17, in the form \[ \epsilon_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\tau,\psi) =w_{\mathrm{mat}}(\tau,\psi)\, q^{a_{\mathrm{mat}}(\tau)(1/2-s)}. \tag{2.26a} \] Its uniquely determined integer exponent \(a_{\mathrm{mat}}(\tau)\) is nonnegative by Corollary 1.24c. This is the analytic exponent of the actual matrix integral; its identification with a separately assigned Artin conductor is a further assertion.

Theorem 2.3cf. Let \(\rho\) be a unitary-centered actual Jacquet-cuspidal irreducible of rank \(d\), let \(\ell\ge1\), and let \(\chi\) be any smooth character. Put \(\vartheta=\rho\otimes(\chi\circ\det)\), \(a=a_{\mathrm{mat}}(\vartheta)\), and \(w=w_{\mathrm{mat}}(\vartheta,\psi)\). Let \(\delta=1\) if \(d=1\) and the character \(\vartheta\) is unramified, and let \(\delta=0\) otherwise. Then \[ \begin{split} A&=a_{\mathrm{mat}} \bigl(S_\ell(\rho)\otimes(\chi\circ\det)\bigr) =\ell a+(\ell-1)\delta,\\ \epsilon_{\mathrm{mat}} \bigl(s,S_\ell(\rho)\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi\bigr) &=Wq^{A(1/2-s)},\\ W&=\begin{cases} (-\vartheta(\varpi))^{\ell-1},&\delta=1,\\ w^\ell,&\delta=0 . \end{cases} \end{split} \tag{2.26b} \] For the actual generic presentation (2.24a), define \(A_i,W_i\) by (2.26b) with \(\rho_i,\ell_i,\chi\). Then the complete analytic epsilon factor is \[ \begin{split} \epsilon_{\mathrm{mat}} \bigl(s,\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi\bigr) &=\prod_i W_iq^{A_i(1/2-s-u_i)},\\ a_{\mathrm{mat}}\bigl(\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det)\bigr) &=\sum_i A_i,\qquad w_{\mathrm{mat}}\bigl(\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi\bigr) =\prod_iW_iq^{-u_iA_i}. \end{split} \tag{2.26c} \] All repetitions contribute separately. In particular the exponent is unchanged by any further unramified norm twist.

Proof: the actual gamma product. Tensoring by a determinant character preserves Jacquet-cuspidality: it is trivial on every unipotent radical, and its ordinary Jacquet quotient is the corresponding twist of the original quotient. Thus \(\vartheta\) is cuspidal and generic by Corollary 2.3ar. Let \(c=(\ell-1)/2\). Theorem 2.3bd gives the actual whole-string surjection from the induction of \(\rho\nu^{-c},\rho\nu^{1-c},\ldots,\rho\nu^c\) onto \(S_\ell(\rho)\). Twisting gives the same surjection with \(\rho\) replaced by \(\vartheta\). Lemma 2.3ak identifies its Whittaker function space and reflected test space with those of the target. Theorem 2.3ac gives the full induced gamma product; alternatively Corollary 2.3ad gives exactly the same scalar on this specified subquotient. Theorem 2.3n identifies each rank-one pairing with its matrix Fourier scalar. Therefore \[ \gamma_{\mathrm{mat}} \bigl(s,S_\ell(\rho)\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi\bigr) =\prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1} \gamma_{\mathrm{mat}}(s-c+j,\vartheta,\psi). \tag{2.26d} \] These are equalities of the meromorphic rational scalars of the actual integral families, not merely equalities of a spherical test.

The cuspidal cases with no Euler denominator. If \(\delta=0\), Theorem 2.3af and Theorem 2.3l give \(L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\vartheta)= L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\vartheta^\vee)=1\). Corollary 2.3ce gives the same two statements for the string and its dual: duality of the centered string is (2.19aa). Here \(\gamma=\epsilon\), so (2.26d) equals \[ \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1} wq^{a(1/2-s+c-j)} =w^\ell q^{\ell a(1/2-s)} . \] The shift sum is zero because \(\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}(-c+j)=0\). This proves (2.26b) in this case, including \(\ell=1\).

The unramified character case and its missing endpoints. Suppose \(\delta=1\), and put \(z=\vartheta(\varpi)\). Proposition 1.2, including its norm-shift extension, gives \(a=0,w=1\) for this character. Its gamma is \[ \gamma_{\mathrm{mat}}(s+t,\vartheta,\psi) =\frac{1-zq^{-s-t}} {1-z^{-1}q^{-1+s+t}} . \tag{2.26e} \] The direct string factor in (2.25b) keeps the endpoint \(t=c\). The dual factor at \(1-s\) keeps \(t=c\) for \(\vartheta^{-1}\), namely \((1-z^{-1}q^{-1+s-c})^{-1}\). Since \(\epsilon=\gamma L(s)/L(1-s,\tau^\vee)\), (2.26d) consequently reduces to the ratio whose numerator has \(t=-c,-c+1,\ldots,c-1\) and whose denominator has \(t=-c+1,\ldots,c\). For every numerator index \(t\), \[ \frac{1-zq^{-s-t}} {1-z^{-1}q^{-1+s+(t+1)}} =-zq^{-s-t}. \tag{2.26f} \] This is an identity of rational functions, so it also holds meromorphically at cancelled roots. There are \(\ell-1\) such indices and their sum is \(-(\ell-1)/2\). Their product is \((-z)^{\ell-1}q^{(\ell-1)(1/2-s)}\). For \(\ell=1\) the product is empty and equals one. This proves the remaining case of (2.26b). The extra exponent \(\ell-1\) comes from the endpoint cancellation.

Finally, the unique unlinked presentation of \(\pi\) is a full irreducible induction by Theorems 2.3bf and 2.3bg. Theorem 2.3ac makes its gamma the product of the block gammas. Corollary 2.3cd makes its \(L\)-factor the product of the block factors; applying it to the contragredient gives the corresponding dual product, with every \(u_i\) negated. Thus the defining gamma-to-epsilon ratios give the product of the block epsilons, evaluated at \(s+u_i\). This is (2.26c). Replacing \(s\) by \(s+b\) multiplies each root constant by \(q^{-bA_i}\) and leaves the exponent unchanged. Uniqueness of the Laurent exponent in (2.26a) proves the assertion. \(\square\)

Tensor strings and the exact Rankin–Selberg epsilon exponent

The same endpoint cancellation works for a pair of strings. When the cuspidal child factor has degree \(t\), the extra exponent is \(t(\ell k-\min(\ell,k))\): the grid has \(\ell k\) cells and \(\min(\ell,k)\) surviving chains. A child with factor one has no endpoint contribution.

Theorem 2.3cg. Let \(\rho,\zeta\) be actual unitary-centered Jacquet-cuspidal irreducibles, and let \(\ell,k\ge1\). For conductor-zero \(\psi\), write the cuspidal-pair epsilon factor as \[ \epsilon(s,\rho\times\zeta,\psi) =w_0q^{a_0(1/2-s)},\qquad w_0\ne0,\quad a_0\in\mathbb Z. \tag{2.27a} \] Put \(b=\ell k\), \(m=\min(\ell,k)\). Let \(t=0\) when \(L(s,\rho\times\zeta)=1\); otherwise use the notation of Theorem 2.3af, so that \[ L(s,\rho\times\zeta)=(1-z^tq^{-ts})^{-1}, \qquad t=|T(\rho)|,\quad \zeta\simeq\rho^\vee\otimes(\chi_z\circ\det). \tag{2.27b} \] Then \[ \begin{split} \epsilon(s,S_\ell(\rho)\times S_k(\zeta),\psi) &=Wq^{A(1/2-s)},\\ A&=\ell k\,a_0+(\ell k-\min(\ell,k))t,\\ W&=\begin{cases} w_0^{\ell k},&t=0,\\ w_0^{\ell k}(-z^t)^{\ell k-\min(\ell,k)},&t>0 . \end{cases} \end{split} \tag{2.27c} \] The power \(z^t\), and hence the formula, is independent of the choice of the unramified character representing the given \(\zeta\).

For the unique generic data in (2.24a), define \(A_{ij},W_{ij}\) by (2.27c) for \(\rho_i,\zeta_j,\ell_i,k_j\). The full epsilon factor is \[ \epsilon(s,\pi\times\sigma,\psi) =\prod_{i,j}W_{ij} q^{A_{ij}(1/2-s-u_i-v_j)} . \tag{2.27d} \] Thus its Laurent exponent is \(\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\). These formulas compute the integral-theoretic exponent from the cuspidal-pair exponents. They do not presume that \(a_0\) has already been identified with an Artin conductor.

Proof. Proposition 2.3i supplies (2.27a). The full increasing strings map onto \(S_\ell(\rho),S_k(\zeta)\) by Theorem 2.3bd. Their actual generic quotient maps and Lemma 2.3ak preserve the Whittaker function families and Fourier scalars. Iterating Theorem 2.3ac in both arguments gives \[ \gamma(s,S_\ell(\rho)\times S_k(\zeta),\psi) =\prod_{p=0}^{\ell-1}\prod_{r=0}^{k-1} \gamma(s-C+p+r,\rho\times\zeta,\psi), \qquad C=\frac{\ell+k-2}{2}. \tag{2.27e} \] The same conclusion follows by restriction to these specified generic subquotients in Corollary 2.3ad. All the norm shifts in the product have sum zero: each first-string shift occurs \(k\) times and each second-string shift occurs \(\ell\) times. Their cuspidal epsilon contributions are consequently \(w_0^{\ell k}q^{\ell k a_0(1/2-s)}\).

If \(t=0\), both the cuspidal-pair and its dual have factor one by Theorem 2.3af. The segment-pair and its dual have factor one by Theorem 2.3al. Hence gamma equals epsilon throughout, proving this case.

Now suppose \(t>0\). On dualizing both cuspidals, Theorem 2.3af replaces \(z\) by \(z^{-1}\) and leaves \(t\) unchanged. For an arbitrary shift \(x\), put \[ P_x=1-z^tq^{-t(s+x)},\qquad D_x=1-z^{-t}q^{-t(1-s-x)}. \] The cuspidal gamma at \(s+x\) is its epsilon there times \(P_x/D_x\). To cancel these factors we need the following finite multiset identity: \[ \{-C+p+r:0\le p<\ell,\ 0\le r<k\} =\coprod_{h=0}^{m-1} \{-H_h,-H_h+1,\ldots,H_h\}, \quad H_h=C-h. \tag{2.27f} \] This retains multiplicities. To prove it, exchange \(\ell,k\) if necessary so that \(\ell\ge k=m\). At the value \(-C+j\), \(0\le j\le\ell+k-2\), the left-hand multiplicity is the number of integers \(r\) with \[ \max(0,j-\ell+1)\le r\le\min(k-1,j). \] It is \(j+1\) before \(j=k-1\), then \(k\) through \(j=\ell-1\), then \(\ell+k-1-j\). On the right, an index \(h\) contributes exactly when \(0\le h<k\) and \(h\le j\le\ell+k-2-h\). Its number is the same \(\min(k,j+1,\ell+k-1-j)\). This proves (2.27f), including \(\ell=1\) or \(k=1\).

Theorem 2.3al keeps precisely the direct factor \(P_{H_h}^{-1}\) for each of these chains. By (2.19aa), its dual at \(1-s\) keeps \(D_{-H_h}^{-1}\). In the identity \(\epsilon=\gamma L(s)/L(1-s,\pi^\vee\times\sigma^\vee)\), the direct upper endpoint and the reflected lower endpoint are therefore removed from each chain. Its remaining ratio is \[ \prod_{x=-H_h}^{H_h-1}\frac{P_x}{D_{x+1}} =\prod_{x=-H_h}^{H_h-1} \bigl(-z^tq^{-t(s+x)}\bigr). \] The elementary identity follows by factoring \(1-y^{-1}=-y^{-1}(1-y)\) with \(y=z^tq^{-t(s+x)}\). The chain has \(2H_h\) remaining indices, whose sum is \(-H_h\). Its contribution is \[ (-z^t)^{2H_h}q^{2H_ht(1/2-s)}. \] Every \(2H_h\) is a nonnegative integer. The chain lengths \(2H_h+1\) sum to \(\ell k\): (2.27f) counts exactly \(\ell k\) entries. There are \(m\) chains, so \(\sum_h2H_h=\ell k-m\). Multiplying proves (2.27c), with the indicated sign even when \(t\) is even. Theorem 2.3af proves the invariance of \(z^t\).

Finally the presentations of both generic irreducibles are full irreducible unlinked inductions. Theorem 2.3ac gives the product of their block-pair gammas, and Corollary 2.3cd gives the direct and dual block-pair factors. Their ratios give (2.27d), with the real norm shifts \(u_i+v_j\). Equality of the Laurent exponents then gives their sum. \(\square\)

Weil–Deligne special blocks and their conductors

These calculations concern supplied finite-dimensional complex Weil representations with finite inertial image, over every nonarchimedean local field in either characteristic. We fix the Frobenius and ramification conventions and compute the factors and conductors from their actual finite operators.

Frobenius, the norm and the local factor

Let \(F\) have residue cardinality \(q\), let \(I\) be its inertia group, and choose a geometric Frobenius lift \(\Phi\in W_F\). Thus its residue action is the inverse of \(x\mapsto x^q\). Use

\[ v_W:W_F\longrightarrow\mathbf Z,\qquad v_W(\Phi)=1,\qquad |w|=q^{-v_W(w)},\qquad |\Phi|=q^{-1}. \tag{2.28a} \]

All Weil representations in this note are finite dimensional over \(\mathbf C\) and smooth on inertia; their inertial images are finite. This implies that their inertial kernels are open. The quotient \(W_F/I\) is discrete, so Frobenius can act by any invertible complex matrix. Frobenius semisimplicity is not needed in the proofs below. For \(t\in\mathbf C\), the unramified character \(|w|^t\) means \(\exp(t\log |w|)\), with the real logarithm of the positive number \(|w|\). In particular, its value on \(\Phi\) is \(q^{-t}\), without a branch choice.

A Weil–Deligne pair is \(D=(r,V,N)\), where \(r\) is such a Weil representation, \(N\) is nilpotent and

\[ r(w)Nr(w)^{-1}=|w|N. \tag{2.28b} \]

For \(i\in I\), equation (2.28b) says that \(r(i)\) commutes with \(N\). Put \(V_N=\ker N\) and define

\[ L(s,D)=\det\bigl(1-q^{-s}r(\Phi)\mid V_N^I\bigr)^{-1},\qquad L(s,\rho)=\det\bigl(1-q^{-s}\rho(\Phi)\mid V_\rho^I\bigr)^{-1}. \tag{2.28c} \]

Here the second notation regards \(\rho\) as a pair with zero monodromy. The determinant is a polynomial in \(X=q^{-s}\) with constant term one. This also defines it without any analytic convergence question. If the indicated space is zero its determinant is one.

These restrictions make sense: normality of \(I\) shows that \(r(\Phi)\) preserves \(V^I\), and (2.28b) shows that it preserves \(\ker N\). Replacing \(\Phi\) by \(i\Phi\), \(i\in I\), gives the same operator on \(V_N^I\), since \(r(i)\) is the identity there. Thus (2.28c) is independent of the chosen geometric lift.

For arithmetic Frobenius \(A=\Phi^{-1}\), the same definition is

\[ L(s,D)=\det\bigl(1-q^{-s}r(A)^{-1}\mid V_N^I\bigr)^{-1},\qquad |A|=q. \tag{2.28d} \]

One cannot replace the inverse matrix in this formula by \(r(A)\) while keeping the same factor and the same parameter. This observation fixes all Frobenius signs in the following statements.

A finite ramification definition of the conductor

The ramification groups here are the ones of the actual local extension, rather than an arbitrary filtration on the finite inertial image. In particular, the image filtration alone cannot be assigned new lower indices after passage to a quotient.

For a finite Galois \(E/F\), put \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\). Normalize \(v_E(E^\times)=\mathbf Z\) and put

\[ i_G(\sigma)=\min_{x\in\mathcal O_E}v_E(\sigma x-x),\qquad G_i=\{\sigma:i_G(\sigma)\ge i+1\},\qquad G_u=G_{\lceil u\rceil}\ (u\ge-1). \tag{2.28e} \]

Use \(i_G(1)=+\infty\). These are decreasing normal groups, \(G_0\) is inertia, and \(G_i=1\) for all sufficiently large \(i\). The intrinsic groups and their termination are proved in Ramification groups and the different of a local extension, Proposition 1.1. Let

\[ \varphi_{E/F}(u)=\int_0^u\frac{|G_t|}{|G_0|}\,dt\quad(u\ge0),\qquad \psi_{E/F}=\varphi_{E/F}^{-1},\qquad G^b=G_{\psi_{E/F}(b)}. \tag{2.28f} \]

For negative indices the rescaling is the identity. The finite upper groups are compatible with Galois quotients, and the inverse-limit upper group \(I^b\), \(b\ge0\), projects onto \(G^b\) at every finite Galois level. These are the quotient and inverse-limit assertions of Herbrand's function and the upper numbering, Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 4.1. No Hasse–Arf statement is used.

For a supplied \(\rho\) define its ordinary Artin conductor by

\[ a(\rho)=\dim V_\rho-\dim V_\rho^I +\int_0^\infty\bigl(\dim V_\rho-\dim V_\rho^{I^b}\bigr)\,db. \tag{2.28g} \]

This is a finite ramification calculation. To see that explicitly, the kernel of \(\rho|_I\) is open in \(I\). The profinite topology on \(G_F\) therefore supplies an open normal subgroup \(U\) with \(U\cap I\) contained in that kernel: take a neighbourhood whose intersection with \(I\) is contained in the kernel and then a finite Galois kernel inside that neighbourhood. Put \(E=(F^{\mathrm{sep}})^U\). The action of \(I\) on \(V_\rho\) factors through \(G_0\). The surjectivity just stated identifies its \(I^b\)-invariants with its \(G^b\)-invariants. On a positive lower interval \(i-1<u<i\), the group is \(G_i\) and \(db=|G_i|\,du/|G_0|\) under (2.28f). Consequently

\[ a(\rho)=\sum_{i\ge0}\frac{|G_i|}{|G_0|} \bigl(\dim V_\rho-\dim V_\rho^{G_i}\bigr). \tag{2.28h} \]

Every term after the finite lower filtration becomes trivial is zero. Values at the finitely many endpoints do not change the integral. Formula (2.28g) makes the definition independent of the chosen finite Galois \(E\); formula (2.28h) computes that same definition at every adequate finite level. For several representations one may choose a common level by intersecting the finitely many open normal subgroups. The finite inertial action, not the possibly infinite Frobenius image, is what factors through this level.

For a Weil–Deligne pair define

\[ a(D)=a(r)+\dim V^I-\dim(\ker N)^I. \tag{2.28i} \]

Since \(N\) commutes with inertia, the added term is \(\operatorname{rank}(N|_{V^I})\), a nonnegative integer. Equations (2.28h)–(2.28i) prove that these conductors are nonnegative rational numbers from the finite data. They do not prove that \(a(\rho)\), or hence every \(a(D)\), is an integer. No assertion of that general integrality is made here.

Lemma 2.3ch (the additivity and twist properties actually used). Ordinary Artin conductors are additive on a short exact sequence of these Weil representations. Weil–Deligne conductors and their local factors are additive, respectively multiplicative, on direct sums. For an unramified character \(\chi\),

\[ a(\rho\otimes\chi)=a(\rho),\qquad a(D\otimes\chi)=a(D). \tag{2.28j} \]

If \(\chi=|\cdot|^t\), then \(L(s,D\otimes\chi)=L(s+t,D)\). More generally \(\chi(\Phi)\) multiplies the Frobenius matrix in (2.28c).

Proof. Choose one adequate finite Galois level for a short exact sequence \(0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0\). For any one of its finite groups \(H=G_i\), an invariant vector \(v''\in(V'')^H\) has a lift \(v\in V\); the average

\[ |H|^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}r(h)v \tag{2.28k} \]

is an invariant lift of \(v''\). Thus the sequence of \(H\)-invariants is exact, and both dimension and invariant dimension are additive. Subtracting gives additivity of every summand of (2.28h), proving the first assertion. This averaging is in \(\mathbf C\), so it works when the residue characteristic divides \(|H|\).

On a direct sum, \(\ker(N_1\oplus N_2)=\ker N_1\oplus\ker N_2\), and all inertia-fixed spaces split in the same way. Equations (2.28h)–(2.28i) therefore give additivity. The restricted Frobenius matrix is block diagonal, so its determinant is the product of the two determinants, proving local-factor multiplicativity. Repeating this proves the assertions for any finite direct sum.

An unramified character is trivial on \(I\), and hence on every \(G_i\) in (2.28h). Tensoring by it leaves all those fixed spaces unchanged. It also leaves \(N\), its kernel and their inertia-fixed spaces unchanged under the natural underlying-vector-space identification. This proves (2.28j). Its Frobenius scalar is \(\chi(\Phi)\); for \(|\cdot|^t\) it is \(q^{-t}\). Substitute in (2.28c) to obtain the factor shift. \(\square\)

The direct-sum qualification for (2.28i) is necessary. For example, the pair \(\mathrm{Sp}_2\) defined below has a short exact sequence whose two ends are unramified one-dimensional pairs with zero monodromy, both of conductor zero, whereas \(a(\mathrm{Sp}_2)=1\). Thus (2.28i) is not generally additive on arbitrary exact sequences of Weil–Deligne pairs. The proof never uses that false assertion.

A single centered special block

For a positive integer \(\ell\), put \(a=\ell-1\) and let \(S_\ell\) have basis \(e_0,\ldots,e_a\). Define

\[ r_\ell(w)e_j=|w|^{a/2-j}e_j,\qquad N_\ell e_0=0,\qquad N_\ell e_j=e_{j-1}\quad(1\le j\le a). \tag{2.28l} \]

Denote this pair by \(\mathrm{Sp}_\ell\). It has finite trivial inertial action. For \(j>0\), conjugation scales \(N_\ell e_j\) by \(|w|^{(a/2-(j-1))-(a/2-j)}=|w|\); on \(e_0\) both sides are zero. Thus it satisfies (2.28b). Its kernel is exactly \(\mathbf C e_0\).

For a Weil representation \(\rho\), the notation \(\rho\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\ell\) regards \(\rho\) as having zero monodromy. Its pair is

\[ r(w)=\rho(w)\otimes r_\ell(w),\qquad N=1\otimes N_\ell. \tag{2.28m} \]

Theorem 2.3ci (special-block local factor and conductor). For every such \(\rho\),

\[ L(s,\rho\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\ell) =\det\bigl(1-q^{-s-(\ell-1)/2}\rho(\Phi) \mid V_\rho^I\bigr)^{-1} =L\bigl(s+(\ell-1)/2,\rho\bigr), \tag{2.28n} \] \[ a(\rho\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\ell) =\ell\,a(\rho)+(\ell-1)\dim V_\rho^I. \tag{2.28o} \]

Proof. A vector in \(V_\rho\otimes S_\ell\) has unique coordinates \(\sum_{j=0}^a v_j\otimes e_j\). Its image under \(N\) is \(\sum_{j=1}^a v_j\otimes e_{j-1}\), so it is killed exactly when all \(v_j\) for \(j>0\) vanish. Hence \(\ker N=V_\rho\otimes e_0\), with inertia invariants \(V_\rho^I\otimes e_0\). The geometric Frobenius on this space is \(q^{-a/2}\rho(\Phi)\), proving (2.28n).

The underlying Weil representation is the actual direct sum

\[ \bigoplus_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\rho\otimes|\cdot|^{(\ell-1)/2-j}. \tag{2.28p} \]

Lemma 2.3ch gives conductor \(\ell a(\rho)\) for this Weil part and inertia-fixed dimension \(\ell\dim V_\rho^I\). Its monodromy-kernel fixed dimension is \(\dim V_\rho^I\), already computed. Substitution in (2.28i) proves (2.28o). \(\square\)

For \(\ell=1\), one has \(\mathrm{Sp}_1=(1,\mathbf C,0)\): (2.28n) is the ordinary factor, and (2.28o) is \(a(\rho)\). For the zero representation both sides of the conductor formula are zero and its factor is one. If \(V_\rho^I=0\), the special-block factor is one and its conductor is \(\ell a(\rho)\). These conclusions do not require \(\rho\) to be irreducible.

An explicit finite-matrix tensor decomposition

For this section let \(\ell,k\ge1\), put \(a=\ell-1\), \(b=k-1\), and set \(m=\min(\ell,k)\). On \(S_\ell\) define three auxiliary matrices

\[ E e_j=e_{j-1},\qquad F e_j=(j+1)(a-j)e_{j+1},\qquad H e_j=(a-2j)e_j. \tag{2.29a} \]

Here \(e_{-1}=e_{a+1}=0\); in particular \(E=N_\ell\). Define the same matrices on \(S_k\), using basis \(f_0,\ldots,f_b\) and replacing \(a\) by \(b\). On their tensor product use

\[ E=E_\ell\otimes1+1\otimes E_k,\quad F=F_\ell\otimes1+1\otimes F_k,\quad H=H_\ell\otimes1+1\otimes H_k. \tag{2.29b} \]

Thus its actual tensor monodromy is \(E\), and its Weil matrix on \(e_i\otimes f_j\) is the scalar \(|w|^{(a+b)/2-i-j}\).

Lemma 2.3cj (finite commutators and a positive form). The matrices in (2.29a), and then those in (2.29b), satisfy

\[ [H,E]=2E,\qquad [H,F]=-2F,\qquad [E,F]=H. \tag{2.29c} \]

There is a positive Hermitian inner product for which \(E^*=F\) and \(H^*=H\), on both individual spaces and on the tensor product.

Proof. On \(e_j\), the first two commutators are the difference of the weights \(a-2(j-1)\), \(a-2j\), and \(a-2(j+1)\), giving the indicated factors \(2\) and \(-2\). The third is

\[ \bigl((j+1)(a-j)-j(a-j+1)\bigr)e_j=(a-2j)e_j. \tag{2.29d} \]

At \(j=0\) and \(j=a\) the absent term has coefficient zero, so this calculation covers the endpoints, also \(a=0\). Tensor operators on different factors commute, which proves (2.29c) for (2.29b).

Make the \(e_j\) orthogonal, with

\[ \langle e_j,e_j\rangle=\frac{(a-j)!}{j!\,a!}. \tag{2.29e} \]

These are positive real numbers. Their recurrence is

\[ \langle e_j,e_j\rangle=(j+1)(a-j) \langle e_{j+1},e_{j+1}\rangle\quad(j<a). \tag{2.29f} \]

This is exactly the adjoint identity for \(E e_{j+1}=e_j\) and \(F e_j=(j+1)(a-j)e_{j+1}\). All other matrix entries vanish, so \(E^*=F\). The real diagonal entries of \(H\) give \(H^*=H\). Define the analogous inner product on the \(f_j\) and the product inner product on the tensor basis. Tensoring and summing adjoint identities proves the claim there. \(\square\)

For \(0\le h<m\), define the explicit highest vector and its weight

\[ v_h=\sum_{i=0}^h(-1)^i e_i\otimes f_{h-i},\qquad c_h=a+b-2h=\ell+k-2-2h. \tag{2.29g} \]

All indices occur in the supplied bases, since \(h\le a,b\), and \(c_h\ge0\). The vector is nonzero: its coefficient at \(e_0\otimes f_h\) is one. Each term has \(H\)-weight \(c_h\). In \(Ev_h\), the coefficients at \(e_i\otimes f_{h-1-i}\), \(0\le i<h\), are \((-1)^{i+1}+(-1)^i=0\); there are no other terms. Thus

\[ Ev_h=0,\qquad Hv_h=c_hv_h. \tag{2.29h} \]

Lemma 2.3ck (the complete length of each chain). For \(j\ge1\),

\[ EF^jv_h=j(c_h-j+1)F^{j-1}v_h,\qquad HF^jv_h=(c_h-2j)F^jv_h. \tag{2.29i} \]

The vectors \(F^jv_h\), \(0\le j\le c_h\), are nonzero and linearly independent, and \(F^{c_h+1}v_h=0\).

Proof. The second identity follows by induction from \([H,F]=-2F\). For the first, \([E,F]=H\) and (2.29h) give the case \(j=1\). If it holds at \(j\), then

\[ \begin{aligned} EF^{j+1}v_h &=FEF^jv_h+HF^jv_h\\ &=\bigl(j(c_h-j+1)+c_h-2j\bigr)F^jv_h\\ &=(j+1)(c_h-j)F^jv_h. \end{aligned} \tag{2.29j} \]

This proves (2.29i) at every \(j\), without assuming any vector is nonzero. Lemma 2.3cj now gives the exact norm recurrence

\[ \|F^jv_h\|^2=j(c_h-j+1)\|F^{j-1}v_h\|^2. \tag{2.29k} \]

The coefficient is positive for \(1\le j\le c_h\), proving nonvanishing inductively from \(v_h\ne0\). At \(j=c_h+1\) it is zero, so positive definiteness forces \(F^{c_h+1}v_h=0\). For \(c_h=0\), this latter argument immediately gives \(Fv_h=0\). The nonzero vectors through \(j=c_h\) have distinct \(H\)-eigenvalues by (2.29i); they are therefore linearly independent. For completeness, apply the polynomial projector \(\prod_{\substack{0\le t\le c_h\\t\ne j}}(H-(c_h-2t))/((c_h-2j)-(c_h-2t))\) to any proposed relation. Its denominators are nonzero, and it isolates exactly the \(j\)-th vector. \(\square\)

Define their normalized versions by

\[ u_{h,j}=\frac{(c_h-j)!}{j!\,c_h!}F^jv_h\quad(0\le j\le c_h). \tag{2.29l} \]

Equation (2.29i) and the quotient of the two consecutive coefficients in (2.29l) give

\[ Eu_{h,0}=0,\qquad Eu_{h,j}=u_{h,j-1}\ (j>0),\qquad Hu_{h,j}=(c_h-2j)u_{h,j}. \tag{2.29m} \]

Also \(Fu_{h,j}=(j+1)(c_h-j)u_{h,j+1}\), with zero at the last position. Every \(F\) step replaces one index by its successor, so \(F^jv_h\) is a combination of tensor basis vectors with index sum \(h+j\). Consequently the actual Weil action, for every \(w\in W_F\), is

\[ r(w)u_{h,j}=|w|^{c_h/2-j}u_{h,j}. \tag{2.29n} \]

The map from the basis of \(\mathrm{Sp}_{c_h+1}\) to \(u_{h,0},\ldots,u_{h,c_h}\) is therefore an actual intertwiner of both Weil matrices and monodromy, by (2.29m)–(2.29n).

Theorem 2.3cl (centered tensor decomposition, with an explicit isomorphism). The preceding intertwiners together give

\[ \mathrm{Sp}_\ell\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_k \simeq\bigoplus_{h=0}^{m-1}\mathrm{Sp}_{\ell+k-1-2h},\qquad e_j^{(h)}\longmapsto u_{h,j}. \tag{2.29o} \]

Proof. It remains to prove that the different actual chains are independent and span. Define one more finite matrix

\[ C=H^2+2H+4FE. \tag{2.29p} \]

It is Hermitian: \(H^*=H\) and \((FE)^*=FE\). The commutators (2.29c) give

\[ \begin{aligned} [C,E]&=2HE+2EH+4E-4HE=0,\\ [C,F]&=-2HF-2FH-4F+4FH=0,\\ [C,H]&=-8FE+8FE=0. \end{aligned} \tag{2.29q} \]

In the first two lines, use \(EH-HE=-2E\) and \(FH-HF=2F\) to obtain zero. On \(v_h\), equation (2.29h) gives \(Cv_h=c_h(c_h+2)v_h\). Commutation with \(F\) gives that same eigenvalue on its whole chain. The numbers \(c_h\) are distinct nonnegative integers, and \(c(c+2)\) is strictly increasing there. Thus different chains lie in eigenspaces with different eigenvalues. They are mutually orthogonal: if \(Cx=\lambda x\), \(Cy=\mu y\) with distinct real \(\lambda,\mu\), the Hermitian identity gives \((\lambda-\mu)\langle x,y\rangle=0\). In particular, their sum is direct.

The dimensions found in Lemma 2.3ck sum to

\[ \sum_{h=0}^{m-1}(\ell+k-1-2h) =m(\ell+k-1)-m(m-1) =m(\ell+k-m)=\ell k. \tag{2.29r} \]

The last equality uses \(m=\min(\ell,k)\). This is the dimension of the tensor product, so the direct sum of chains is the whole space. Equations (2.29m)–(2.29n) prove that the stated bijection is an isomorphism of pairs, completing the proof. \(\square\)

The explicit finite operators and highest vectors give the entire tensor isomorphism. All factorial denominators and Hermitian averages are in \(\mathbf C\). They require no division by an integer in the local field, and therefore impose no field- or residue-characteristic restriction.

Tensor local factors and conductors

If \(D_1=(r_1,V_1,N_1)\), \(D_2=(r_2,V_2,N_2)\), their tensor pair has

\[ r=r_1\otimes r_2,\qquad N=N_1\otimes1+1\otimes N_2. \tag{2.30a} \]

The two summands in \(N\) commute. If \(N_1^A=N_2^B=0\), its \((A+B-1)\)-st power is zero by the binomial expansion: each term has an exponent at least \(A\) in the first summand or at least \(B\) in the second. Conjugation by \(r(w)\) multiplies each summand by \(|w|\), proving (2.28b) for the tensor. These facts prove that (2.30a) is indeed a Weil–Deligne pair.

Theorem 2.3cm (the tensor factor and exact tensor conductor). Let \(\rho,\zeta\) be supplied Weil representations with zero monodromy, put \(R=\rho\otimes\zeta\), and let \(m=\min(\ell,k)\). Then

\[ (\rho\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\ell)\otimes (\zeta\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_k) \simeq\bigoplus_{h=0}^{m-1} R\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_{\ell+k-1-2h}, \tag{2.30b} \] \[ \begin{aligned} L\bigl(s,(\rho\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\ell)\otimes (\zeta\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_k)\bigr) &=\prod_{h=0}^{m-1}L\bigl(s+(\ell+k-2)/2-h,R\bigr)\\ &=\prod_{h=0}^{m-1}\det\bigl(1-q^{-s-(\ell+k-2)/2+h} R(\Phi)\mid V_R^I\bigr)^{-1}, \end{aligned} \tag{2.30c} \] \[ a\bigl((\rho\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\ell)\otimes (\zeta\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_k)\bigr) =\ell k\,a(R)+(\ell k-m)\dim V_R^I. \tag{2.30d} \]

Proof. The actual reordering isomorphism

\[ (V_\rho\otimes S_\ell)\otimes(V_\zeta\otimes S_k) \longrightarrow(V_\rho\otimes V_\zeta)\otimes(S_\ell\otimes S_k),\qquad (v\otimes x)\otimes(z\otimes y)\longmapsto(v\otimes z)\otimes(x\otimes y) \tag{2.30e} \]

intertwines all Weil operators and carries monodromy to \(1\otimes E\). Apply Theorem 2.3cl and the explicit maps \(1_{V_R}\otimes u_{h,j}\) to obtain (2.30b). This tensor Weil representation still has finite inertial image, since the product of the two finite inertial images is finite.

Direct-sum multiplicativity in Lemma 2.3ch and (2.28n) give (2.30c), because the highest exponent of its \(h\)-th block is \((\ell+k-2)/2-h\). Let \(d_h=\ell+k-1-2h\). Direct-sum additivity and (2.28o) give

\[ \sum_{h=0}^{m-1}\bigl(d_h a(R)+(d_h-1)\dim V_R^I\bigr). \tag{2.30f} \]

Formula (2.29r) says that \(\sum_hd_h=\ell k\), and there are exactly \(m\) summands. Therefore (2.30f) is (2.30d). \(\square\)

There is also a direct check of the monodromy term. Theorem 2.3cl exhibits exactly \(m\) independent kernel vectors \(v_h\), so the tensor kernel has inertia-fixed dimension \(m\dim V_R^I\). Its full inertia-fixed dimension is \(\ell k\dim V_R^I\), and its ordinary Weil conductor is \(\ell k\,a(R)\), since its Weil part is a sum of \(\ell k\) unramified twists of \(R\). Substituting those three quantities in (2.28i) gives (2.30d) again.

When \(\ell=1\) or \(k=1\), there is one chain and its length is the other integer. When both are one, tensor monodromy is zero, (2.30c) is \(L(s,R)\), and (2.30d) is \(a(R)\). In general the spaces \(V_\rho^I\otimes V_\zeta^I\) and \(V_R^I\) need not agree. Both the determinant and conductor in these formulas use \(V_R^I\). Cancellation of a ramified character with its inverse is an elementary example of strict inequality of their dimensions.

Supplied sums, twists and repetitions

The same calculation applies to supplied block sums

\[ D=\bigoplus_{i=1}^t (\rho_i\otimes|\cdot|^{z_i})\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_{\ell_i},\qquad D'=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{t'} (\zeta_j\otimes|\cdot|^{w_j})\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_{k_j}. \tag{2.30g} \]

No assertion that every pair has this form is required. Lemma 2.3ch and Theorem 2.3ci prove

\[ L(s,D)=\prod_i L\bigl(s+z_i+(\ell_i-1)/2,\rho_i\bigr),\qquad a(D)=\sum_i\bigl(\ell_i a(\rho_i)+(\ell_i-1)\dim V_{\rho_i}^I\bigr). \tag{2.30h} \]

Distributing the actual tensor of finite direct sums and then applying (2.30c)–(2.30d) proves

\[ L(s,D\otimes D') =\prod_{i,j}\prod_{h=0}^{\min(\ell_i,k_j)-1} L\bigl(s+z_i+w_j+(\ell_i+k_j-2)/2-h,\rho_i\otimes\zeta_j\bigr), \tag{2.30i} \] \[ a(D\otimes D')=\sum_{i,j}\left[ \ell_i k_j\,a(\rho_i\otimes\zeta_j) +(\ell_i k_j-\min(\ell_i,k_j)) \dim(V_{\rho_i}\otimes V_{\zeta_j})^I\right]. \tag{2.30j} \]

All indices in these formulas are positions in the supplied direct sums. Repeated isomorphic blocks and coincident eigenvalues retain their full multiplicities: repeated determinants are multiplied repeatedly and their conductors are added repeatedly. No hypothesis of distinct Frobenius roots, distinct blocks or unitary twists is used.

The Weil topology and geometric Frobenius convention are fixed in Representations of Weil groups, §1. The integral generators used in ramification are proved in Unramified and totally ramified extensions, Theorem 5.1, Proposition 6.1 and Corollary 6.2.

For further reading on the conventions and block formulas, see Wedhorn, arXiv math/0011210v2, §§3.2.1–3.2.3 and Bisatt–Paterson, arXiv 2309.02782v2, Definition 2.3 and Lemmas 3.2–3.3.

From cuspidal compatibility to generic parameters

Corollary 2.3cn (supplied cuspidal parameters imply generic-pair factor and conductor compatibility). Suppose that, for the unitary-centered actual cuspidal bases occurring in two generic presentations (2.24a), irreducible smooth complex Weil representations \(R_i,Z_j\) with finite inertial image and the corresponding ranks are supplied. Suppose these cuspidal-pair identities hold:

\[ L_{\mathrm{RS}}(s,\rho_i\times\zeta_j)=L(s,R_i\otimes Z_j),\qquad a_{\mathrm{RS}}(\rho_i\times\zeta_j)=a(R_i\otimes Z_j). \tag{2.32a} \]

The analytic exponent here is the one in (2.27a) for the same conductor-zero additive character and measures. Define the supplied block parameters

\[ D_\pi=\bigoplus_i (R_i\otimes|\cdot|^{u_i})\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_{\ell_i},\qquad D_\sigma=\bigoplus_j (Z_j\otimes|\cdot|^{v_j})\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_{k_j}. \tag{2.32b} \]

Then the actual analytic formulas of Corollary 2.3cd and Theorem 2.3cg imply

\[ L_{\mathrm{RS}}(s,\pi\times\sigma)=L(s,D_\pi\otimes D_\sigma),\qquad a_{\mathrm{RS}}(\pi\times\sigma)=a(D_\pi\otimes D_\sigma). \tag{2.32c} \]

This implication retains every repeated base and block. It assumes neither general Artin integrality nor a generic newvector-conductor identification.

Proof. Put \(T_{ij}=R_i\otimes Z_j\) and \(d_{ij}=\dim T_{ij}^I\). The restricted \(T_{ij}(\Phi)\) is invertible on \(T_{ij}^I\): both it and its inverse preserve that space. Hence

\[ \deg\det(1-XT_{ij}(\Phi)\mid T_{ij}^I)=d_{ij}. \tag{2.32d} \]

Indeed, the coefficient of \(X^{d_{ij}}\) is \((-1)^{d_{ij}}\det(T_{ij}(\Phi)|_{T_{ij}^I})\ne0\); for \(d_{ij}=0\) the polynomial is one. The normalized reciprocal polynomial of the analytic cuspidal-pair factor has degree exactly \(t_{ij}\): it is one when \(t_{ij}=0\), and otherwise is \(1-z^{t_{ij}}X^{t_{ij}}\) with nonzero \(z\), by (2.27b). Equality of the two normalized reciprocal polynomials in (2.32a) therefore proves \(d_{ij}=t_{ij}\). Repetition of Frobenius roots cannot reduce this degree.

Apply the first equality in (2.32a), with the shifts of (2.24b), to every child factor of that actual analytic product. Equation (2.30i) is the identical parameter product, proving the first equality in (2.32c). For the conductor, (2.27c) gives

\[ A_{ij}=\ell_i k_j\,a_{\mathrm{RS}}(\rho_i\times\zeta_j) +(\ell_i k_j-\min(\ell_i,k_j))t_{ij}. \tag{2.32e} \]

Use the second equality in (2.32a) and \(t_{ij}=d_{ij}\). The result is exactly the \(i,j\) summand of (2.30j). The analytic full-pair exponent is \(\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\) by (2.27d); the parameter exponent is that same sum by (2.30j), unaffected by the unramified twists. This proves the second equality. \(\square\)

These identities concern the supplied block parameters. Identifying them with the parameters of the actual representations requires the cuspidal parameter construction and the base compatibility (2.32a). A generic newvector level and epsilon root constants also require their own identification arguments.

Real norm weights and the unitary epsilon phase

Corollary 2.3co. Suppose that the generic \(\pi\) of (2.24a) has a compatible unitary realization, and that \(\chi\) is unitary. For the nonnegative analytic string exponents \(A_i\) in (2.26b), \[ \sum_i u_iA_i=0,\qquad w_{\mathrm{mat}}\bigl(\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi\bigr) =\prod_iW_i,\qquad |W_i|=1 . \tag{2.33a} \] The conductor-weight identity is distinct from the scalar-center identity \(\sum_i d_i\ell_i u_i=0\).

Proof. Each base \(\rho_i\) has unitary center. Corollary 2.3ar and the positive coefficient integral (2.16h) give it a compatible unitary realization. Tensoring by the unitary character preserves that realization and its invariant norm. The unitary phase consequence of Theorem 1.17 gives \(|w_{\mathrm{mat}}(\rho_i\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi)|=1\). In the unramified rank-one case, \(|(\rho_i\chi)(\varpi)|=1\); in every other case the base constant has absolute value one. Both alternatives in (2.26b) therefore give \(|W_i|=1\).

The given realization of \(\pi\), twisted by the same unitary character, also has matrix epsilon constant of absolute value one. Taking absolute values in (2.26c) gives \[ 1=\left|\prod_iW_iq^{-u_iA_i}\right| =q^{-\sum_i u_iA_i}. \tag{2.33b} \] Every \(u_i,A_i\) is real and \(q>1\), so the real exponent is zero. This proves (2.33a). On scalar matrices, each centered base has unitary character, and the real norm of the \(i\)-th string is \(|z|^{d_i\ell_i u_i}\). Unitarity of the whole scalar character gives the second weighted identity, with ranks as weights. The weights \(A_i\) measure epsilon exponents instead. \(\square\)

Standard matrix factors for every finite-place irreducible

Canonical decreasing data have now been constructed for every irreducible representation. To compute its standard matrix factor, we need actual tests in the head itself. The following Schur-complement construction transfers the two endpoint families; their pole bounds then eliminate the possible polynomial correction. Repeated factors keep their full multiplicities.

An actual embedding transfers the smaller matrix family

Put \(G_j=\operatorname{GL}_j(k)\), \(K_j=G_j(\mathcal O)\), \(X=q^{-s}\), \(\mathscr R=\mathbb C[X,X^{-1}]\), and \[ C_j=\prod_{h=1}^j(1-q^{-h}),\qquad dg_j=C_j^{-1}|\det g|^{-j}\,dM_j(g), \qquad dM_j(M_j(\mathcal O))=1. \tag{2.34a} \] These are the programme's measures, with \(K_j\) of volume one. To check the constant directly, reduction modulo \(\varpi\) gives \(|\operatorname{GL}_j(\mathbb F_q)|=\prod_{h=0}^{j-1}(q^j-q^h)\): the next column must avoid the span of the preceding independent columns. Its proportion in \(M_j(\mathbb F_q)\) is \(C_j\). Left and right multiplication scale additive matrix measure by \(|\det g|^j\), so (2.34a) is Haar measure with the required normalization.

Lemma 2.3cp (matrix-family transfer from an actual embedding). Let \(r,t\ge1\), \(n=r+t\), let \(A,B\) be irreducible smooth admissible representations of \(G_r,G_t\), and suppose that an actual irreducible smooth admissible \(V\) embeds in the normalized upper induction \(A\times B\). Then \[ \mathcal I_A\subset\mathcal I_V. \tag{2.34b} \] The inclusion is realized by finite actual vectors, smooth dual functionals and matrix Schwartz tests, with the same integral variable.

Proof. Write \(j:V\hookrightarrow A\times B\) and evaluate its sections at the identity: \[ L(v)=j(v)(1),\qquad L(V(p)v)=\delta_P(p)^{1/2}(A\boxtimes B)(p)L(v). \tag{2.34c} \] Thus \(L\) is invariant under the upper radical and is a normalized Levi intertwiner. It is nonzero: otherwise \(j(v)(g)=L(V(g)v)=0\) for every \(v,g\). Its image is an invariant nonzero subspace of \(A\boxtimes B\). Here is the irreducibility check. In a nonzero submodule choose a tensor of minimal length \(\sum_{h=1}^kv_h\otimes w_h\); both lists are linearly independent, since a dependence would shorten it. Choose compact levels fixing these lists. Their two fixed spaces are finite-dimensional simple corner modules. The full simple-corner matrix argument proved in Lemma 2.0i supplies an operator on the first corner taking \(v_1\) to itself and all other \(v_h\) to zero. Its action puts \(v_1\otimes w_1\) in the submodule. Independent group translates of this tensor span the whole tensor product, because each factor is irreducible. Thus the outer tensor product is irreducible, and the image of \(L\) is all of it.

Fix any matrix coefficient \(\ell_A(A(a)v_A)\). Choose \(v_B,\ell_B\) with \(\ell_B(v_B)=1\), and lift \(v_A\otimes v_B\) to \(v\in V\). Choose \(d\ge1\) large enough that the principal congruence group \(J=1+\varpi^dM_n(\mathcal O)\) fixes \(v\), that its Levi part fixes \(\ell_A,\ell_B\), and that \(J_{t,d}\) fixes \(v_B\). Define the actual smooth dual vector \[ \ell_V=(\ell_A\otimes\ell_B)L e_J. \tag{2.34d} \] It is \(J\)-fixed because \(e_J\) is the normalized probability average. No functional on a quotient kernel is extended by an unsupported choice.

The exact block factorization and probability identity (1.21d)–(1.21e) give \(e_J=e_{J_U}e_{J_M}e_{J_{U^-}}\). For \(a\in G_r\cap M_r(\mathcal O)\), \(D\in J_{t,d}\), put \(m=\operatorname{diag}(a,D)\). Its inverse conjugation on a lower off-diagonal block is \(W\mapsto D^{-1}Wa\). Consequently \(m^{-1}J_{U^-}m\subset J_{U^-}\), including arbitrarily singular integral \(a\). The lower average therefore fixes \(V(m)v\). The upper average disappears under \(L\), and the Levi average disappears under the chosen Levi-fixed functional. Equation (2.34c) now proves the exact identity \[ \ell_V(V(m)v) =|\det a|^{t/2}\ell_A(A(a)v_A). \tag{2.34e} \] Here \(|\det D|=1\) and \(\ell_B(B(D)v_B)=1\).

Initially let \(\phi\in\mathcal S(M_r(k))\) have support in \(M_r(\mathcal O)\). On the clopen set \(D\in J_{t,d}\), use the Schur coordinate \(a=Z-CD^{-1}W\) and set \[ \Phi\!\begin{pmatrix}Z&C\\W&D\end{pmatrix} =\phi(Z-CD^{-1}W) 1_{\varpi^dM_{r,t}(\mathcal O)}(C) 1_{\varpi^dM_{t,r}(\mathcal O)}(W) 1_{J_{t,d}}(D), \tag{2.34f} \] extending it by zero elsewhere. This is locally constant with compact support on the whole matrix space. Its group points factor as \[ \begin{pmatrix}Z&C\\W&D\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1&CD^{-1}\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&D\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\D^{-1}W&1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2.34g} \] The outer factors are in \(J\). Since \(\ell_V\) and \(v\) are \(J\)-fixed, their coefficient is exactly (2.34e).

The additive change from \(Z\) to \(a\) has Jacobian one. Using \(\det g=\det a\det D\) and (2.34a), group Haar in these coordinates is \[ dg_n=\frac{C_rC_t}{C_n} |\det a|^{-t}|\det D|^{-r}\, dg_r(a)\,dg_t(D)\,dC\,dW. \tag{2.34h} \] The coefficient power \(t/2\), the global zeta weight \(s+(n-1)/2\), and the Haar power \(-t\) add to \(s+(r-1)/2\). Thus, in a common absolute-convergence half-plane, \[ Z_V(s,\Phi,v,\ell_V)=\kappa_{r,t,d} Z_A(s,\phi,v_A,\ell_A),\qquad \kappa_{r,t,d}=\frac{C_r}{C_n}q^{-d(t^2+2rt)}>0. \tag{2.34i} \] Indeed \(\operatorname{vol}(J_{t,d})=q^{-t^2d}/C_t\), and the two additive block volumes are \(q^{-drt}\) each. Rational continuation gives the identity everywhere.

Every original \(\phi\) has support in some \(\varpi^{-b}M_r(\mathcal O)\). The test \(\phi_b(a)=\phi(\varpi^{-b}a)\) has integral support and satisfies \[ Z_A(s,\phi_b,v_A,\ell_A) =\omega_A(\varpi)^b q^{-br(r-1)/2}X^{br} Z_A(s,\phi,v_A,\ell_A),\qquad X=q^{-s}. \tag{2.34j} \] This follows by \(a=\varpi^b h\), using multiplicative Haar and the actual scalar center of \(A\). The multiplier is a Laurent unit. The entire matrix family is a Laurent module by Proposition 1.3, with its multipliers realized by determinant translations. Dividing by this unit and by \(\kappa\) proves (2.34b) for every actual test. Finite sums remain finite sums of actual \(V\)-integrals. \(\square\)

Both canonical endpoints really embed

Corollary 2.3cq. Let \[ I=\tau_1\nu^{a_1}\times\cdots\times\tau_m\nu^{a_m} \twoheadrightarrow\pi,\qquad a_1>\cdots>a_m,\quad m>1, \tag{2.35a} \] be the canonical grouped data of Theorem 2.3cb. Let \(H_{\rm tail}\) and \(H_{\rm prefix}\) be the actual canonical heads omitting the first and the last blocks, respectively. There are actual embeddings \[ \pi\hookrightarrow H_{\rm tail}\times\tau_1\nu^{a_1}, \qquad \pi^\vee\hookrightarrow H_{\rm prefix}^\vee \times\tau_m^\vee\nu^{-a_m}. \tag{2.35b} \]

Proof. Exact induction maps \(I\) onto \(\tau_1\nu^{a_1}\times H_{\rm tail}\). The latter is nonzero, admissible and finite length, by the actual compact-section construction and Lemma 1.23a/Theorem 1.23v. An irreducible quotient of it is a quotient of \(I\), hence is \(\pi\) by the unique-head theorem. Smooth duality, proved exactly in Lemma 1.23j and for normalized induction in Lemma 1.23a, gives \[ \pi^\vee\hookrightarrow \tau_1^\vee\nu^{-a_1}\times H_{\rm tail}^\vee. \tag{2.35c} \] Use the programme's involution \(\theta_n(g)=w_n\,{}^tg^{-1}w_n\). Section pullback \(f\mapsto f\circ\theta_n\), followed by the actual tensor flip, identifies \[ (A\times B)\circ\theta_n \simeq(B\circ\theta_t)\times(A\circ\theta_r). \tag{2.35d} \] This is an identity of full smooth induction models. It sends the upper parabolic of ranks \(r,t\) to the upper parabolic of ranks \(t,r\); on its diagonal it sends \((a,D)\) to \((\theta_t(D),\theta_r(a))\). The two modular characters agree, since \[ |\det D^{-1}|^r|\det a^{-1}|^{-t} =|\det a|^t|\det D|^{-r}. \tag{2.35e} \] Theorem 2.0j applies to every irreducible admissible representation, including these nongeneric heads, and identifies \(A^\vee\circ\theta_r\) with \(A\). Applying this to (2.35c) proves the first embedding. The symmetric exact quotient \(H_{\rm prefix}\times\tau_m\nu^{a_m}\twoheadrightarrow\pi\) and its ordinary smooth dual prove the second. No second-adjointness or Jacquet-duality premise is required. \(\square\)

The entire matrix ideal of every head

Theorem 2.3cr (standard matrix factors for all finite-place irreducibles). For every actual irreducible smooth admissible \(\pi\), with the canonical data (2.35a), allowing \(m=1\) as well, \[ \mathcal I_\pi=D(s)\mathbb C[X,X^{-1}],\qquad L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)=D(s) =\prod_{i=1}^mL_{\rm mat}(s+a_i,\tau_i). \tag{2.36a} \] The generator is attained by a finite sum of actual \(\pi\)-tests. All ranks, ramification, repeated blocks and ties before canonical grouping, and both local field characteristics are included.

Proof. Proceed by rank, for the assertion for every irreducible of that rank. When \(m=1\), \(\pi=\tau_1\nu^{a_1}\); a determinant twist shifts the integral directly. For \(m>1\), exact matrix descent and its attaining sections in Lemma 1.23b, iterated in the full admissible compact models, give \(\mathcal I_I=D\mathscr R\). The actual constituent inclusion in Corollary 1.23c gives \[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)=R(X)D(s),\qquad R\in\mathbb C[X],\quad R(0)=1. \tag{2.36b} \] Write \(P_i(X)=L_{\rm mat}(s+a_i,\tau_i)^{-1}\). Both smaller heads have smaller positive rank. The rank induction, Corollary 2.3cq and Lemma 2.3cp therefore construct \[ \prod_{i=2}^mL_{\rm mat}(s+a_i,\tau_i)\in\mathcal I_\pi, \qquad \prod_{i=1}^{m-1}L_{\rm mat}(z-a_i,\tau_i^\vee) \in\mathcal I_{\pi^\vee}. \tag{2.36c} \] For the second product, \(H_{\rm prefix}^\vee\) is the decreasing head of the reversed list \(\tau_{m-1}^\vee\nu^{-a_{m-1}},\ldots,\tau_1^\vee\nu^{-a_1}\). This follows by applying (2.35d) and Theorem 2.0j to its actual quotient map. Each dual block is coefficient-tempered, since inversion preserves the coefficient \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) property and unitary center. Its reversed real exponents are decreasing.

Apply Corollary 1.23c also to the actual dual constituent, and write its correction \(\widetilde R\) relative to \(\widetilde D(z)=\prod_iL_{\rm mat}(z-a_i,\tau_i^\vee)\). The two containments (2.36c) imply \[ R\mid P_1,\qquad \widetilde R\mid\widetilde P_m \quad\text{in }\mathscr R,\qquad \widetilde P_m(q^{-z}) =L_{\rm mat}(z-a_m,\tau_m^\vee)^{-1}. \tag{2.36d} \] The actual whole matrix gamma product in Theorem 1.23 and Corollary 1.23c, and the Laurent-unit epsilon factors of Theorem 1.17, give \[ R(X)=bX^e\widetilde R(q^{-1}X^{-1}),\qquad b\ne0,\qquad e=\deg R=\deg\widetilde R. \tag{2.36e} \] For completeness, cancel \(\widetilde D(1-s)/D(s)\) from the two gamma expressions. Their epsilon quotient is a Laurent unit, so gives the first equality with some integer \(e\). The lowest power on the right is \(e-\deg\widetilde R\) and its highest is \(e\). The nonzero constant terms of both normalized corrections force the lowest power to be zero; their leading terms are nonzero. This proves both degree identities and retains the required monomial.

If \(R\ne1\), choose a nonzero root \(X=q^{-s_0}\). Its existence is the polynomial root argument already proved in Theorem 2.3aj; its nonzeroness follows from \(R(0)=1\). Divisibility by \(P_1\) forces a pole of \(L_{\rm mat}(s+a_1,\tau_1)\) there. The coefficient-tempered classification and the exact generic specialization in Corollary 2.3ce give its pole bound \(\operatorname{Re}s_0+a_1\le0\). The reflected root and the second divisibility give a pole of \(L_{\rm mat}(1-s-a_m,\tau_m^\vee)\), hence \(1-\operatorname{Re}s_0-a_m\le0\). Adding gives \[ 1+a_1-a_m\le0, \tag{2.36f} \] contrary to the decreasing order. Thus \(R=1\). The argument excludes every possible root, including repeated roots. Proposition 1.3 gives finite actual attainment once the entire ideals are equal; (2.36c) already used actual finite attaining families. This closes the rank induction. \(\square\)

Every irreducible's exact analytic conductor data

Decompose each actual unitary coefficient-tempered \(\tau_i\) into its unique unitary \(L^2\) blocks, and then their actual segments, using Theorems 2.3bi and 2.3cc. Write the resulting repeated list as \[ S_{\ell_b}(\rho_b)\nu^{u_b},\qquad \rho_b\text{ unitary-centered actual cuspidal},\quad d_b=\operatorname{rank}\rho_b. \tag{2.37a} \] Here each \(u_b\) is the real exponent of its canonical grouped block. These segments need not be unlinked across different real groups.

Corollary 2.3cs. Let \(\chi\) be any smooth character and put \(\theta_b=\rho_b\otimes(\chi\circ\det)\). With the conductor-zero additive character and the measures already fixed, write the actual cuspidal matrix epsilon as \[ \epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\theta_b,\psi) =w_bq^{a_b(1/2-s)},\qquad a_b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}. \tag{2.37b} \] Let \(\delta_b=1\) precisely when \(d_b=1\) and \(\theta_b\) is unramified; otherwise let it be zero. Put \[ A_b=\ell_ba_b+(\ell_b-1)\delta_b,\qquad W_b= \begin{cases} (-\theta_b(\varpi))^{\ell_b-1},&\delta_b=1,\\ w_b^{\ell_b},&\delta_b=0. \end{cases} \tag{2.37c} \] For every irreducible \(\pi\), including every nongeneric one, \[ \begin{split} L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det)) &=\prod_{\delta_b=1} (1-\theta_b(\varpi)q^{-u_b-(\ell_b-1)/2}q^{-s})^{-1},\\ \epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi) &=\prod_bW_bq^{A_b(1/2-s-u_b)},\\ a_{\rm mat}(\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det))&=\sum_b A_b . \end{split} \tag{2.37d} \] All multiplicities are retained.

Proof. Theorem 2.3cr computes both the head and dual factors as the products of their actual block factors. The whole gamma product of Theorem 1.23 therefore identifies the epsilon as the block epsilon product, with no remaining correction. Each block is actual generic, so Corollary 2.3ce and Theorem 2.3cf compute its factors and epsilon. Multiplying gives every formula in (2.37d). For a nonunitary \(\chi\), write \(\chi=\chi_0|\cdot|^v\), with \(\chi_0\) unitary and \(v\) real. The unit group has compact image, so its absolute value is one, and the value at \(\varpi\) determines this unique real \(v\). Twisting the actual head changes all grouped exponents by the same \(v\) and twists every centered cuspidal by \(\chi_0\). Rewriting this common shift as \(\theta_b\) gives exactly the displayed formulas, including their constants. Nonnegativity and integrality of each \(a_b\) were already proved for the actual matrix epsilon; no Artin or newvector equality is inserted. \(\square\)

Corollary 2.3ct (necessary unitary weights for every head). If \(\pi\) has a compatible positive unitary realization and \(\chi\) is unitary, then \[ \sum_bu_bA_b=0,\qquad w_{\rm mat}(\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det),\psi)=\prod_bW_b, \qquad \left|\prod_bW_b\right|=1. \tag{2.37e} \] The scalar-center equation is separately \(\sum_b d_b\ell_bu_b=0\); neither equation is asserted sufficient for unitarity.

Proof. The actual centered cuspidals have compatible positive unitary realizations, and a unitary character twist preserves them. The unitary matrix phase in Theorem 1.17 gives \(|w_b|=1\); in the unramified rank-one case \(|\theta_b(\varpi)|=1\). Thus \(|W_b|=1\). The critical constant in (2.37d) has modulus \(q^{-\sum_bu_bA_b}\). The same proved compatible-unitary phase applied to \(\pi\otimes(\chi\circ\det)\) gives modulus one, proving the first equality and then the two constant assertions. The unitary centered segments have unitary scalar center, so the absolute value of the actual scalar center in (2.37a) separately gives the rank-weight equation. \(\square\)

Corollary 2.3cu (the precise remaining single-cuspidal comparison). Suppose that irreducible smooth complex Weil representations \(R_b\) with finite inertia and rank \(d_b\) are supplied for the actual centered cuspidals in (2.37a), and suppose that \[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\rho_b)=L(s,R_b),\qquad a_{\rm mat}(\rho_b)=a(R_b). \tag{2.38a} \] Then the supplied block sum \[ D_\pi=\bigoplus_b(R_b\otimes|\cdot|^{u_b})\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_{\ell_b} \tag{2.38b} \] satisfies, for every \(\pi\), generic or nongeneric, \[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)=L(s,D_\pi),\qquad a_{\rm mat}(\pi)=a(D_\pi). \tag{2.38c} \]

Proof. In this untwisted comparison, specialize \(\chi=1\) in (2.37b)–(2.37c): \(a_b=a_{\rm mat}(\rho_b)\), and \(\delta_b=1\) exactly for a rank-one unramified \(\rho_b\). The reciprocal determinant polynomial for \(R_b\) has degree \(\dim R_b^I\), since its highest coefficient is a nonzero determinant of the invertible Frobenius restriction. The actual cuspidal reciprocal polynomial has degree \(\delta_b\), by the proved cuspidal specialization. The first identity (2.38a) therefore gives \(\dim R_b^I=\delta_b\), retaining repeated roots and Jordan matrices. The special-block identities of Theorem 2.3ci now give the same shifted factors as (2.37d) and the same conductor summands \(\ell_ba_b+(\ell_b-1)\delta_b\). Direct-sum multiplicativity and conductor additivity from Lemma 2.3ch prove (2.38c). This is a proved implication from both displayed cuspidal premises. It constructs no cuspidal correspondence and identifies neither canonical Weil epsilon root constants nor minimal newvector levels. \(\square\)

The generic minimal level and the analytic conductor

For a generic representation the analytic conductor also describes the first compact subgroup that fixes a vector. We first construct the essential Whittaker vector from its derivatives. A universal spherical transform then proves both minimality of its level and dimension one at that level.

Conventions and precise earlier providers

Let \(F\) be a nonarchimedean local field, of either characteristic,

\[ \mathcal O=\mathcal O_F,\quad \mathfrak p=\varpi\mathcal O, \quad |\varpi|=q^{-1},\quad G_d=\mathrm{GL}_d(F), \quad K_d=\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathcal O). \]

The nontrivial additive character \(\psi\) has annihilator of \(\mathcal O\) equal to \(\mathcal O\). Additive measures are self-dual, and the measures of \(K_d\), \(N_d(\mathcal O)\) and multiplicative unit shells are one. Whittaker characters on paired spaces are inverse. All inductions and derivatives are normalized exactly as in (2.19b–e). Right translation is \(R(h)W(g)=W(gh)\).

For \(n\ge2\), set \(m=n-1\) and

\[ H(c)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}h&v\\0&1\end{pmatrix}: h\in K_m,\ v\in(\mathfrak p^c)^m\right\},\qquad c\in\mathbb Z. \tag{2.40a} \]

Here \((\mathfrak p^c)^m\) means the column lattice \((\mathfrak p^c)^m\). Define \(K_1(\mathfrak p^0)=K_n\), and, for \(c>0\),

\[ K_1(\mathfrak p^c)= \left\{\begin{pmatrix}h&v\\u&x\end{pmatrix}\in K_n: u\in(\mathfrak p^c)^m,\ x\equiv1\pmod{\mathfrak p^c}\right\}. \tag{2.40b} \]

For \(n=1\) this means \(\mathcal O^\times\) at zero and \(1+\mathfrak p^c\) at positive levels.

The actual earlier inputs are the following complete programme proofs:

  • Theorem 2.0: Whittaker uniqueness and inverse-transpose contragredience; (2.9p–s), Lemma 2.3ap: exact Fourier fibres, compact sections and the simple bottom mirabolic module.
  • Lemma 2.3av, (2.19b–e): the exact normalized derivative filtration; Theorem 2.3bd and (2.19z–aa): constructed segment derivatives and ordinary duality; Theorems 2.3bf–bg: unlinked induction, its mirabolic homogeneity, and actual generic classification.
  • Proposition 2.1a, Lemma 2.1b, Proposition 2.1c: the complete spherical recurrence, Schur formula and rectangular Cauchy identity; Theorem 2.3ae: the whole spherical ideal, not just its test value. LG-GLOB-02 Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.2 supply the actual spherical occurrence and Hecke character. Their cyclic-submodule statement is not being strengthened to cyclicity of a reducible whole principal series.
  • Propositions 2.3b–d, Theorem 2.3h and Proposition 2.3i: rational integral families, entire normalized quotients and the exact scalar Fourier equation; Theorem 2.3ac and Corollary 2.3cd: full gamma multiplicativity and actual generic-pair factor products; Theorems 2.3l–n: equality of rank-one and matrix factors/scalars.
  • Corollary 2.3ce and Theorem 2.3cf: the actual generic standard factor and analytic epsilon exponent. Proposition 1.16 in rank one gives the character conductor calculation. Finite length and admissibility needed by the derivative filtration are proved in Theorem 1.23v and the actual geometric Jacquet calculation.

These providers are proof inputs, not an assumed newvector theorem. In particular Theorem 2.3aq supplies an essential irreducible submodule, not an essential Whittaker vector, and is not used as the latter.

Write

\[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)=P_\pi(q^{-s})^{-1},\qquad \epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\pi,\psi)=C_\pi(q^{-s})^{a_\pi}, \quad C_\pi\ne0,\ a_\pi\in\mathbb Z. \tag{2.40c} \]

Thus \(C_\pi=w_\pi q^{a_\pi/2}\). Keeping \(C_\pi\) and \(w_\pi\) distinct prevents a half-conductor normalization error.

Injectivity of the actual mirabolic restriction

Lemma 2.3cv. For a generic irreducible admissible \(\pi\), the map

\[ W\longmapsto W|_{P_n},\qquad P_n=G_mU_n, \tag{2.40d} \]

is injective.

Proof. Theorem 2.3bg writes \(\pi\) as the actual full induction of its pairwise unlinked segments. The proof of Theorem 2.3bf says that this full module has no nonzero \(P_n\)-submodule with zero final generic coinvariant. This statement applies to \(\pi\) itself.

The kernel \(M\) of (2.40d) is a \(P_n\)-submodule. If its final generic coinvariant were nonzero, the natural bottom inclusion (2.9r) would embed a nonzero copy of \(A_n=\mathrm{c\!-\!Ind}_{N_n}^{P_n}\psi_n\) in \(M\), and hence in \(\pi|_{P_n}\). Exactness and naturality identify its generic fibre with a nonzero subspace of the one-dimensional generic fibre of \(\pi\). On this bottom copy the actual Whittaker functional is the nonzero evaluation functional: this is proved by the local-section construction in (2.9q–s), starting with \(P_1\). Its translates therefore have nonzero restrictions to \(P_n\). That contradicts the definition of \(M\). Thus \(M\) is nongeneric; the stated homogeneity makes it zero. \(\square\)

The lemma also shows that \(K_m\)- or \(H(c)\)-invariance checked on the mirabolic restriction is invariance of the actual vector.

Two elementary function realizations of Fourier fibres

Let \(T\subset C^\infty(N_k\backslash P_k,\psi_k)\) be a smooth submodule, and write its functions on \(\operatorname{diag}(g,1)\), \(g\in G_{k-1}\). If \(u(x)\in U_k\), its right action is multiplication by

\[ \psi(e_{k-1}gx). \tag{2.40e} \]

For every compact additive lattice \(L\subset F^{k-1}\), ordinary probability averaging multiplies a function by \(1_{e_{k-1}g\in L^\perp}\). Averaging with weight \(\psi(e_{k-1}x)^{-1}\) multiplies it by \(1_{e_{k-1}g\in e_{k-1}+L^\perp}\). These are actual finite sums on a smooth vector. The vector minus either average is a finite sum of the corresponding ordinary or twisted differences.

Lemma 2.3cw. The normalized nonzero fibre \(\Phi^-T\) is the function model obtained by restriction

\[ f\longmapsto\bigl[p\longmapsto |\det p|^{-1/2}f(\operatorname{diag}(p,1))\bigr], \quad p\in P_{k-1}. \tag{2.40f} \]

The kernel is exactly the \(U_k,\psi(e_{k-1}\cdot)\) difference space. The ordinary \(U_k\)-difference space consists exactly of functions vanishing whenever the last row of \(g\) lies in a sufficiently small neighborhood of zero, with that neighborhood depending on the vector.

Proof. Twisted differences vanish on the indicated restriction, since \(e_{k-1}p=e_{k-1}\). Conversely, suppose that restriction is zero. Choose a principal congruence subgroup \(J\subset G_{k-1}\) fixing \(f\) on the right. Its row orbit \(e_{k-1}J\) contains a neighborhood of \(e_{k-1}\): if a row is congruent to \(e_{k-1}\) modulo a sufficiently high power of \(\mathfrak p\), it is the last row of \(1+A\) for a matrix \(A\) in that power. Every \(g\) with last row in this neighborhood has \(g=pj\), \(p\in P_{k-1}\), \(j\in J\). Hence \(f(g)=0\) there. Choose \(L\) so that the weighted average's frequency box is contained in that neighborhood. Its average of \(f\) is zero; subtracting the average expresses \(f\) by twisted differences. This proves the kernel. The actual fibre and its restriction image are therefore isomorphic; the negative half determinant in (2.40f) is precisely (2.19b).

An ordinary difference is \((\psi(e_{k-1}gx)-1)f(g)\), which vanishes for all sufficiently small last rows. A finite sum of differences has one common such bound. Conversely, if \(f\) vanishes in a small row ball, average over a lattice whose annihilator is contained in that ball. The average is zero, so the same finite-difference identity puts \(f\) in the ordinary kernel. No compactness of the other rows is required. \(\square\)

Lemma 2.3cx (compact lifting). \(\Phi^-\) maps \(T^{P_k(\mathcal O)}\) onto \((\Phi^-T)^{P_{k-1}(\mathcal O)}\). Ordinary \(\Psi^-\) maps \(T^{K_{k-1}}\) onto \((\Psi^-T)^{K_{k-1}}\).

Proof. The ordinary assertion is compact averaging of a lift. For the first assertion the nonzero-orbit submodule of \(T\) is the actual \(\Phi^+\Phi^-T\) of (2.19c); its existence, kernel and compact section identification are proved in (2.9p–q). Let \(v\) be a \(P_{k-1}(\mathcal O)\)-fixed vector of its fibre. Write an element of \(G_{k-1}\) as \(zpk\), with \(z\in F^\times\), \(p\in P_{k-1}\), \(k\in K_{k-1}\). This decomposition follows by normalizing the primitive last row, using elementary integral column operations. In the vector-valued compact-section model of \(\Phi^+\Phi^-T\), define the section

\[ f\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}zpk&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\right) =|\det p|^{1/2}\psi(x_{k-1})\,1_{\mathcal O^\times}(z) (\Phi^-T)(p)v. \tag{2.40g} \]

If two decompositions have unit \(z,z'\), then \(z'/z\in\mathcal O^\times\) and their \(p\)'s differ by a member of \(P_{k-1}(\mathcal O)\), after absorbing that central unit. The section is consequently well-defined; outside the unit-row locus it is zero. Its support on the nonzero row orbit is the compact set of primitive integral rows. The displayed covariance is exactly the positive half determinant of \(\Phi^+\). Right \(K_{k-1}\)-invariance is explicit. Right \(U_k(\mathcal O)\) adds \(zpkx_0\) to the column; on its support the last coordinate is integral, so its \(\psi\)-multiplier is one. The section is therefore \(P_k(\mathcal O)\)-fixed and evaluates to \(v\) in its fibre. It is an actual vector of the compact-section submodule of \(T\). This proves surjectivity, including zero-size groups. \(\square\)

The single spherical derivative line

Use the actual presentation of Theorem 2.3bg,

\[ \pi=\prod_i S([u_i,v_i]_{\rho_i}), \qquad v_i-u_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}. \tag{2.40h} \]

The segments are pairwise unlinked, with repetitions allowed. Let \(r\) be the number of those segments whose cuspidal base has rank one and is unramified. For each of these take its terminal actual character \(\chi_i=\rho_i\nu^{v_i}\), and put \(b_i=\chi_i(\varpi)\). Thus

\[ P_\pi(X)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(1-b_iX) \tag{2.40i} \]

by Corollary 2.3ce. These are slots in the actual segment multiset; equal \(b_i\)'s are counted separately.

Lemma 2.3cy. If \(0<r<n\), then \((\partial_{n-r}\pi)^{K_r}\) is a line. Its Hecke character is the Satake evaluation at \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\), and its central character is \(c(z)=\prod_i\chi_i(z)\). The assertions concern that line and the module it generates; they do not presume that a whole reducible unramified principal series is cyclic.

Proof. Evaluation at one in the compact picture gives, for any parabolic product, the equality of its \(K\)-fixed space with the tensor of the inducing blocks' compact fixed spaces. Indeed \(G=PK\), the half modulus is one on \(P\cap K\), and a constant right-\(K\) section is determined by its value fixed by \(P\cap K\). The radical acts trivially, leaving precisely the block compact groups.

A generic segment of rank \(d\ell>1\) has no compact spherical vector. If it had one, Theorem 2.3ae paired with the trivial rank-one character would give a standard reciprocal polynomial of degree \(d\ell\). Corollary 2.3ce gives degree at most one for this segment. These degrees contradict each other. A rank-one segment is spherical exactly when its character is unramified.

The exact derivative filtration (2.19e), with (2.19z), has one quotient for each allocation of removed ranks to the original segment slots. Its nonzero quotients are products of the remaining terminal segments. For such a quotient to have a \(K_r\)-fixed vector, each original unramified rank-one-base slot must leave at most one character, and every other slot must leave zero rank. Their total remaining rank is \(r\), the number of the former slots. Consequently all those slots must leave exactly their one terminal character. This is one allocation, even with repeated or nested segments. Its quotient is the full unramified character induction of the \(\chi_i\), in the inherited order, and its fixed space is one-dimensional. Every other quotient has zero fixed space. Exact compact averaging along the finite filtration therefore proves the claimed dimension and identifies its Hecke and central actions with those of that single quotient. The actual Satake calculation identifies the character with \(b\). \(\square\)

If \(r=n\), every original segment has rank and length one and is unramified; its full irreducible induction is spherical. If \(r=0\), the final derivative is the one-dimensional generic fibre.

A central ordinary fibre as an actual Whittaker germ

Here is the scalar-germ argument needed for existence; it is proved locally rather than imported from a derivative asymptotics theorem.

Lemma 2.3cz. Suppose \(T\subset C^\infty(N_{d+1}\backslash P_{d+1},\psi)\) and \(\Psi^-T\) has scalar central character \(c\). Then its ordinary fibre has the actual function realization

\[ S(f)(g)=|\det g|^{-1/2} \lim_{z\to0}c(z)^{-1}|z|^{-d/2} f(\operatorname{diag}(zg,1)),\quad g\in G_d. \tag{2.40j} \]

The expression is eventually constant for each \(g\); the kernel is exactly the ordinary difference space. It is a \(G_d\)-equivariant injective model of \(\Psi^-T\), with the ordinary normalized action.

Proof. The relation

\[ R(\operatorname{diag}(zI_d,1))f-c(z)|z|^{d/2}f \in T(U_{d+1},1) \tag{2.40k} \]

is precisely the scalar central action after the negative half determinant in \(\Psi^-\). By Lemma 2.3cw each such relation vanishes whenever the last row is sufficiently small. Take \(z=\varpi\). For \(g\in P_d\), that row in \(zg\) is \(ze_d\), independent of the other entries of \(g\). There is thus one integer \(B_f\) for which

\[ f(\operatorname{diag}(\varpi zg,1)) =c(\varpi)q^{-d/2}f(\operatorname{diag}(zg,1)) \quad(g\in P_d,\ v(z)\ge B_f). \tag{2.40l} \]

The unit part causes no new limit: smoothness gives an open unit subgroup fixing \(f\) under the central unit action and lying in the kernel of \(c\). Apply (2.40k) to the finitely many remaining unit coset representatives and enlarge \(B_f\). The normalized values are then independent of both the valuation and the unit of sufficiently small \(z\). For any fixed \(g\in G_d\), write \(g=z_0pk\) with \(p\in P_d\), \(k\in K_d\), and apply the same argument to \(R(k)f\). This proves existence of the limit. On each compact set there are finitely many right smooth cosets, so the resulting function is smooth.

Ordinary differences give zero limit by Lemma 2.3cw. If \(S(f)=0\), use the finite right-\(K_d\) cosets of a subgroup fixing \(f\). Applying the uniform bound (2.40l) to those finitely many translates shows that \(f\) vanishes whenever the last row is in one sufficiently small ball. Lemma 2.3cw makes it an ordinary difference. This proves the kernel, and also nondegeneracy of the induced model.

For \(h\in G_d\), inserting the normalized action \(|\det h|^{-1/2}R(h)\) into (2.40j) gives exactly \(S(f)(gh)\), because \(|\det(gh)|^{-1/2}=|\det g|^{-1/2}|\det h|^{-1/2}\). For \(u\in N_d\), its determinant is one and it commutes with the scalar \(zI_d\); the left Whittaker multiplier is therefore \(\psi_d(u)\). Thus the model is equivariant with the claimed character. \(\square\)

Construction of the essential vector

Theorem 2.3da. There is an actual \(H(0)\)-fixed Whittaker vector \(W_\pi^e\), normalized by \(W_\pi^e(1)=1\), with the following restriction when \(0\le r<n\). For \(a=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\) and \(a'=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\),

\[ W_\pi^e(\operatorname{diag}(a,1))= W_b^0(a')|\det a'|^{(n-r)/2} 1_{\mathcal O}(a_r)\prod_{r<j\le m}1_{\mathcal O^\times}(a_j) \quad(r>0), \tag{2.40m} \]

and for \(r=0\) it is \(\prod_{j=1}^{m}1_{\mathcal O^\times}(a_j)\). Here \(W_b^0\) is the normalized spherical Whittaker function given by the actual Schur recurrence at \(b\); no cyclicity theorem is an input. For \(r=n\), \(W_\pi^e\) is the normalized spherical vector of \(\pi\).

Proof. Assume \(0<r<n\). Repeated Lemma 2.3cw realizes

\[ T=(\Phi^-)^{n-r-1}(\pi|_{P_n}) \subset C^\infty(N_{r+1}\backslash P_{r+1},\psi), \qquad \Psi^-T=\partial_{n-r}\pi. \]

Let \(v_0\) generate the fixed line of Lemma 2.3cy. Compact averaging gives a \(K_r\)-fixed lift \(\widetilde f\in T\). Let \(T_0\) be its \(P_{r+1}\)-span. Its ordinary quotient is the \(G_r\)-span of \(v_0\), since ordinary unipotent action disappears in that quotient. The center acts on this span by \(c=\prod_i\chi_i\): it acts that way on \(v_0\) by Lemma 2.3cy and commutes with \(G_r\). Thus Lemma 2.3cz applies to \(T_0\).

The nonzero function \(S(\widetilde f)\) is \(K_r\)-fixed and is an eigenfunction for the Satake character \(b\), since the quotient's fixed line has that character. The full recurrence proof of Proposition 2.1a applies to any such Whittaker eigenfunction. Its lattice-coset calculation and induction show that all its values are its value at one times \(\delta_r^{1/2}s_\lambda(b)\); if its value at one were zero, Iwasawa and that recurrence would make the function zero. Rescale the lift so that its nonzero germ is \(W_b^0\). This uses no irreducibility, faithfulness or generation assertion for a whole reducible unramified principal series.

The central recurrence (2.40l) for this \(K_r\)-fixed lift is uniform in \(p\in P_r\). Choose \(B\ge0\) above its bound and set \(t=\varpi^B\). Replace the lift by

\[ \widetilde f_t(g)=c(t)^{-1}|t|^{-r/2} \widetilde f(g\operatorname{diag}(tI_r,1)). \]

It remains \(K_r\)-fixed. For \(g=zp\), \(p\in P_r\), \(v(z)\ge0\), the recurrence and the normalized germ give the exact equality

\[ \widetilde f_t(\operatorname{diag}(g,1)) =|\det g|^{1/2}W_b^0(g). \tag{2.40n} \]

Indeed the central scalar on the germ is \(c(z)\), and \(|\det(zp)|^{1/2}=|z|^{r/2}|\det p|^{1/2}\); these are exactly the two factors in (2.40j). Right \(K_r\)-invariance extends (2.40n) to every \(g\) whose last row is integral. Average over \(U_{r+1}(\mathcal O)\). By (2.40e) this multiplies the restriction by the indicator that its last row is integral, while preserving right \(K_r\). The resulting vector \(f_0\) is \(P_{r+1}(\mathcal O)\)-fixed and on its diagonal is

\[ f_0(\operatorname{diag}(a',1)) =|\det a'|^{1/2}W_b^0(a')1_{\mathcal O}(a_r). \tag{2.40o} \]

Now lift this vector backwards through each successive \(\Phi^-\), using Lemma 2.3cx. At a step from \(P_k\) to \(P_{k+1}\), take a compact-fixed lift and apply the difference of the two ordinary column averages whose annihilators are \(\mathcal O^k\) and \((\mathfrak p)^k\). It remains \(P_{k+1}(\mathcal O)\)-fixed and multiplies the restriction by the indicator that the last row is primitive integral. For a diagonal \(g=\beta_k(z)p\), with \(p\in P_k\), this indicator is \(1_{\mathcal O^\times}(z)\), and the normalized restriction (2.40f) gives exactly

\[ f_{\rm new}(\operatorname{diag}(p zI_k,1)) =|\det p|^{1/2}f_{\rm old}(p) 1_{\mathcal O^\times}(z). \tag{2.40p} \]

The unit scaling on the restriction has no effect, since the lift is compact fixed. This is the promised exact extension rather than an arbitrary lift. In the simple-root coordinates \(\beta_j(z)=\operatorname{diag}(zI_j,I_{n-j})\), each new variable after \(r\) is restricted to a unit. Every positive half determinant in these \(n-r\) steps restricts on \(G_r\) to \(|\det|^{1/2}\). Their product is \(|\det|^{(n-r)/2}\), including the first ordinary step (2.40o). Since the later variables are units, conversion from simple-root coordinates to diagonal entries gives precisely (2.40m).

For \(r=0\) start with the constant one on \(P_1=\{1\}\), the final generic fibre, and perform the same nonzero-fibre lifts and primitive row cutoffs. All diagonal variables are then units. For \(r=n\), Lemma 2.3cy's boundary observation gives the actual spherical representation and its normalized vector by Proposition 2.1a.

The resulting vector is genuinely \(P_n(\mathcal O)=H(0)\)-fixed in the actual representation. Lemma 2.3cv ensures that the last lift is a unique actual Whittaker vector with the specified restriction. Its value at one is one in every case. \(\square\)

A universal spherical transform and its separation

For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in(\mathbb C^\times)^m\), let \(W_x^0\) denote the spherical function with inverse character and diagonal values \(\delta_m(a_\lambda)^{1/2}s_\lambda(x)\) for dominant integer \(\lambda\), and zero otherwise. These values define the universal Laurent-polynomial function through Iwasawa. For \(K_m\)-fixed \(W\), set

\[ \Psi(X,W;x)=\int_{N_m\backslash G_m} W(\operatorname{diag}(g,1))W_x^0(g) |\det g|^{s-1/2}\,dg,\qquad X=q^{-s}. \tag{2.40q} \]

It can initially be read as the series from the far-right convergent integral. Its coefficient on a fixed determinant shell is a finite symmetric Laurent polynomial. To see finiteness without a spectral decomposition, choose a column lattice fixing \(W\). (2.40e) bounds the last-row norm wherever \(W\ne0\). For a contributing dominant diagonal tuple \(\lambda\), its last coordinate is consequently bounded below. At a fixed sum \(|\lambda|\), dominance and that lower bound allow only finitely many tuples. The same argument gives one lower bound on \(|\lambda|\) for the whole series.

Lemma 2.3db (separation). If this universal series is zero for a \(K_m\)-fixed actual \(W\), then \(W=0\).

Proof. On one determinant shell its coefficient is a linear combination of the \(s_\lambda(x)\), over those finitely many dominant integer tuples, with coefficient

\[ W(\operatorname{diag}(a_\lambda,1)) \delta_m(a_\lambda)^{-1/2}|\det a_\lambda|^{-1/2}. \]

Those Laurent Schur polynomials are linearly independent. Multiply a relation by the Vandermonde alternant. Their numerators have exponent multisets \(\{\lambda_j+m-j\}\), which are strictly decreasing and different for distinct dominant \(\lambda\). Their monomial supports are disjoint, including negative central powers. Every coefficient therefore vanishes. Iwasawa gives zero restriction to \(P_n\), and Lemma 2.3cv gives \(W=0\). \(\square\)

Lemma 2.3dc. The vector constructed in Theorem 2.3da satisfies

\[ \Psi(X,W_\pi^e;x)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}P_\pi(Xx_j)^{-1}. \tag{2.40r} \]

Proof. For \(0<r<n\), (2.40m) leaves the tuples \(\lambda=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r,0^{m-r})\), with \(\mu\) a nonnegative partition. The moduli and half shifts cancel exactly because

\[ \delta_m(a_{(\mu,0)}) =\delta_r(a_\mu)|\det a_\mu|^{m-r}. \]

Thus (2.40q) is \(\sum_\mu s_\mu^{(r)}(b)s_{(\mu,0)}^{(m)}(x)X^{|\mu|}\). The fully proved rectangular Cauchy identity makes it \(\prod_{i,j}(1-b_iXx_j)^{-1}\), which is (2.40r). At \(r=0\) only the identity unit shell contributes, giving one. At \(r=n=m+1\), the ordinary all-rank spherical integral calculation has the same cancellation and gives the \(n\)-by-\(m\) Cauchy product. This also proves uniqueness of a \(K_m\)-fixed vector satisfying (2.40r), by Lemma 2.3db. \(\square\)

Finite normalized polynomials and the exact reflection

Define the normalized transform

\[ F_W(X;x)=\Psi(X,W;x)\prod_jP_\pi(Xx_j). \]

Lemma 2.3dd. For every \(K_m\)-fixed actual \(W\) there is a finite symmetric Laurent polynomial \(\Xi_W\) such that

\[ F_W(X;x)=\Xi_W(Xx_1,\ldots,Xx_m). \tag{2.40s} \]

For \(\widetilde W(g)=W(w_ng^{-t})\), the exact relation is

\[ \Xi_{\widetilde W}(q^{-1}x_1^{-1},\ldots,q^{-1}x_m^{-1}) =C_\pi^m(x_1\cdots x_m)^{a_\pi}\Xi_W(x). \tag{2.40t} \]

If \(W\) is \(H(0)\)-fixed then \(\Xi_W\) is an ordinary symmetric polynomial, with every individual-variable exponent nonnegative.

Proof. First take tuples satisfying \(x_i/x_j\notin\{q,q^{-1}\}\) for \(i\ne j\). The corresponding full unramified character induction is irreducible generic by Theorem 2.3az, including repeated parameters. Its spherical Whittaker function is the actual \(W_x^0\), by Proposition 2.1a. The actual generic-pair factor product gives \(L(s,\pi\times I_x)=\prod_jP_\pi(Xx_j)^{-1}\). Its reflected dual has parameters \(x_j^{-1}\). Full gamma multiplicativity, rank-one/matrix identification, and the direct norm substitution give

\[ \epsilon(s,\pi\times I_x,\psi) =C_\pi^m X^{ma_\pi}(x_1\cdots x_m)^{a_\pi}. \tag{2.40u} \]

This uses actual factors and their duals. A scalar gamma product by itself would not justify (2.40u). Since all inducing characters are unramified, their value at \(-1\) is one; the central sign in (2.9at) is exactly one here. In rank difference one the matrix \(w_{n,m}\) in (2.9ai) is the identity. The normalized spherical reflected function is \(W_{x^{-1}}^0\), because it is compact fixed, has inverse Satake parameters, and its value at one is \(W_x^0(w_m)=1\). The full scalar equation consequently reads

\[ F_{\widetilde W}(q^{-1}X^{-1};x^{-1}) =C_\pi^mX^{ma_\pi}(x_1\cdots x_m)^{a_\pi}F_W(X;x). \tag{2.40v} \]

For each of these tuples both normalized test integrals are actual Laurent polynomials in \(X\), by the whole fractional-ideal proof. The determinant-shell argument preceding Lemma 2.3db supplies a lower bound for each transform independent of \(x\). Equation (2.40v) therefore supplies an upper bound for the first polynomial, independent of \(x\), from the lower bound for the reflected one. This step compares finite Laurent polynomials; it does not compare two incompatible expansions of a rational function at zero and infinity.

Every shell coefficient of \(F_W\) is already a symmetric Laurent polynomial in \(x\), homogeneous of its shell degree. Above the uniform upper bound it vanishes on the stated dense open set of tuples, hence identically. The density assertion is elementary: the excluded sets are the finitely many nonzero polynomial equations \(x_i-q^{\pm1}x_j=0\); a Laurent polynomial vanishing on their open complement is zero, by clearing denominators and induction on the number of variables for an ordinary polynomial.
