For each \(f\in I\), its Whittaker function is the function of \(qf\), multiplied by \(c\). Surjectivity lifts every \(\pi\)-vector, proving both inclusions and equality. All the actual integral families and normalized factors agree. For \(U/V\), Corollary 2.3ad constructs only the inclusion of its Whittaker space and test ideal in those of \(I\); its normalized denominator divides that of \(I\) and the L-factor has the stated polynomial correction. An actual surjection is additional mathematical information.

Exercise 9.33 (medium). In the coefficient criterion take \(n=3,i=1\), and suppose an actual compact Jacquet eigenvalue has absolute value \(q^{-1}\). Show that this root prevents square integrability but satisfies the necessary bounds for every \(L^{2+\epsilon}\). Explain why a polynomial factor from a Jordan block does not spoil the latter summability.

Solution. The quotient shell volume grows as \(q^{2h}\). The eigenvector coefficient in (2.18i) has absolute value \(q^{-h}\), so its squared integral contains \(\sum_{h\ge1}1\), which diverges. At \(p=2+\epsilon\), the corresponding geometric ratio is \(q^2q^{-(2+\epsilon)}=q^{-\epsilon}<1\). A Jordan block contributes at most a fixed power of \(1+h\). For a polynomial weight of degree \(A\), the ratio of successive terms of \((1+h)^Aq^{-\epsilon h}\) tends to \(q^{-\epsilon}<1\), so its series converges. This single root meets the weak criterion; all other proper-cut roots must meet it as well to conclude that every coefficient is in all \(L^{2+\epsilon}\).

Exercise 9.34 (medium). In Lemma 2.3am explain why one power of \(T_i\) kills the entire compact Jacquet kernel, rather than only each vector separately. If that kernel has dimension three and the quotient has nonzero roots \(\alpha,\alpha,\beta,\gamma\), determine the characteristic polynomial of \(T_i\), including multiplicities.

Solution. The compact kernel is finite-dimensional. Choose a basis and write each basis vector as a finite sum of actual upper-unipotent differences. One compact additive lattice contains every unipotent element in these finitely many expressions. Every sufficiently expanded upper average contains that lattice and kills all the basis vectors. The semigroup identity turns that uniform vanishing into \(T_i^hB=0\) for one common \(h\). In a basis adapted to the kernel, \(T_i\) is block triangular. The nilpotent three-dimensional block has characteristic polynomial \(t^3\); the quotient block has the stated invertible roots. Their product is \[ t^3(t-\alpha)^2(t-\beta)(t-\gamma). \] This includes any coincident values among the three named nonzero roots with their summed multiplicities.

Exercise 9.35 (hard). Let \(V\) satisfy Theorem 2.3aq and let \(Q\) be its faithful Whittaker quotient. Prove that the \(G_n\)-span of the bottom mirabolic module is irreducible. Why does this argument identify every generic irreducible subquotient of \(V\) without a composition series?

Solution. Every nonzero submodule \(M\subset Q\) has a function with a nonzero value. Translating that value to the identity makes evaluation nonzero on \(M\). Its exact generic fibre is therefore the full one-dimensional generic fibre of \(Q\). Naturality of (2.9r) identifies its bottom inclusion with \(A_n\) tensored with that fibre isomorphism, so \(M\) contains the same bottom module \(A\). Its \(G_n\)-span \(S\) is nonzero. Every nonzero submodule of \(S\) contains \(A\) and hence all of \(S\), proving irreducibility. For a supplied generic simple \(U/W\) of \(V\), exactness gives \(\dim U_{N,\psi}=1\) and \(W_{N,\psi}=0\). The full functional restricts to \(U\) and kills every translate of \(W\), giving a nonzero Whittaker map \(U/W\hookrightarrow Q\). Its simple image contains \(S\), so equals \(S\). No finite-length selection was used. This is a subquotient construction; it supplies no surjection from the whole \(V\) unless such a map is separately proved.

Exercise 9.36 (hard). Let a unitary-centre Jacquet-cuspidal \(\rho\) have rank \(d=2\), and take the centered string of length \(\ell=3\). Compute the candidate root absolute values at the cuts \(i=2,4\). Compare them with the square-integrability boundary and with the value selected by the proved formula (2.18x).

Solution. The three twist exponents are \(-1,0,1\). At \(i=2\), the subsets have cardinality one; at \(i=4\), they have cardinality two. In both cases their possible sums are \(-1,0,1\). The raw half-modulus in (2.18wa) is \(q^{-4}\), and the twists contribute \(q^{-2\sum t}\). The possible absolute values are therefore \[ \{q^{-2},q^{-4},q^{-6}\}. \] Both cuts have boundary \(q^{-i(6-i)/2}=q^{-4}\). The candidate set alone includes one value above that boundary and one on it, so it does not establish square integrability. For (2.18x), the additional normalized exponent \(ad(\ell-a)/2\) equals two for \(a=1,2\). The selected raw root has absolute value \(q^{-4}q^{-2}=q^{-6}<q^{-4}\). The cuts \(1,3,5\) have zero Jacquet modules by Lemma 2.3as. Theorem 2.3bd proves (2.18x) at both divisible cuts, and Proposition 2.3at therefore proves square integrability. The arithmetic identifies the candidates; the adjacent-kernel proof selects the descending tuple.

Exercise 9.37 (medium). Suppose a rank-three Jacquet-cuspidal \(\rho\) has \(|\omega_\rho(\varpi)|=q^{-6}\). Compute the unique real exponent \(e(\rho)\) and the twist making its centre unitary. Explain why dualizing the cuspidal embedding gives an actual quotient without changing its upper parabolic or permuting its blocks.

Solution. Formula (1.39j) gives \(e(\rho)=-(-6\log q)/(3\log q)=2\). The normalized block is \(\tau=\rho\nu^{-2}\); at \(\varpi I_3\), its central modulus is \(q^{-6}q^6=1\). The unit group already has modulus one. The dual has exponent \(-2\). Lemma 1.23a identifies the ordinary smooth dual of normalized induction with induction of the ordinary dual data on the same upper parabolic. Exact admissible duality in Lemma 1.23j turns an injection of \(\pi^\vee\) into an onto map to \((\pi^\vee)^\vee=\pi\). Lemma 1.23i preserves Jacquet vanishing for the dual blocks. This operation supplies the unordered actual quotient of Theorem 1.23k with its original block order.

Exercise 9.38 (hard). In Lemma 1.23s take \(H(w,w)=1\) and \(e=f_{ww}\). Prove that an occurrence of the cuspidal \(\rho\) as a subquotient of an actual smooth module with the same scalar centre produces an embedding into that module. Explain the role of the fixed central character.

Solution. The convolution identity gives \(e*e=e\), and the action on \(\rho\) is \(u\mapsto H(u,w)w\), so \(e\rho\ne0\). Applying an idempotent is exact: for a surjection, lift a vector and apply \(e\); its kernel is the intersection with the original kernel. The subquotient occurrence therefore forces \(eV\ne0\). For a nonzero \(u\in eV\), the formula \(T_u(v)=f_{vw}u\) is equivariant and satisfies \(T_u(w)=u\). It is a nonzero map from the irreducible \(\rho\), hence injective. The representative cancellation in \(\int_{Z\backslash G}f(g)\pi_V(g)v\,d\bar g\) uses \(f(zg)=\omega(z)^{-1}f(g)\) and \(\pi_V(z)=\omega(z)\mathrm{id}\). Those exact inverse weights are why the relative action, and this argument, has the stated fixed scalar central-character category.

Exercise 9.39 (hard). For three actual Jacquet-cuspidal irreducible blocks, derive the uniform length bound \(12\) for their full induction from Theorem 1.23v. Derive the bound \(6\) if each of the three two-block subinductions is known to be irreducible. Why does the proof use all nonzero subquotients?

Solution. For two blocks the bound in (1.39ad) has two proper nonempty subsets, each with single irreducible factors, so its length is at most two. For three blocks there are six proper nonempty subsets. Each corresponding product of lengths has one single-block length one and one two-block length at most two, giving \(6\cdot2=12\). If all the pair products are irreducible, each term is one and the bound becomes six. No such pair irreducibility is inferred from the bound itself. Every nonzero subquotient of the full induction has an actual irreducible subquotient. Corollary 1.23t excludes a cuspidal one, so a proper Jacquet functor detects it. Thus for every strict submodule inclusion \(W\subsetneq W'\), some Jacquet length increases. The finite integer (1.39ae) strictly increases and bounds both ascending and descending chains. Detecting only quotients of the whole induction would not establish this strict increase for every intermediate \(W'/W\).

Exercise 9.40 (hard). In Theorem 1.23x explain why a Jacquet-cuspidal factor in the comparison embedding must match a single original inducing position. Account explicitly for repeated factors and real norm twists.

Solution. Reciprocity makes the tensor of the comparison cuspidal factors an actual quotient of the corresponding Jacquet module of \(\pi\). Exactness puts it in the Jacquet module of the original cuspidal induction. Intersecting a representative of this simple subquotient with the finite filtration locates it in one actual ordered-partition quotient. Tensoring the finite composition series of that quotient identifies its factors with constituents of the assigned subinductions. An assigned set with two or more positions would make its cuspidal constituent a subquotient of a proper cuspidal induction, excluded by Corollary 1.23t. Each set is nonempty by its positive rank, so it has exactly one position. The disjoint partition matches every position once. Identical representations in different positions remain separate entries, so multiplicities are preserved. Factor isomorphism concerns the actual twisted representation, rather than only its real central exponent or its unitary normalization. All twists therefore remain part of the unique multiset.

Segments, pooling and canonical data

Let \(k\) be a nondiscrete nonarchimedean local field of either characteristic, \(q\) its residue cardinality, \(|\varpi|=q^{-1}\), \(G_n=GL_n(k)\), and \(\nu(g)=|\det g|\). All representations below are actual complex smooth admissible modules. The product \(\times\) means normalized induction from the upper block parabolic, with covariance \(\delta_P^{1/2}\) and right translation. Write \(r_P\) for normalized Jacquet coinvariants. Fix a nontrivial smooth additive character \(\psi\) of \(k\), put \(\psi_n(u)=\psi(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}u_{i,i+1})\), and use \(V_{N,\psi}\) for the corresponding generic coinvariant.

A coefficient-tempered irreducible has unitary scalar centre and all smooth coefficients in every \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) modulo that centre. Fix an irreducible Jacquet-cuspidal \(\rho\) of \(G_d\) with unitary centre, allowing arbitrary ramification. The centered segment \(S_\ell(\rho)\) is the constructed generic head of \[ \rho\nu^{-(\ell-1)/2}\times\cdots\times \rho\nu^{(\ell-1)/2}. \] For \([u,v]\), with \(v-u\) a nonnegative integer, write \(S([u,v]_\rho)=S_{v-u+1}(\rho)\nu^{(u+v)/2}\).

Exercise 9.41 (medium; ascending and descending maps). Put \(L=\rho\nu^{-1/2}\), \(H=\rho\nu^{1/2}\), \(I_\uparrow=L\times H\), and \(I_\downarrow=H\times L\). Determine the kernels and images of the two nonzero adjacent exchange maps. Give the normalized \((d,d)\)-Jacquet modules of their simple factors and the generic dimensions. Specialize to \(d=1\), \(\rho=\mathbf1\), and identify the nongeneric factor and an actual map onto it. Use Theorem 2.3az–Theorem 2.3bb, especially (2.19p), (2.19t).

Solution. Both inductions have length two. Let \(D=S_2(\rho)\) and let \(T\) be the nongeneric simple kernel of the ascending product. The actual maps give \[ \begin{array}{c} 0\longrightarrow T\xrightarrow{j_T}I_\uparrow \xrightarrow{p_D}D\longrightarrow0,\\ 0\longrightarrow D\xrightarrow{j_D}I_\downarrow \xrightarrow{p_T}T\longrightarrow0. \end{array} \] The exchange maps, up to nonzero scalar, are \(j_Dp_D:I_\uparrow\to I_\downarrow\) and \(j_Tp_T:I_\downarrow\to I_\uparrow\). Their kernels are \(T,D\), their images are \(D,T\), respectively, and both composites are zero. The maps arise by projecting the actual Jacquet module to the exchanged tensor and applying normalized reciprocity; no inverse exchange is asserted.

The descending product has no nongeneric submodule by Theorem 2.3ay. Its nonzero forward exchange image is therefore generic. An image of length two would be an isomorphism and would transport the ascending nongeneric submodule into it. Thus that image is the simple \(D\). Reciprocity and exact Jacquet detection then give \[ r_{d,d}D=H\boxtimes L,\qquad r_{d,d}T=L\boxtimes H,\qquad \dim D_{N,\psi}=1,\quad \dim T_{N,\psi}=0. \] The reverse map has image \(T\) and kernel \(D\) by the same length-two argument.

When \(d=1,\rho=\mathbf1\), the ascending inducing covariance is \[ |a/b|^{1/2}|a|^{-1/2}|b|^{1/2}=1. \] Its constant section embeds \(\mathbf1\), which is nongeneric because \(N_2\) acts trivially and \(\psi\) is nontrivial. Hence \(T=\mathbf1\). Ordinary smooth duality turns this injection into \(I_\downarrow\twoheadrightarrow\mathbf1\) on the same upper parabolic. Explicitly the quotient is \(f\mapsto\int_{GL_2(\mathcal O)}f(k)\,dk\), with compact volume one: pairing with the constant ascending section gives its invariance, and the descending section equal to one on the compact picture maps to one. Thus the two block orders have different simple heads.

Exercise 9.42 (hard; length three and the selected roots). Set \(\rho_1=\rho\nu^{-1}\), \(\rho_2=\rho\), \(\rho_3=\rho\nu\), and \(I=\rho_1\times\rho_2\times\rho_3\). Let \(K_1,K_2\) be obtained by inducing the ascending adjacent kernels in positions \(1,2\) and \(2,3\). Determine the survivor in the full cuspidal Jacquet module of \(I/(K_1+K_2)\). Compute its two proper divisible Jacquet cuts and compare their raw first-central root magnitudes with the \(L^2\) boundary. Use Lemma 2.3bc–Theorem 2.3bd, equations (2.19v)–(2.19y).

Solution. The full Jacquet module is the direct sum of the six actual tensors indexed by permutations. Distinct joint block-central characters separate them. \(K_1\) contains precisely the summands with \(1\) before \(2\); \(K_2\) contains those with \(2\) before \(3\): \[ \begin{array}{c|c} 123&K_1,K_2\\ 132&K_1\\ 213&K_2\\ 231&K_2\\ 312&K_1\\ 321&\text{survives}. \end{array} \] Their sum has zero generic coinvariant, so the actual quotient is nonzero with generic dimension one. Every nonzero subquotient is detected by the full cuspidal Jacquet functor. Its one surviving simple tensor therefore forces the quotient to be irreducible: it is \(S_3(\rho)\), and the whole induction maps onto it.

The selected full tuple is \(\rho\nu\boxtimes\rho\boxtimes\rho\nu^{-1}\). Grouping its first one or two positions gives \[ \begin{aligned} r_{d,2d}S_3(\rho) &=\rho\nu\boxtimes S_2(\rho)\nu^{-1/2},\\ r_{2d,d}S_3(\rho) &=S_2(\rho)\nu^{1/2}\boxtimes\rho\nu^{-1}. \end{aligned} \] The first normalized central scalars are \(\omega_\rho(\varpi)q^{-d}\) and \(\omega_\rho(\varpi)^2q^{-d}\), respectively. At either cut the raw half-modulus contributes \(q^{-d^2}\). Both raw magnitudes are consequently \(q^{-d^2-d}\), strictly less than the boundary \(q^{-d^2}\). All other proper cuts vanish, and the total centre is the unitary \(\omega_\rho^3\). The complete coefficient criterion Theorem 2.3an thus gives \(L^2\).

Exercise 9.43 (medium; repeated nested centered segments). Prove that \[ V=S_3(\rho)\times S_3(\rho)\times\rho \] is an irreducible coefficient-tempered representation of \(G_{7d}\) with generic dimension one and a compatible unitary realization. Determine its full cuspidal support with multiplicities and explain why these multiplicities reconstruct its segment multiset uniquely. Use Lemma 2.3be–Theorem 2.3bi.

Solution. Its intervals are two copies of \([-1,1]\) and one copy of \([0,0]\). Equal intervals contain one another, and the singleton is contained in both longer intervals. Thus no pair is linked. Theorem 2.3bf proves irreducibility, while the exact generic induction calculation gives \[ \dim V_{N,\psi}=1\cdot1\cdot1=1. \] Repetition of a generic factor does not add the dimensions. All three segments are centered with unitary centre. Their coefficient \(L^2\) properties and Theorem 2.3ao give temperedness; the coefficient-integral and compact-induction forms of Theorem 2.3bi give the compatible unitary realization.

Its actual support multiplicities at twists \(-1,0,1\) are \((2,3,2)\), so its rank is \(d(2+3+2)=7d\). The level-one and level-two components are both \([-1,1]\); the level-three component is \([0,0]\). In any unlinked family, maximal intervals are disjoint with a missing integer between them. They must therefore be the connected components of the level-one support. Remove one copy and repeat on the remaining multiplicities. This forces exactly those three intervals, including both repeated copies. Theorem 2.3bg then identifies the actual generic representation, rather than only its central character. It is not \(L^2\): a whole-segment Jacquet cut of this three-factor induction has normalized central modulus one, the forbidden boundary equality in Theorem 2.3bj.

Exercise 9.44 (medium; finite level reconstruction). On the integral line \(\rho\nu^{\mathbb Z}\), prescribe \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr} j&-3&-2&-1&0&1&2&3\\ \hline m(j)&1&2&2&3&1&0&2. \end{array} \] Construct the unique unlinked segment multiset, its irreducible generic induction, its rank and its real central exponent. Show the reconstruction terminates and is unique. Use Lemma 2.3be–Theorem 2.3bg and formula (2.21a).

Solution. Taking connected components at every positive level gives \[ \begin{array}{c|l} 1&[-3,1],\ [3,3]\\ 2&[-2,0],\ [3,3]\\ 3&[0,0]. \end{array} \] There are no higher levels. The intervals \([-2,0]\), \([0,0]\) are nested inside \([-3,1]\); the two copies of \([3,3]\) are separated from that component by the missing integer \(2\). Thus the family is unlinked. Its induction, in any order, is \[ S_5(\rho)\nu^{-1}\times S_3(\rho)\nu^{-1} \times\rho\times\rho\nu^3\times\rho\nu^3. \] Theorem 2.3bf makes it irreducible generic; actual string quotient maps and exact induction make it a quotient of a cuspidal induction having the prescribed support.

The lengths are \(5,3,1,1,1\), totaling \(11\). The weighted sum of real exponents is \(5(-1)+3(-1)+1(0)+1(3)+1(3)=-2\). The rank and central exponent are therefore \[ n=11d,\qquad e=-\frac2{11}. \] Equivalently the support sum \(-3-4-2+0+1+0+6=-2\) gives the same answer. The unitary-centre normalization is the twist \(\nu^{2/11}\).

For uniqueness, maximal intervals of any unlinked family must be exactly the connected support components. Remove one copy of each maximal interval; its rank multiplicities decrease by one on those components. Repeat. The maximal multiplicity falls from \(3\) to \(0\), so this finite procedure terminates and forces the displayed level table, including repetitions.

Exercise 9.45 (hard; rank weights and strict gain at norm zero). For weights \(d=(1,2,1)\), project \(z=(3,0,2)\) onto \(C=\{y_1\le y_2\le y_3\}\) in the weighted norm \(\|z\|^2=\sum d_jz_j^2\). Verify the projection directly. If an irreducible \(\pi\) embeds in \(V_1\times V_2\times V_3\), where \(V_1,V_2,V_3\) are actual irreducible admissible blocks with these ranks and real exponents, describe the actual coarsened embedding. Separately split the old rank-three profile \(x=0\) into ranks \(2,1\) with values \(-1,2\). Verify strict norm gain even though \(\|x\|=0\). Use Lemma 2.3bp–Lemma 2.3br.

Solution. Pool the first two entries, whose weighted average is \((1\cdot3+2\cdot0)/3=1\). The result is \(y=(1,1,2)\), with grouped ranks \(3,1\). The weighted residual is \((2,-2,0)\), hence for every \(u\in C\), \[ \langle z-y,u-y\rangle=2(u_1-u_2)\le0. \] Expanding \(\|z-u\|^2\) now gives \(\|z-u\|^2\ge\|z-y\|^2+\|u-y\|^2\). This proves both minimality and uniqueness. Numerically \[ \|z\|^2=13,\quad \|y\|^2=7,\quad \|z-y\|^2=6. \]

For the supplied embedding, let \(J=V_1\times V_2\). Induction in stages identifies the ambient module with \(J\times V_3\). It has a finite filtration induced from the composition series of \(J\). Intersect it with the embedded simple image of \(\pi\), and take the first nonzero intersection. Projection to that successive quotient is injective on \(\pi\), giving the actual embedding \[ \pi\hookrightarrow W\times V_3 \] for one actual irreducible constituent \(W\) of \(J\). Its rank is \(3\) and its exponent is \((1\cdot3+2\cdot0)/3=1\). No permutation of the original blocks or whole-module quotient \(J\twoheadrightarrow W\) is required by this construction.

For the separate split, \(2(-1)+1(2)=0\) preserves the old weighted mean. The refined profile is already increasing, so pooling gives \(y=(-1,2)\), with \[ A=\|x\|^2=0,\qquad B=\|\delta\|^2=2+4=6,\qquad \|y\|^2=6>0. \] For \(0<\epsilon\le1\), \(u=x+\epsilon\delta\) is increasing. The strict-gain estimate (2.21f) is well defined and equals \((\epsilon B)^2/(\epsilon^2B)=B=6\). It never divides by the zero old norm. When such a split comes from Lemma 2.3bs, its refinement is an actual embedding and Lemma 2.3bp realizes the pooled groups by the same filtration maps.

Exercise 9.46 (hard; canonical grouped data and supplied ties). Let \(A,B,C\) be actual irreducible coefficient-tempered blocks of ranks \(a,b,c>0\), allowing \(A=B\). Set \(\tau=A\times B\). Compare the supplied weakly decreasing list \[ (A\nu^2,\ B\nu^2,\ C\nu^{-1}) \] with the strictly decreasing grouped list \[ (\tau\nu^2,\ C\nu^{-1}). \] Give the actual induction isomorphism and canonical datum of their unique irreducible quotient. Explain precisely which uniqueness assertion permits the two different lists. Use Theorem 2.3bn and Theorem 2.3ca–Theorem 2.3cb for tied tempered blocks, together with Theorem 2.3bx–Theorem 2.3bz.

Solution. Theorem 2.3bn supplies compatible unitary forms; Theorem 2.3ca proves that the full \(\tau=A\times B\) is irreducible coefficient-tempered, independent of the order of \(A,B\), including repetitions. Its proof uses finite length and semisimplicity: every simple constituent is generic, while the full generic coinvariant has dimension \(1\cdot1=1\). Its total length is consequently one.

Normalized induction in stages gives the actual isomorphism \[ (A\nu^2)\times(B\nu^2)\times(C\nu^{-1}) \ \simeq\ (\tau\nu^2)\times(C\nu^{-1}). \] For clarity, before identifying the inner common twist with \(\tau\nu^2\), its section map is \[ F(g)(h)= \delta_{P_{a+b,c}}(\operatorname{diag}(h,I_c))^{-1/2} f(\operatorname{diag}(h,I_c)g). \] The inner covariance is that of \((A\nu^2)\times(B\nu^2)\); multiplication of the inner and outer moduli gives the original three-block modulus. Evaluation at \(h=1\) is the inverse section map. On the inner section space, \(f(h)\mapsto\nu(h)^{-2}f(h)\) identifies that common twist with the representation \((A\times B)\nu^2\), with its twisted right action. Thus these are actual inverse induction maps.

The strict exponents \(2>-1\) allow Theorem 2.3bz to give an onto map from this common full induction to a unique irreducible \(\pi\), with head multiplicity one. Its canonical grouped datum is \[ (a+b,c;\ \tau,C;\ 2,-1). \] Its real central exponent is \((2(a+b)-c)/(a+b+c)\), because row ranks weight the actual central characters. Theorem 2.3by–Theorem 2.3bz identify the grouped ranks, actual blocks and distinct exponents whenever the quotients are isomorphic. They do not assert that an ungrouped tied list is unique. Replacing the single block \(\tau\) by its two tempered factors produces exactly the displayed alternative list describing the same full induced module. Theorem 2.3ca also permits an internal permutation of that tied group. These conclusions use no exchange across the unequal exponents \(2,-1\).

Exercise 9.47 (standard factors and repeated roots). Let \(\eta\) be an unramified unitary character with \(\eta(\varpi)=a\). Compute the matrix factor of \[ \pi=S_3(\eta)\times S_1(\eta)\times S_1(\eta). \] Justify that the full induction is irreducible and generic, calculate its rank and reciprocal degree, and list its poles with multiplicities. Explain what a character twist \(\chi\) does if \(\eta\chi\) is ramified.

Solution. The three strings on the cuspidal line of \(\eta\) have exponent intervals \([-1,1]\), \([0,0]\), \([0,0]\). The shorter ones are contained in the first, and the last two are identical. They are therefore unlinked, including with repetitions. Theorems 2.3bf and 2.3bg make the full induction irreducible and generic. Its rank is \(3+1+1=5\), while (2.25b) gives \[ L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\pi) =\frac{1}{(1-aq^{-s-1})(1-aq^{-s})^2}. \] The reciprocal degree is three. Write \(a=e^{i\theta}\). The first factor has simple poles at \(s=-1+i(\theta+2\pi m)/\log q\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\); the last two give double poles at \(s=i(\theta+2\pi m)/\log q\). The two families have distinct real parts and do not intersect. If \(\eta\chi\) is ramified, all three rank-one bases fail the unit-invariance condition, so \(J_\chi\) is empty and the twisted matrix factor is one. This removes the Euler denominators; it does not assert that the twisted representation has conductor zero.

Exercise 9.48 (the two rank-two constituents). Compare the matrix factors of the centered string \(S_2(1)\) and the trivial representation of \(G_2(k)\). Identify the whole increasing string that maps onto the former and the decreasing principal series whose head is the latter. Explain why the two factors differ.

Solution. By Theorem 2.3bd, the whole normalized induction \(\nu^{-1/2}\times\nu^{1/2}\) maps onto \(S_2(1)\). This is generic, and (2.25b) gives \[ L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,S_2(1))=(1-q^{-s-1/2})^{-1}. \] The opposite order \(\nu^{1/2}\times\nu^{-1/2}\) has the trivial representation as head by the actual adjacent map and quotient calculation in Theorem 2.3bb and Exercise 9.41. The trivial representation is a determinant character, and Proposition 1.16 gives \[ L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,1_{G_2}) =\frac{1}{(1-q^{-s-1/2})(1-q^{-s+1/2})}. \] The generic constituent retains one endpoint of its length-two string. The one-dimensional trivial representation has a different matrix coefficient family and two denominator factors. The increasing generic-string factor cannot be transferred to the opposite nongeneric quotient by merely reversing the order.

Exercise 9.49 (Euler denominator and conductor carry different information). For the representation of Exercise 9.47, compute the matrix epsilon factor for conductor-zero \(\psi\). Then twist by a unitary character \(\chi\) such that \(\eta\chi\) has analytic rank-one conductor \(f>0\) and rank-one epsilon constant \(w\). Compute the resulting standard factor and analytic conductor.

Solution. Before twisting, the length-three block has exponent \(3-1=2\) and constant \((-\eta(\varpi))^2=a^2\); each length-one block has exponent zero and constant one. Equation (2.26c) gives \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\pi,\psi)= a^2q^{2(1/2-s)}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{mat}}(\pi)=2\). After twisting, the character \(\eta\chi\) is ramified. Corollary 2.3ce gives \(L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\pi\otimes\chi)=1\). Equation (2.26b) gives conductor \(3f\) and constant \(w^3\) on the length-three block, and conductor \(f\), constant \(w\), on each length-one block. Hence the total conductor is \(5f\) and the epsilon factor is \(w^5q^{5f(1/2-s)}\). An absent standard Euler denominator therefore allows a positive, and potentially large, analytic conductor.

Exercise 9.50 (the length-three and length-two pair). Compute the local factor and the conductor-zero epsilon factor of \(S_3(1)\times S_2(1)\). Give the gamma-product shifts, explain their multiplicities, and identify the surviving endpoint shifts.

Solution. The two centered strings have shifts \(-1,0,1\) and \(-1/2,1/2\). Their six pair shifts are \(-3/2,-1/2,-1/2,1/2,1/2,3/2\). They split as the four-entry chain \([-3/2,-1/2,1/2,3/2]\) and the two-entry chain \([-1/2,1/2]\), preserving the repeated middle weights. Corollary 2.3cd keeps shifts \(3/2\) and \(1/2\), so \[ L(s,S_3(1)\times S_2(1)) =\frac{1}{(1-q^{-s-3/2})(1-q^{-s-1/2})}. \] The underlying rank-one cuspidal pair is \(1\times1\); Proposition 1.2 gives \(a_0=0,w_0=1\), and Theorem 2.3af gives \(t=1,z=1\). Equation (2.27c) therefore gives \(A=6-2=4\), \(W=(-1)^4=1\), and \(\epsilon(s)=q^{4(1/2-s)}\). The four residual ratios supply the four epsilon powers, while the Euler denominator records the two surviving chain endpoints.

Exercise 9.51 (a single block and zero monodromy). Let \(\chi\) be an unramified one-dimensional Weil representation with \(\chi(\Phi)=\alpha\ne0\). Compute the factor and conductor of \(\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_3\). Compare with the same Weil part but zero monodromy, and then with two repeated copies of the original pair.

Solution. Every ramification group acts trivially on \(\chi\), so (2.28h) gives \(a(\chi)=0\) and \(\dim\chi^I=1\). On the three Weil basis vectors the Frobenius eigenvalues are \(\alpha q^{-1},\alpha,\alpha q\). The monodromy kernel is exactly the first basis line. Thus

\[ L(s,\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_3)=(1-\alpha q^{-s-1})^{-1},\qquad a(\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_3)=2. \tag{2.31a} \]

Setting monodromy to zero gives an actual different pair with full three-dimensional kernel and conductor zero. Its factor is

\[ \bigl((1-\alpha q^{-s-1})(1-\alpha q^{-s})(1-\alpha q^{-s+1})\bigr)^{-1}. \tag{2.31b} \]

Two repeated copies of the original pair have factor \((1-\alpha q^{-s-1})^{-2}\) and conductor \(4\). This also shows why the ordinary conductor of the Weil part alone cannot replace (2.28i).

Exercise 9.52 (all six vectors of a tensor). Construct the full \(\mathrm{Sp}_3\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2\) splitting, and compute its factor and conductor.

Solution. Use \(e_0,e_1,e_2\) and \(f_0,f_1\). The two highest vectors from (2.29g) are

\[ v_0=e_0\otimes f_0,\qquad v_1=e_0\otimes f_1-e_1\otimes f_0. \tag{2.31c} \]

Their weights \(c_h\) are \(3\) and \(1\). Abbreviating \(e_i\otimes f_j\) by \(e_if_j\), the normalized full chains of (2.29l) are

\[ \begin{array}{c|cccc} \mathrm{Sp}_4& e_0f_0& (2e_1f_0+e_0f_1)/3& (e_2f_0+e_1f_1)/3& e_2f_1/3\\ \mathrm{Sp}_2& e_0f_1-e_1f_0& e_1f_1-2e_2f_0&& \end{array}. \tag{2.31d} \]

In each row, \(N\) takes a vector after the first to the preceding one and takes the first to zero. Direct substitution in \(N(e_if_j)=e_{i-1}f_j+e_if_{j-1}\) verifies every arrow, including \(N(e_1f_1-2e_2f_0)=e_0f_1-e_1f_0\). The two middle pairs at index sums \(1\) and \(2\) are independent: their coordinate matrices both have determinant \(-1\), in the respective coordinate orders \((e_0f_1,e_1f_0)\) and \((e_1f_1,e_2f_0)\). The remaining two vectors occupy the unique index sums \(0\) and \(3\). Thus the six vectors are a basis, agreeing with the general proof of Theorem 2.3cl.

The two kernel Frobenius eigenvalues are \(q^{-3/2}\) and \(q^{-1/2}\). The underlying six-dimensional Weil representation is unramified, and the kernel has dimension \(2\). Therefore

\[ L(s,\mathrm{Sp}_3\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2) =\bigl((1-q^{-s-3/2})(1-q^{-s-1/2})\bigr)^{-1},\qquad a(\mathrm{Sp}_3\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2)=6-2=4. \tag{2.31e} \]

Exercise 9.53 (ramification cancellation in a repeated character). Let \(F=\mathbf Q_2\), \(E=\mathbf Q_2(i)\), and let \(\chi:G_F\to\{\pm1\}\) be the nontrivial quotient character of \(\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\), restricted to \(W_F\). Compute the individual conductors for \(\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_4\) and \(\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2\), and the factor and conductor of their tensor.

Solution. The polynomial of \(i-1\) is \(X^2+2X+2\), which is Eisenstein, so \(E/F\) is totally ramified quadratic, \(v_E(2)=2\), and \(i-1\) is a uniformizer. Conjugation moves it by \(-2i\), of value \(2\). The intrinsic uniformizer formula (Ramification groups and the different of a local extension, equation (2.2)) gives \(G_0=G_1=C_2\), \(G_2=1\). The nontrivial character has no \(C_2\)-fixed vector, so directly from (2.28h),

\[ \chi^I=0,\qquad a(\chi)=1+1=2. \tag{2.31f} \]

Thus the individual special-block conductors are \(4\cdot2=8\) and \(2\cdot2=4\), and their individual factors are one. On the tensor Weil representation, however, \(R=\chi\otimes\chi=1\), since \(\chi^2=1\) on the whole Weil group. Hence \(a(R)=0\), \(R^I=\mathbf C\), and its Frobenius is one. Formula (2.30b) gives \(\mathrm{Sp}_5\oplus\mathrm{Sp}_3\), so

\[ L\bigl(s,(\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_4)\otimes (\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2)\bigr) =\bigl((1-q^{-s-2})(1-q^{-s-1})\bigr)^{-1},\qquad q=2, \tag{2.31g} \] \[ a\bigl((\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_4)\otimes (\chi\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2)\bigr) =8\cdot0+(8-2)\cdot1=6. \tag{2.31h} \]

In this example \(\dim\chi^I\cdot\dim\chi^I=0\), whereas \(\dim(\chi\otimes\chi)^I=1\). This proves concretely that substituting the former product in (2.30d) would give the wrong conductor. The integrality of the displayed numbers is proved by their explicit finite sums; it supplies no claim of general conductor integrality.

Exercise 9.54 (unitary center does not supply a unitary model). Consider the actual normalized induction \[ \pi=S_2(1)\nu^{1/4}\times S_1(1)\nu^{-1/2}. \] Prove that it is irreducible, generic and has unitary scalar center. Compute its standard factor and conductor-zero matrix epsilon. Use (2.33a) to rule out a compatible unitary realization.

Solution. Its cuspidal strings have exponent sets \(\{-1/4,3/4\}\) and \(\{-1/2\}\). They lie on distinct integer-step levels: the differences between the second exponent and the two first exponents are \(-1/4\) and \(-5/4\), neither an integer. They are unlinked, so Theorems 2.3bf and 2.3bg make the full induction irreducible and generic. The real exponent of its scalar character is \(2(1/4)+1(-1/2)=0\); the underlying centered bases have trivial scalar character. Its scalar character is therefore trivial.

Corollary 2.3ce and Theorem 2.3cf give \[ L_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\pi) =\frac{1}{(1-q^{-s-3/4})(1-q^{-s+1/2})}, \qquad \epsilon_{\mathrm{mat}}(s,\pi,\psi) =-q^{1/2-s-1/4}. \] The two analytic string exponents are \(A_1=1,A_2=0\). Thus \(\sum_i u_iA_i=1/4\ne0\), contrary to (2.33a) for a compatible unitary model. Equivalently its epsilon constant is \(-q^{-1/4}\), whose absolute value is less than one. The actual representation and its scalar center exist as stated; the missing property is an invariant positive unitary realization.

Exercise 9.55 (one actual endpoint test). For the decreasing \(GL_2\) trivial head, write an actual matrix test attaining \(L_k(s-\tfrac12,1)\), calculate its precise constant, and check that it belongs to the whole two-factor head ideal.

Solution. The trivial representation embeds as the constant section in \(I(\nu^{-1/2},\nu^{1/2})\), since normalized upper covariance is \(|a/D|^{1/2}|a|^{-1/2}|D|^{1/2}=1\). Take \(r=t=1\), \(d\ge1\), \(\phi=1_{\mathcal O}\), and the test (2.34f). Its coefficient is one. Formula (2.34i) gives \[ Z(s,\Phi,1)= \frac{q^{2-3d}}{q^2-1}\, \frac1{1-q^{1/2}X}. \tag{2.39a} \] The constant follows from \(C_1/C_2=(1-q^{-2})^{-1}\) and \(t^2+2rt=3\). Multiplying the test by its reciprocal attains exactly the claimed Tate factor. The full head generator is \([(1-q^{-1/2}X)(1-q^{1/2}X)]^{-1}\), by Theorem 2.3cr or the already proved Proposition 1.16. The endpoint test is that generator times \(1-q^{-1/2}X\), so is in the entire head ideal. It is an actual test, rather than a quotient-induced inclusion assumed without a vector construction.

Exercise 9.56 (repeated nongeneric head endpoints). Let \(\tau=1_{G_1}\times1_{G_1}\), and let \(\pi\) be the canonical head of \(\tau\nu^{1/2}\times\tau\nu^{-1/2}\). Compute its rank, matrix factor, epsilon exponent and pole multiplicities.

Solution. The repeated tied induction \(\tau\) is actual irreducible unitary coefficient-tempered by Theorem 2.3ca. The canonical segment list has four length-one trivial cuspidals, with two centers \(1/2\) and two centers \(-1/2\). Thus \(\pi\) has rank four and \[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)= (1-q^{-1/2}X)^{-2}(1-q^{1/2}X)^{-2},\qquad \epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\pi,\psi)=1. \tag{2.39b} \] Every child has \(a_b=0,\ell_b=1,W_b=1\), so the conductor exponent is zero. On the real axis the two poles are at \(-1/2\) and \(1/2\), each of order two; their imaginary translates have period \(2\pi/\log q\). The canonical length-one strings at the two different centers are linked. If the head were generic, its unique generic unlinked segment list and the canonical uniqueness of Theorems 2.3cb–cc would make this same list unlinked, a contradiction. This nongeneric head retains every repeated factor.

Exercise 9.57 (why the newvector statement needs genericity). Let \(n\ge2\), let \(\chi\) have positive scalar conductor \(f\), and put \(\pi=\chi\circ\det\) on \(G_n\). Compute its matrix factor and conductor exponent. Determine whether it has a \(K_1(\varpi^c)\)-fixed vector at any level.

Solution. The exact determinant-character calculation of Proposition 1.16 gives \[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)=1,\qquad \epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\pi,\psi) =w_\chi^nq^{nf(1/2-s)},\qquad a_{\rm mat}(\pi)=nf. \tag{2.39c} \] It is also the decreasing head of the length-one characters \(\chi\nu^{(n+1)/2-j}\), \(1\le j\le n\). The exact compact duality with the ascending induction containing \(\chi^{-1}\circ\det\) constructs that quotient; canonical decreasing uniqueness identifies it with this one-dimensional representation. The common centered normalization of \(\chi\) leaves the decreasing real order intact.

For \(c\ge1\), \(K_1(\varpi^c)\) is the subgroup of \(G_n(\mathcal O)\) whose last row is congruent to \((0,\ldots,0,1)\) modulo \(\varpi^c\); at \(c=0\) it is \(G_n(\mathcal O)\). Every \(\operatorname{diag}(u,1,\ldots,1)\), \(u\in\mathcal O^\times\), belongs to every one of these groups. Choose \(u\) with \(\chi(u)\ne1\), possible since \(f>0\). It acts by that scalar on the one-dimensional \(\pi\), so all these fixed spaces are zero. The upper unipotent acts trivially, making \(\pi\) nongeneric. A finite matrix conductor does not give a minimal \(K_1\) level for every nongeneric representation. At rank one, in contrast, the subgroup is \(1+\varpi^c\mathcal O\) for positive \(c\); the scalar character's first fixed level is exactly \(f\) and its fixed dimension is one. This follows directly from the definition of \(f\), without an all-rank newvector theorem.

Exercise 9.58 (same standard factors, different monodromy). Compare the canonical head \(\pi\) of \(S_2(1)\nu^{1/2}\times S_2(1)\nu^{-1/2}\) with the actual generic irreducible \(\sigma=S_3(1)\times1_{G_1}\). Compute their matrix factors and conductors, and compare the supplied WD pairs \[ D=(|\cdot|^{1/2}\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2) \oplus(|\cdot|^{-1/2}\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_2),\qquad E=\mathrm{Sp}_3\oplus\mathrm{Sp}_1. \tag{2.39d} \]

Solution. The two centered length-two blocks of \(\pi\) have cuspidal strings \(\{0,1\}\) and \(\{-1,0\}\). They are linked, so canonical uniqueness and generic unlinked exhaustion show that \(\pi\) is nongeneric. The strings for \(\sigma\) are \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and \(\{0\}\), which are nested and unlinked; Theorem 2.3bf proves actual irreducibility and genericity. Both representations have rank four and \[ L_{\rm mat}(s,\pi)=L_{\rm mat}(s,\sigma) =L_k(s+1,1)L_k(s,1),\qquad \epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\pi,\psi) =\epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\sigma,\psi)=q^{2(1/2-s)}. \tag{2.39e} \] For \(\pi\), the two string exponents are one and their constants are both \(-1\); the real shifts cancel. For \(\sigma\), the length-three block has exponent two and constant \((-1)^2\); the length-one block contributes exponent zero and constant one. This proves every equality above using actual integrals.

Both supplied pairs have the same four Frobenius eigenvalues \(q^{-1},1,1,q\). Their monodromy chain lengths are respectively \((2,2)\) and \((3,1)\). Their kernels have the same two Frobenius eigenvalues \(q^{-1},1\), and both Weil parts are unramified; Theorem 2.3ci therefore gives the same factor in (2.39e) and conductor \(4-2=2\). They are not isomorphic: the square of \(N\) is zero on \(D\) and nonzero on \(E\). No general cuspidal correspondence is used in this explicit comparison. Standard factors, even together with the conductor and the Weil eigenvalue multiset, do not determine monodromy or the genericity of the actual representation.

Exercise 9.59 (nested and repeated contributing endpoints). Let \(\rho=1\) on \(G_1\), and take the two nested segments \([0,2]_\rho\) and \([0,1]_\rho\). Their full induction is an actual generic irreducible of \(G_5\). Compute its reciprocal standard factor, analytic conductor, essential torus restriction, and first fixed-space dimension. Explain why one may not assume its auxiliary spherical derivative is irreducible.

Solution. The segments are nested, hence unlinked. Their terminal characters are \(\nu^2\) and \(\nu\), so \(r=2\),

\[ P_\pi(X)=(1-q^{-2}X)(1-q^{-1}X). \]

In centered notation their data are \(S_3(1)\nu\) and \(S_2(1)\nu^{1/2}\). The actual formula (2.26b–c) gives conductor \((3-1)+(2-1)=3\), independent of those norm shifts. Its epsilon constant in the \(wq^{a(1/2-s)}\) convention is \((-1)^2q^{-2}\cdot(-1)q^{-1/2}=-q^{-5/2}\). Thus \(\epsilon(s,\pi,\psi)=-q^{-1-3s}\).

For \(a=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)\),

\[ W_\pi^e(\operatorname{diag}(a,1)) =W^0_{(q^{-2},q^{-1})}(\operatorname{diag}(a_1,a_2)) |a_1a_2|^{3/2}1_{\mathcal O}(a_2) 1_{\mathcal O^\times}(a_3)1_{\mathcal O^\times}(a_4). \]

At \(a_1=\varpi^{\lambda_1}\), \(a_2=\varpi^{\lambda_2}\), with \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge0\), this is \(q^{-(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)/2} s_{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)}(q^{-2},q^{-1}) q^{-3(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)/2}\), and it is zero off the displayed support. It equals one at the identity. Theorem 2.3dg gives no fixed vector at levels zero, one or two, and a one-dimensional space at level three. The unique spherical derivative quotient is the full induction \(\nu^2\times\nu\); its two parameters are adjacent, so it is reducible by the actual adjacent calculation. Lemmas 2.3cy–2.3cz and Theorem 2.3da use its fixed line's Hecke character and the scalar germ, and require no irreducibility of that whole quotient. Replacing the two segments by two copies of \([0,2]\) would give two equal terminal parameters and count both copies in the derivative line allocation and the conductor sum.

Exercise 9.60 (the reflected polynomial obstruction). In rank three suppose \(\epsilon_{\rm mat}(s,\pi,\psi)=Cq^{-4s}\), \(C\ne0\). Let \(W\) be a hypothetical level-three vector. Derive the contradiction with exact constants. At level four determine every possible normalized universal transform and the dimension. Also compute the reflected essential vector's scalar in (2.40x).

Solution. Here \(m=2\), \(a_\pi=4\). Put \(P=\Xi_W\) and \(Q=\Xi_{R(t_{-3})\widetilde W}\). They are ordinary symmetric polynomials. Equation (2.40aa) is

\[ Q(q^{-1}x_1^{-1},q^{-1}x_2^{-1}) =C^2q^{-3}x_1x_2P(x_1,x_2). \]

All exponents on the left are at most zero; on the right they are at least one in both variables. Coefficient comparison forces \(P=Q=0\), and separation forces \(W=0\). At level four the equation is \(Q(q^{-1}x^{-1})=C^2q^{-4}P(x)\). Both must be constants, so \(P=d\), and the actual vector is \(dW_\pi^e\). The essential vector is nonzero and at this level, hence the dimension is exactly one. Finally (2.40x) gives \(\widetilde{W_\pi^e}=C^2q^{-4}R(t_4)W_{\pi^\vee}^{e,\psi^{-1}}\). The \(q^{-4}\) comes from the two half determinant shifts and cannot be replaced by a unit-modulus assertion about \(C\).

Exercise 9.61 (rank-one and ramified strings). Let \(\chi\) be a rank-one character of conductor \(d>0\), and let \(\pi=S_\ell(\chi)\nu^u\), \(\ell\ge2\), \(u\in\mathbb R\). Find its essential restriction and first compact level, and compare with the unramified character string.

Solution. Every terminal character in this one ramified slot is ramified, so \(r=0\), \(P_\pi=1\), and \(W_\pi^e(\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_{\ell-1},1)) =\prod_j1_{\mathcal O^\times}(a_j)\). The actual analytic formula gives \(a_\pi=\ell d\), with no endpoint correction, and \(\epsilon=w_\chi^\ell q^{\ell d(1/2-s-u)}\). Theorem 2.3dg therefore makes the first fixed level \(\ell d\), of dimension one. With unramified \(\chi\), the same string has \(r=1\), terminal parameter \(b=\chi(\varpi)q^{-u-(\ell-1)/2}\), reciprocal factor \(1-bX\), and conductor \(\ell-1\). Formula (2.40m) becomes \(\chi(a_1)|a_1|^{u+\ell-1}1_{\mathcal O}(a_1) \prod_{j>1}1_{\mathcal O^\times}(a_j)\), since its normalized rank-one spherical function is the terminal character. Its first fixed level is \(\ell-1\), again a line. The rank-one theorem itself has first level \(d\) and one-dimensional character space.

10. What this lesson does not prove

The determinant computation, Landau's lemma, Cauchy's identity and coarse initial convergence are proved above. Assuming the analytic identification and complete pole theorem in Theorems 2.1 and 3.1, the subsequent proofs establish absolute convergence for \(\operatorname{Re}s>1\), the strict local bound, boundary nonvanishing, strong multiplicity one and uniqueness of the cuspidal constituent multiset. These are conditional deductions until those general analytic proofs are supplied.

The degree-one analytic theory has a preceding complete proof in Hecke L-functions and the Dedekind zeta function, Theorems 10.1–10.2. For \(GL_2/\mathbb Q\), the standard-function construction, fixed local test vectors, entireness and twisted functional equation have preceding proofs in Global Whittaker functions and the L-function of a cuspidal representation, §§3–5. These statements have the field and rank scope indicated; they do not supply a proof of the general \(GL_n\times GL_m\) analytic theorem.

The following statements made in this lesson still require the indicated general-rank constructions.

  • For Theorem 1.1, the remaining local input 1.1c consists of standard-conductor and standard-factor identification for general finite-place irreducibles, and explicit archimedean standard-factor identification. Theorem 1.31 proves Gaussian-ideal existence, finite attainment, entire Schwartz division and compatible factor conjugation in every prescribed actual complete smooth moderate dual-pair model. Theorems 1.21–1.22 prove general archimedean full-Schwartz continuation, a common pole majorant with entire quotients and strip bounds, and the scalar Fourier equation in actual smooth dual-pair models; Proposition 1.21b and Corollary 1.22e prove canonical division and constant epsilon under the genuine Gaussian-ideal premise. Corollary 1.22f proves the unitary scalar critical-line phase. These results do not identify the canonical factor. Proposition 1.3 has proved the entire finite-place matrix ideal and its attaining generator in every rank, including ramification; Theorem 1.17 proves the scalar Fourier equation for every finite-place smooth admissible irreducible representation; the Laurent-unit, reflection-sign, character-scaling and compatible-unitary consequences in (1.7j)–(1.7m) therefore apply. Proposition 1.16 does prove the full finite-place theory and exact nonnegative conductor in the matrix/Tate-product normalization for determinant characters in every rank, including ramification. Lemma 1.20a proves compact-mod-center coefficient support from zero proper Jacquet modules. Theorem 1.20 proves strictly positive exponent for every irreducible admissible compact induction from finite-dimensional data on an open compact-mod-center subgroup, including positive-depth data; Corollary 1.20c constructs the depth-zero family and proves exponent n. Lemma 1.20d proves the polynomial degree correction, whose parabolic identities are now proved by Theorem 1.23 and Corollary 1.23c for the full induced matrix family and every irreducible subquotient. Theorem 1.23e proves general cuspidal-support embedding. Theorem 1.23k constructs an actual unordered cuspidal quotient by exact duality; Lemma 1.23l proves the real normalization and compatible unitarity of its blocks. Lemmas 1.23m–1.23n prove cyclic induction and finite semisimple heads. Lemmas 1.23h and 1.23q–1.23s prove the normalized quotient measure, smooth formal degree and exact coefficient idempotents in the fixed scalar central-character category. Corollary 1.23t excludes cuspidal subquotients of proper cuspidal induction; Theorem 1.23v proves full finite length of admissible finite-length induction and Jacquet modules. Lemma 1.23w and Theorem 1.23x prove the intrinsic cuspidal multiset, and Corollary 1.23y gives the full supercuspidality criterion. Lemmas 1.23f–1.23g prove compact inducing realization from the stated finite-subspace or compact-intertwining criteria. Theorem 1.24 proves strict matrix-exponent positivity for every terminal higher-rank cuspidal block by finite spectral charts, full unipotent-fiber cancellation and the exact Fourier-shell extraction. Corollary 1.24c consequently proves the nonnegative matrix exponent for every irreducible, and Corollary 1.24d gives the factor-degree bound and exponent-zero consequence. Universal compact-induction data are unnecessary for these conclusions. Theorem 2.3cr and Corollary 2.3cs now identify the standard matrix factor and its analytic epsilon conductor for every finite-place irreducible from actual cuspidal data. Theorems 2.3da and 2.3dg construct the generic essential vector and identify its minimal compact level with the matrix epsilon exponent, with a one-dimensional first fixed space. Parameter and canonical epsilon root compatibility remain required. Propositions 1.5–1.7 prove polynomial-module closure and the full Gaussian ideal for determinant characters over both real and complex fields, and Theorem 1.18 proves their full-Schwartz continuation, normalized division and Fourier equation with exact real/complex phases. Theorem 1.25 proves the full canonical Gaussian ideal, finite attainment, entire Schwartz division, Fourier equation and exact dual/conjugation formulas for every norm-twisted symmetric power in each rank, its complex antiholomorphic companion and their duals. Theorem 1.26 now proves the exact Gaussian product and whole-Schwartz Fourier package for every full Borel induction. Theorems 1.26a–1.26b construct actual closure, quotient and admissible dual models for every supplied principal-core subquotient, with an exact finite monic polynomial correction, finite attainment, entire division, Fourier reflection and unitary conjugation normalization. Theorems 1.27–1.31 prove nilpotent finite generation, nonzero Jacquet quotient, principal-core occurrence, analytic coefficient comparison, a complete common refinement and the full Gaussian package in every prescribed actual dual-pair realization. Theorems 1.32–1.34 prove existence and full Borel occurrence for every abstract irreducible admissible core. Full onto/closed-image comparison and explicit standard-factor/scalar identification remain required. Theorems 1.11 and 1.13 prove compatible unitary realization and tensor pairings for an actual admissible Hilbert cusp constituent; Proposition 1.14 and Lemma 1.15 give the stated reverse-comparison routes. Theorem 1.19 proves realization and admissibility for every abstract cuspidal subquotient: local elliptic estimates, rapid decay without a prior realization, bounded covering multiplicity, compact cusp energy embedding, finite-dimensional constrained cusp spaces, compact convolution and discrete Hilbert spectrum, constituent admissibility, and the positive-central Jordan filtration are all supplied. Proposition 1.1a proves general adelic reduction, and Proposition 1.2 proves the whole unramified matrix family and its Fourier equation with epsilon factor one. Lemmas 1.1b and 1.1d supply the cusp and matrix estimates; singular-orbit cancellation, Poisson, Mellin continuation, strip bounds, Euler-product recovery and the global functional-equation deduction are proved in §1 from the remaining precise inputs. The free readings are [Goldfeld–Jacquet, §§2–5 and 8–9] and [Getz–Hahn, 22 April 2022 draft, Theorem 6.5.1].
  • Theorem 2.1: the general archimedean Rankin–Selberg local factors and their equation remain required. Theorems 2.3au–2.3cd prove the universal finite-place classification and exact generic-pair factor product: normalized derivatives and nondegenerate highest-derivative pairing, adjacent reducibility and exact kernel directions, whole-string generic surjection and descending Jacquet selection (2.18x), square-integrable segment construction and exhaustion, unique unlinked generic data, coefficient-tempered classification and compatible unitarity, every supplied tied induction, universal decreasing unique head and canonical actual grouped data. Repetitions, ramification, both field characteristics and every rank are included. Lemmas and Theorems 2.3am–2.3at provide the exact coefficient criteria and preliminary construction; Proposition 2.3at now applies through the locally proved selection. Theorems 2.3af–2.3al prove cuspidal self-twist factors, the coefficient-tempered pole bound, all-rank trailing ideal insertion, exact ordered products, quotient transfer and segment-pair factors. Theorems 2.3ac–2.3ae prove finite-place parabolic gamma multiplicativity, the exact polynomial correction and the full spherical generator. Propositions 2.3b–2.3d prove the entire finite-place rational ideal and finite actual test-sum attainment in all ranks and both field characteristics. Corollary 2.3f proves index independence, Proposition 2.3g proves generic pairing uniqueness by orbit depth and global derivative polynomials, Theorem 2.3h proves the scalar functional equation, and Proposition 2.3i and Corollary 2.3j prove Laurent epsilon, reflection and exact character/norm laws. Theorems 2.3l–2.3n prove the complete finite-place rank-one ideal, gamma and epsilon identification with the twisted matrix factors and the stated generic-block multiplicativity. Theorem 2.3ac and Corollary 2.3ad below prove higher-rank finite-place multiplicativity with its exact polynomial correction; Theorem 2.3ae identifies the whole spherical generator. Theorem 2.3cb supplies universal ordered data and actual quotient maps; Theorem 2.3aj and Lemma 2.3ak give their exact factors, and Corollary 2.3cd computes every finite-place generic-pair product. Corollary 2.3ce and Theorems 2.3cf–2.3cg now compute its rank-one standard specialization and all analytic string/pair epsilon exponents; Lemmas and Theorems 2.3ch–2.3cm prove the full supplied Weil–Deligne block and tensor conductor calculations. Corollary 2.3cn retains the precise cuspidal-pair compatibility hypotheses; Corollary 2.3co gives the compatible-unitary conductor-weight constraint. Lemma 2.3cp constructs the actual matrix test transfer, Corollary 2.3cq supplies both canonical endpoint embeddings, and Theorem 2.3cr proves the complete standard matrix-factor product for every irreducible canonical head, including nongeneric heads. Corollaries 2.3cs–2.3ct give their exact analytic epsilon/conductor formulas and necessary unitary weights. Corollary 2.3cu retains both single-cuspidal premises for standard Weil–Deligne factor/conductor comparison. Lemmas 2.3cv–2.3cz and Theorem 2.3da prove the mirabolic restriction, compact lifting, single spherical derivative line, scalar germ and essential-vector construction. Lemmas 2.3db–2.3df prove transform separation, exact reflection and the generated compact subgroup; Theorem 2.3dg proves the generic minimal level equals the analytic conductor and its fixed space is a line. Cuspidal parameter existence and base compatibility and canonical epsilon root compatibility remain required. Theorem 2.0 proves finite-place Whittaker uniqueness for every irreducible smooth admissible representation, every nondegenerate character and every rank/field, including the zero Hom case. Its localization, Bruhat symmetry, contragredient identification and convolution-kernel proof are written in full. Theorem 2.0n proves the all-rank real/complex distributional-principal-series bound and kills every transverse boundary jet; Corollary 2.0o transports it through a specified continuous-dual embedding. Theorems 2.0x–2.0y now construct it for every prescribed actual complete smooth moderate dual-pair model, and Theorem 2.0z proves the general archimedean bound in that class, including nonunitary and nongeneric representations. Lemmas 2.0p–2.0r and Theorem 2.0s prove generic Casimir eigendistribution symmetry in every real and complex rank by finite transverse-order and explicit Bruhat normal-symbol arguments. Lemmas 2.0t–2.0u prove smoothing of Hilbert distribution vectors and the full smooth-space kernel argument. Theorem 2.0v proves uniqueness for every compatible unitary model with irreducible admissible compact-type core and all determinant twists; Theorems 1.19 and 1.11–1.13 supply these hypotheses for every actual archimedean cusp factor. Together with the preceding local existence proof their cusp-model functional spaces are exactly one-dimensional. No opposite-functional existence or onto model comparison is needed for this general uniqueness proof; Theorem 1.34 proves abstract-core existence; full onto comparison remains a separate obligation. Proposition 2.1a proves uniqueness for every unramified irreducible and the normalized spherical formula whenever it is generic. Lemma 2.1b and Proposition 2.1c prove the all-rank spherical integral values, including unequal ranks and repeated parameters; Theorem 2.3ae now uses the full parabolic polynomial correction to prove that this spherical value is the generator of the whole ideal. Global cuspidal genericity and local Whittaker existence under the precise smooth-realization hypothesis have preceding proofs in Automorphic representations and automorphic L-functions, Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.4; Theorem 1.19 supplies that realization and comparison for every abstract cuspidal subquotient. The precise free sources for the remaining local assertions are [Jacquet–Piatetski-Shapiro–Shalika, Rankin–Selberg convolutions, §§2.7, 3–9.4] and [Getz–Hahn, 22 April 2022 draft, §§11.5–11.6]. Lemma 2.2 proves the entire-reciprocal property once the factor shape is established.
  • Theorem 3.1 for arbitrary number fields and arbitrary positive ranks: complete global continuation, the functional equation with conductor and root number, and the exact simple dual-pairing poles after split-central normalization and imaginary twists. The theorem is [Getz–Hahn, 22 April 2022 draft, Theorem 11.7.1]; the local twist identity extends the normalized statement. The unfolding, analytic estimates and pole calculation are not proved here. Boundary nonvanishing is proved in Theorem 4.6, rather than included among these assumptions.
  • Global automorphic isobaric existence in §6, general archimedean local assembly and agreement with the intended local-parameter convention remain required. The finite-place actual ordered-data assembly and its unique quotient are proved in Theorem 2.3cb, with square-integrable segment identification and unique discrete data in Theorems 2.3bj and 2.3cc. The unitary cuspidal norm normalization is Theorem 1.19. Free further-reading locators for the remaining assertions are [Getz–Hahn, 22 April 2022 draft, Theorem 6.5.1, Theorems 10.5.1–10.5.2, equation (10.21), and Theorem 10.6.5]. The proof of multiset uniqueness does not assume that existence is a consequence of the good-place Euler product.
  • Theorem 7.1: the discrete spectrum consists exactly of the unique Speh pairs, with multiplicity one, and \(m>1\) gives the residual part. [Mœglin–Waldspurger, Le spectre résiduel de GL(n), théorème de l'introduction]; [Getz–Hahn, 22 April 2022 draft, Theorem 10.7.1]. The Eisenstein residues and their exhaustiveness are not constructed here.

For the modular-form example, the precise earlier \(GL_2/\mathbb Q\) dictionary is Global Whittaker functions and the L-function of a cuspidal representation, §6. The good-prime twist factors, recurrence, conductor-normalization constant and shift \(u\mapsto k-u\) are computed in §8.
